The vertex-cover closure modulo the occupancy span: occupancy forms are exempted without a cap, the potential bound and the leaves survive, and the onto lemma extends to the occupancy equations

22 September 2026 · Working proofs for plain unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\): potential, leaves, block sums and the onto lemma, modulo the occupancy span. The Delayer step remains open. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The route review found that block column sums over at least \(\theta\) holes are safe under the vertex-cover closure. It found that the column dichotomy then applies to them, with its depth threshold raised by the factor \(\theta\). It proposed measuring danger modulo the occupancy span, and testing whether the potential bound and the leaf property survive, and whether the onto lemma extends to the occupancy equations. The test ends when each of these holds or fails.

Definitions

Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph between pigeons and holes in which every hole has at least two neighbours. The target is plain PHP on \(G\). Forms are over \(\mathbb F_p\) in the cells \(x_{ih}\in\{0,1\}\), and \(O\) is the occupancy equations \(\mathrm{col}_h=1\), \(h\in H\). For a set \(S\) of rows and holes, \(W_S=\langle\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]:h\notin S\rangle\) is the occupancy span after \(S\) is zeroed.

  • Danger modulo \(W\). For a subspace \(U\subseteq\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\), let \(d_W(U)=\dim\bigl((U+W_S)/W_S\bigr)\). Let \(\tau_W(U)\) be the least cover number \(\tau(\operatorname{supp}U')\) over subspaces \(U'\) with \(U'+W_S=U+W_S\) and \(\dim U'=d_W(U)\), the representatives of \(U\). \(U\) is \(\theta\)-dangerous modulo \(W\) when \(d_W(U)\ge1\) and \(\tau_W(U)<\theta\,d_W(U)\), and \(F[\backslash S]\) is safe modulo \(W\) when no subspace is.
  • Greedy closure. While \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\) has a dangerous subspace \(U\), take a representative \(U'\) with \(\tau(\operatorname{supp}U')=\tau_W(U)\), and add a minimum cover of \(\operatorname{supp}U'\) to \(S\).
  • Absorbed cells and pigeons of \(S\). A cell \(ih\) with \(i\) and \(h\) outside \(S\) is absorbed when every other cell of column \(h\) lies in a row of \(S\). Then \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]=x_{ih}\), and \(O\) determines \(x_{ih}\) from the cells of \(S\). A pigeon counts as a pigeon of \(S\) when each of its cells is zeroed by \(S\) or absorbed. This extends the earlier rule for pigeons whose holes all lie in \(S\).
  • Local consistency. Fix a budget \(\beta\). \(\Phi\) is locally consistent when some \(S\) with \(|S|\le\beta\) makes \(\Phi[\backslash S]\) safe modulo \(W\), and \(\Phi\cup O\) has an \(S\)-injective \(0/1\) solution. That is, every hole of \(S\) holds at most one pigeon, and every pigeon of \(S\) lies in at least one hole, in holes no other pigeon of \(S\) uses.

The potential bound

Lemma A\(_W\). Every step of the greedy closure strictly decreases \(|S|+\theta\dim\bigl((\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S)/W_S\bigr)\). So from \(S_0=\varnothing\), \(|S|\le\theta\dim\bigl((\langle F\rangle+W)/W\bigr)\).

Proof. Zeroing the cover \(K\) maps \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S\) onto \(\langle F[\backslash(S\cup K)]\rangle+W_{S\cup K}\), and it maps \(W_S\) onto \(W_{S\cup K}\), since \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]\) goes to \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash(S\cup K)]\), which is zero for \(h\in K\). So it induces a surjection of the quotients by the occupancy spans. The representative \(U'\) lies in \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S\), meets \(W_S\) only in \(0\), and has dimension \(d=d_W(U)\). Its image in the first quotient therefore has dimension \(d\), and it lies in the kernel, since \(K\) covers \(\operatorname{supp}U'\). So the quotient dimension drops by at least \(d\), while \(|S|\) grows by \(\tau_W(U)<\theta d\). \(\square\)

Block sums \(\sum_{h\in B}\mathrm{col}_h\), and every other form of the occupancy span, have \(d_W=0\), so they are exempted, as Byramji and Impagliazzo exempt column sums. The column dichotomy said exemption fails for fixed \(p\). The reason was the safety cap: with pigeon rows as blocks, a safe system has room for at most \(p\) forms beside the occupancy span. Here danger is measured by covers of representatives modulo the span, not by counting forms against rows, so no cap arises. The exempted values are fixed by \(O\), which local consistency imposes, and any other value of a block sum contradicts \(O\). So the column dichotomy's charged horn does not arise, because block sums are not charged, and its exempted horn is no longer blocked by the cap. Whether the probability bound holds for the remaining safe systems is a separate question.

Leaves and the examples

Proposition B\(_W\). Let \(\theta>1\). The empty system is locally consistent with witness \(\varnothing\): since every hole has at least two neighbours, no cell is absorbed and no pigeon counts as a pigeon of \(\varnothing\), and \(O\) has a \(0/1\) solution, one cell per column.

  1. Hole clauses. \(\{x_{ih}=1,\ x_{jh}=1\}\) is not locally consistent. A single cell \(x_{ih}\) is its own representative, supported in column \(h\), so its \(\tau_W\) is at most \(1\). A witness must therefore make it zero or put it into \(W_S\). The only element of \(W_S\) that can equal \(x_{ih}\) is \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]\). So the witness kills the cell by row \(i\), by hole \(h\), or by absorbing \(ih\), which puts every other neighbour of \(h\) into \(S\). The same holds for \(jh\). If \(h\in S\), then \(h\) holds two pigeons. If \(i,j\in S\), they share \(h\). Otherwise exactly one of \(i,j\) is in \(S\), and the other's cell is absorbed. Then two pigeons lie in \(h\), and all neighbours of \(h\) except the one outside \(S\) are in \(S\). By \(O\) the occupancy of \(h\) is then at least \(p+1\), so at least \(p-1\ge1\) further pigeons of \(S\) lie in \(h\), next to the one of \(i,j\) in \(S\). Two pigeons of \(S\) share a hole.
  2. Pigeon clauses. \(\{x_{ih}=0:h\in N(i)\}\) is not locally consistent. A witness kills every cell of \(i\), by row \(i\), by its hole, or by absorbing it. Then \(i\) counts as a pigeon of \(S\) and must lie in a hole.
  3. The examples. \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}\) is its own representative, supported in column \(a\), so it is dangerous unless the witness makes it zero or puts it into \(W_S\). The witness pins \(a\), or takes rows \(1,2,3\), or takes every neighbour of \(a\) outside \(\{1,2,3\}\), possibly with some of \(1,2,3\). In the last case, with the value \(2\), two of the pigeons \(1,2,3\) lie in \(a\). By \(O\) the occupancy of \(a\) is then at least \(p+1\), so at least \(p-1\ge2\) further pigeons lie in \(a\), all of them in \(S\). So the value \(2\) is rejected in every case, as the rejection argument requires. The calibration family, over \(k\le p-2\) holes, is rejected in the same way when \(\theta>p-2\). For \(\theta\le k\) its form can be safe with \(S=\varnothing\), and then a solution with one hole holding \(p+1\) pigeons outside \(S\) accepts the value \(k+1\).

The onto lemma with the occupancy equations

Lemma C\(_W\). Let \(l\) be as in Lemma C for rank \(r\), the rank of \(\Phi\cup O\). Suppose \(\Phi\) is safe modulo \(W\) with \(\theta\ge2l\), and every hole has at least \(2l\) cells. Then every value of \(\Phi\cup O\) attained over \(\mathbb F_p\) is attained by a \(0/1\) assignment.

Proof. Lemma C needs \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge l\dim U\) for every nonzero \(U\subseteq\langle\Phi\cup O\rangle\). The number \(\tau_W(U)\) depends only on \(U+W\). For \(U\subseteq\langle\Phi\rangle+W\), the modular law gives \(U+W=V+W\) with \(V=(U+W)\cap\langle\Phi\rangle\), so safety of \(\Phi\) modulo \(W\) bounds it for every such \(U\). Let \(d_1=\dim(U\cap W)\) and \(d_2=\dim U-d_1\), and let \(U''\subseteq U\) be a complement of \(U\cap W\). A subspace of \(W\) of dimension \(d_1\) contains, for each of at least \(d_1\) holes, an element in which that column has a nonzero coefficient. Its support therefore covers those columns in full, which is at least \(2l\,d_1\) cells. \(U''\) is a representative of \(U\) modulo \(W\). If \(d_2\ge1\), safety gives \(|\operatorname{supp}U''|\ge\tau(\operatorname{supp}U'')\ge\theta d_2\ge2l\,d_2\). Both supports lie in \(\operatorname{supp}U\), so \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge\max(2ld_1,2ld_2)\ge l(d_1+d_2)\). \(\square\)

In the Delayer step the lemma is applied to the free cells, so every hole outside the closure needs \(2l\) free cells. With \(l\) of order \(p\ln r\), the graph needs degree at least of order \(p\log n\). That is necessary, not sufficient: the closure does not by itself keep \(2l\) free cells in every column, since an absorbed hole has one free cell and closure rows erode columns. The free-cell condition is part of what the expander step must provide. A graph restriction of that degree still transfers lower bounds to full PHP.

What remains

  • The Delayer step. Its greedy reduction was refuted by trapped pigeons, and absorbed cells now trap pigeons too. The next obligation is Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons on an expander, and then (MR′).
  • Row sums, an open question. The random walk's hard distribution is functional, and row sums are fixed for the pigeons it maps. Whether the probability bound also needs a quotient by row sums is open. Two cautions apply. First, \(\sum_i\mathrm{row}_i=\sum_h\mathrm{col}_h\), so modulo \(W\) a row sum over a set of pigeons is minus the row sum over the complement, and its danger depends on both. Second, imposing every row equation together with \(O\) is inconsistent over \(\mathbb F_p\) when the numbers of pigeons and holes differ modulo \(p\). A distribution with occupancy one per hole also leaves some pigeons unmapped. Any row quotient would have to impose only some row equations.
  • Span containment, a canonical closure, the probability bound, the restriction step and search hardness, as recorded in the route review.

Assessment

The candidate remedy works where it was tested. The quotient keeps the potential bound and the leaves, and exempts block column sums without the safety cap. It also makes the free part realizable together with the occupancy equations, provided every hole outside the closure keeps at least \(2l\) free cells, which needs degree at least of order \(p\log n\). Row sums under a functional distribution are an open question on the other side. The Delayer step is still the main open item. The closure sub-line is still weak: several design steps remain, and the payoff is limited to bounded depth.

Sheaf check

Quotienting by the occupancy span treats hole occupancy as data fixed by the distribution, as Byramji and Impagliazzo treat their column sums. The difference from the safety cap is that danger is measured by covers of representatives, not by counting forms against rows. So the quotient costs nothing in the bound. Absorbed cells are the local shadow of the quotient: a cell whose column is otherwise pinned is determined by the global section. Its pigeon joins the closure when all of the pigeon's cells are zeroed or absorbed.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): the Delayer step on an expander of degree of order \(p\log n\), modulo the occupancy span. Add to the closure the pigeons whose free neighbourhood becomes too small, and prove Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons into the holes that are not pinned. The test case is a pigeon of degree \(d\) whose other \(d-1\) holes are pinned or absorbed. In parallel, decide which row equations a functional hard distribution would let local consistency impose.

Verification gate. Re-read in full: the vertex-cover closure (Lemmas A and C, the leaves), the route review (block sums) and the column dichotomy (the safety cap). Record searches for danger modulo the occupancy span, absorbed cells and trapped pigeons, and onto lemmas with occupancy found nothing that implies these statements. Before review, I corrected three points in my own draft: which representatives a single cell has, the mixed witnesses in the example, and why safety covers subspaces of \(\langle\Phi\rangle+W\). A fresh-context reviewer checked the entry. Verdict: sound with fixes. It confirmed Lemma A\(_W\), the hole and pigeon leaves under \(O\), the three-cell example and the split in Lemma C\(_W\). The fixes:

  • the calibration family needs \(\theta>p-2\);
  • block sums are exempted, not merely uncharged, and the entry now names why exemption is no longer blocked;
  • the degree remark is a necessary condition, and realizability is conditional on free cells;
  • the row-sum remark was wrong, since row sums over complementary sets are opposite modulo \(W\) and imposing all row equations with \(O\) is inconsistent, so it is now an open question;
  • the unused two-neighbour hypothesis now carries the local consistency of the empty system;
  • four points of wording.

These fixes remove or weaken claims, and the root statement is elementary, so no second pass was run. No computation was run.

A star closure for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\) satisfies the Delayer step on the full board, after the vertex-cover and matching-edge closures fail it

22 September 2026 · Working proofs for plain unary PHP on the full board over \(\mathbb F_p\): one pigeon per hole, and the star closure's one-node Delayer step. Refutations of two other closures. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The closure modulo the occupancy span left the Delayer step open. The proposed next step was Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons on an expander, followed by the value-matching problem (MR′). This entry tests the Delayer step on the full board, where the graph is not in the way. The test ends with the step proved for some closure, or with an obstruction that does not depend on the graph.

Setting

The board is complete: pigeons \([n+1]\), holes \([n]\), cells \(x_{ih}\in\{0,1\}\). The target is plain PHP, with pigeon clauses and hole clauses. Forms are over \(\mathbb F_p\). \(O\) is the occupancy equations \(\mathrm{col}_h=1\), and danger is measured modulo the occupancy span \(W\), by cover numbers of representatives, as in the previous entry. For a rank \(r\ge1\), \(l_r\) denotes the least integer with \((1-1/p)^{l_r-p+2}\,r<1\), as in Lemma C. Throughout, \(\theta>1\) and every closure has at most \(n/2\) lines.

Hall's condition is not the obstruction on the full board

A pigeon is trapped when all its holes are pinned, and a cell is absorbed when every other cell of its column lies in a closure row. On the full board the first needs \(n\) pinned holes and the second \(n\) closure rows, so neither happens while the closure has fewer than \(n\) lines. With at most \(n/2\) lines, every pigeon keeps at least \(n/2\) free holes, and every hole at least \(n/2\) free cells. The expander step is therefore not needed on the full board. The two failures below occur there all the same.

Two closures that fail the Delayer step

Private holes. Under the vertex-cover closure, a pigeon of the witness \(S\) must avoid the holes of the other pigeons of \(S\), but other pigeons may share its hole. Let \(k=\lceil\theta\rceil\), let \(h_1,\ldots,h_k\) be distinct holes, and let \(1,\ldots,k\) and \(j_1,\ldots,j_k\) be \(2k\) distinct pigeons, with \(n\ge2k+p\). Let

\[ \Phi=\{x_{ih_i}=1\ (i\le k),\quad \textstyle\sum_{i\le k}x_{j_ih_i}=1\}. \]
  • Every \(0/1\) solution collides. The second equation makes \(\#\{i:x_{j_ih_i}=1\}\equiv1\pmod p\), so some \(x_{j_ih_i}=1\), and hole \(h_i\) holds \(i\) and \(j_i\).
  • The vertex-cover closure accepts \(\Phi\). Take \(S=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), as rows. Then \(\Phi[\backslash S]=\{\psi\}\) with \(\psi=\sum_ix_{j_ih_i}\). A representative \(\psi+\sum_hc_h\,\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]\) has nonzero coefficients in each column \(h_i\): at \(j_ih_i\) if \(c_{h_i}\ne-1\), and at every other free cell of the column if \(c_{h_i}=-1\). Choosing one such cell per column, greedily with distinct rows, gives a matching of size \(k\). So \(\tau_W(\psi)\ge k\ge\theta\), and \(\Phi[\backslash S]\) is safe. An \(S\)-injective solution puts pigeon \(i\) only in \(h_i\). It puts \(j_1\) and \(p-1\) further pigeons outside \(S\cup\{j_1\}\) into \(h_1\), and one pigeon outside \(S\) into every hole outside \(\{h_1,\ldots,h_k\}\). The condition \(n\ge2k+p\) is more than the example uses; it is there for convenience.
  • The Delayer step fails. This is the rejection argument, made direct. Query the cells \(x_{j_ih_i}\) one at a time. If each query had an answer that keeps local consistency, the system after all \(k\) queries would be locally consistent, and so it would have a \(0/1\) solution together with \(O\). That solution solves \(\Phi\), so some \(x_{j_ih_i}\) is \(1\) in it, and the answer to that query was \(1\). The system would then contain the equations \(x_{ih_i}=1\) and \(x_{j_ih_i}=1\). Span weakening (Proposition B) holds verbatim modulo \(W\) with \(O\) imposed: danger depends only on the subspace and \(W_S\), and an \(S\)-injective solution of the system with \(O\) solves each subsystem with \(O\). So the negated hole clause would be locally consistent, against the leaf property (Proposition B\(_W\)). Hence some query has no locally consistent answer. The system it is asked of has rank at most \(2k\): \(\Phi\) has rank \(k+1\), and the first \(k-1\) answers add at most \(k-1\).

The same example, with the same witness, refutes the version without occupancy equations in the vertex-cover entry. Both refutations hold for every budget \(\beta\ge k\) and every \(\theta>1\) with \(2\lceil\theta\rceil+p\le n\). That includes the range \(\theta\ge2l\) that Lemma C\(_W\) needs, where \(l\) is of order \(p\log n\), so the failure lies where the closure was meant to work.

Row sums. The natural repair makes each closure pigeon own its hole: closing by matching edges, as the standard PHP restriction does. Local consistency then asks for a partial matching \(\rho\) with \(\Phi|_\rho\) safe modulo \(W_\rho\) and \(\Phi|_\rho\cup O_\rho\) solvable in \(0/1\). This fails for plain PHP at rank two. Let \(R\) be a set of \(k=\lceil\theta\rceil\) pigeons, \(n\ge\max(2k,p)\), and \(v\not\equiv k\pmod p\).

  • \(\{\sum_{i\in R}\mathrm{row}_i=v\}\) is locally consistent with \(\rho=\varnothing\). In a representative \(\sum_R\mathrm{row}_i+\sum_hc_h\,\mathrm{col}_h\), column \(h\) is supported on the rows of \(R\) if \(c_h=0\), on the other rows if \(c_h=-1\), and on the whole column otherwise. If at least \(k\) columns have \(c_h=0\), the support contains a \(k\)-matching inside \(R\). Otherwise at least \(n-k+1\ge k\) columns carry the other rows. Either way \(\tau_W\ge k\ge\theta\). A solution puts one pigeon in each hole, with \(R\) occupying \(v'\) holes for some \(v'\in[0,n]\) with \(v'\equiv v\), which exists since \(n\ge p\).
  • No answer to \(\mathrm{row}_{i_1}\), \(i_1\in R\), is locally consistent. Let \(\rho\) be a witness. A matched row restricts to the constant \(1\). So, up to constants, the restricted span contains \(\mathrm{row}_{i_1}|_\rho\) if \(i_1\) is unmatched, and \(\sum_{i\in R'}\mathrm{row}_i|_\rho\), where \(R'\) is the unmatched part of \(R\setminus\{i_1\}\). A nonzero such form lies outside \(W_\rho\), because another free pigeon and a free hole exist. Its cover number is at most \(1\), respectively \(|R'|\le k-1<\theta\), so it is dangerous. Hence \(\rho\) matches all of \(R\), and then \(\sum_R\mathrm{row}_i=k\not\equiv v\).

In plain PHP a pigeon may lie in several holes. The two examples suggest that a closure pigeon should be allowed several holes, and that its holes should hold no other pigeon.

One pigeon per hole

Lemma E. Let \(\Psi\) be affine equations over \(\mathbb F_p\) in the cells of a complete bipartite board, with pigeons \(P'\ne\varnothing\) and holes \(H'\). Let \(W=\langle\mathrm{col}_h:h\in H'\rangle\) and \(O'=\{\mathrm{col}_h=1:h\in H'\}\). Suppose \(\Psi\cup O'\) is consistent over \(\mathbb F_p\) and \(\langle\Psi\rangle\) is \(\theta\)-safe modulo \(W\). Let \(q=\dim\bigl((\langle\Psi\rangle+W)/W\bigr)\), and \(\theta\ge l_q\) if \(q\ge1\). Then for every map \(d:H'\to P'\) there is a \(0/1\) solution of \(\Psi\cup O'\) in which every hole holds exactly one pigeon, and that pigeon is \(d(h)\) for all but at most \(l_q\,q\) holes \(h\).

Proof. Choose \(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_q\in\langle\Psi\rangle\) with \(\langle\Psi\rangle+W=\langle\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_q\rangle\oplus W\), and an \(\mathbb F_p\) solution \(z\) of \(\Psi\cup O'\). Let \(b_k=\psi_k(z)\).

  1. Reduction. A \(0/1\) point \(x\) that satisfies \(O'\) and \(\psi_k(x)=b_k\) for all \(k\) satisfies \(\Psi\). An equation of \(\Psi\) with linear part \(\sum_k\lambda_k\psi_k+\sum_hc_h\,\mathrm{col}_h\) takes the value \(\sum_k\lambda_kb_k+\sum_hc_h\) at \(x\), as at \(z\). If \(q=0\), put pigeon \(d(h)\) in every hole \(h\) and stop.
  2. Switches. For a cell \(t\) let \(c_t=(\psi_1(t),\ldots,\psi_q(t))\in\mathbb F_p^q\). For \(t=(i,h)\) let \(s_t=c_t-c_{(d(h),h)}\). For a set \(T\) of cells with at most one per column, let \(x_T\) put pigeon \(i\) in hole \(h\) if \((i,h)\in T\), and pigeon \(d(h)\) otherwise. Then every hole holds exactly one pigeon, and \(\psi(x_T)=\sum_hc_{(d(h),h)}+\sum_{t\in T}s_t\). So it suffices to find a set \(Z\) of cells, at most one per column, whose switch vectors contain \(l_q\) disjoint bases of \(\mathbb F_p^q\). By Alon, Linial and Meshulam's Proposition 3.1 their subset sums then cover \(\mathbb F_p^q\), and some \(T\subseteq Z\) gives \(\psi_k(x_T)=b_k\) for all \(k\).
  3. Matroid intersection. Let \(M\) be the linear matroid of the vectors \(s_t\) on the set \(E\) of cells, \(M_1\) the union of \(l_q\) copies of \(M\), and \(M_2\) the partition matroid allowing one cell per column. A common independent set of size \(l_qq\) is the required \(Z\), since each of the \(l_q\) parts is independent of size at most \(q\). By Edmonds' intersection theorem and the Nash-Williams rank formula for \(M_1\), it suffices that \[ |A\setminus B|+l_q\,r_M(B)+\mathrm{cols}(E\setminus A)\ \ge\ l_q\,q\qquad(B\subseteq A\subseteq E), \] where \(\mathrm{cols}(X)\) is the number of columns that meet \(X\). Each column meeting \(E\setminus B\) meets \(E\setminus A\) or contains a cell of \(A\setminus B\), so the left side is at least \(l_q\,r_M(B)+\mathrm{cols}(E\setminus B)\).
  4. Safety gives the count. Let \(S=\langle s_t:t\in B\rangle\) and \(U=\{\sum_k\mu_k\psi_k:\mu\perp S\}\), so \(\dim U=q-r_M(B)\) and \(U\cap W=0\). If some form of \(U\) is not constant on column \(h\), then \(\mu\cdot s_{(i,h)}\ne0\) for some \(\mu\perp S\) and some \(i\), so \((i,h)\notin B\). Hence \(\mathrm{cols}(E\setminus B)\) is at least the number \(\mathrm{nc}(U)\) of columns on which \(U\) is not constant. Subtracting from each basis form of \(U\) its constant value times \(\mathrm{col}_h\), on each column where \(U\) is constant, gives a representative supported on the other columns. Those columns cover it, so \(\tau_W(U)\le\mathrm{nc}(U)\). Safety gives \(\tau_W(U)\ge\theta\dim U\) when \(\dim U\ge1\). So \(\mathrm{cols}(E\setminus B)\ge\theta(q-r_M(B))\ge l_q(q-r_M(B))\), which is the required inequality. \(\square\)

Only the column partition is constrained, because in plain PHP a pigeon may lie in several holes. That keeps the problem to two matroids, where Edmonds' theorem applies. (MR′) also constrained rows, which made it a three-matroid problem. Lemma E needs \(\theta\ge l_q\), not the \(2l\) of Lemma C\(_W\), and it needs no count of free cells per hole. The proof never uses that the board is complete. On a bipartite graph in which every hole has a neighbour, the same argument works with \(d(h)\) a neighbour of \(h\), since \(W\), the switch vectors, \(\mathrm{cols}\) and \(\mathrm{nc}\) are all taken column by column.

The star closure

Definition. A star system \(\sigma\) is a set \(P_\sigma\) of closure pigeons, a set \(H_\sigma\) of closure holes and an owner map \(\mathrm{own}:H_\sigma\to P_\sigma\). It is not required to be onto: a closure pigeon may own no hole. Its size \(|\sigma|\) is \(|P_\sigma|+|H_\sigma|\). Its pattern sets every cell in a row of \(P_\sigma\) or a column of \(H_\sigma\): \(x_{ih}=1\) exactly when \(h\in H_\sigma\) and \(\mathrm{own}(h)=i\). So a closure pigeon lies exactly in the holes it owns, and a closure hole holds exactly its owner. \(\Phi|_\sigma\) substitutes the pattern. \(W_\sigma\), \(O_\sigma\) and danger modulo \(W_\sigma\) refer to the free board: pigeons outside \(P_\sigma\) and holes outside \(H_\sigma\). \(\Phi\) is locally consistent, with budget \(\beta\le n/2\), when some \(\sigma\) with \(|\sigma|\le\beta\) makes \(\Phi|_\sigma\) \(\theta\)-safe modulo \(W_\sigma\) and \(\Phi|_\sigma\cup O_\sigma\) has a \(0/1\) solution.

Proposition S. Let \(\theta>1\) and \(\beta\ge1\).

  1. Hole clauses. The system \(\{x_{ih}=1,\ x_{jh}=1\}\) is not locally consistent. If moreover \(\theta\ge l_r\), and \(\Phi\) has rank at most \(r\) and is locally consistent, then \(\Phi\cup O\) has a \(0/1\) solution in which every hole holds exactly one pigeon. In particular \(\Phi\) then implies no collision over \(0/1\) points.
  2. Pigeon clauses. The system \(\{x_{ih}=0:h\in[n]\}\) is locally consistent, with \(i\) a closure pigeon owning nothing. But no system of rank below \(n/(p-1)\) that has a \(0/1\) solution implies it over \(0/1\) points.
  3. Delayer step, one-node form. Let \(\theta\ge l_r\) and let \(\Phi\) have rank at most \(r\). If \(\Phi\) is locally consistent with witness \(\sigma\), and \(f\) is a form, then for some \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_p\) the system \(\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha)\) is locally consistent with a witness \(\sigma^*\) that extends \(\sigma\), provided the bound below is at most \(\beta\). Let \(D\) and \(D^*\) be the dimensions of \(\langle\Phi|_\sigma\rangle\) and \(\langle(\Phi\cup\{f\})|_{\sigma^*}\rangle\) modulo the occupancy spans of their free boards. Then \(|\sigma^*|+3\theta D^*\le|\sigma|+3\theta(D+1)+l_rD\), so \(|\sigma^*|\le|\sigma|+4\theta(D+1)\).

Proof of 1. For the second claim, apply Lemma E to \(\Phi|_\sigma\) on the free board, whose rank modulo \(W_\sigma\) is at most \(r\). Every closure hole holds exactly its owner, so the combined assignment has one pigeon per hole. For the negated hole clause: a free cell \(x_{ih}\) is a form outside \(W_\sigma\), since its column has other free cells, with cover number \(1<\theta\). So both cells lie in closure lines, and the pattern makes \(x_{ih}=x_{jh}=1\) only if \(h\) has two owners.

Proof of 2. The first claim is immediate. For the second, let \(x\) be a \(0/1\) solution of a system of rank \(r'\) with row \(i\) zero, and let \(v_h\in\mathbb F_p^{r'}\) be the coefficients of the cell \(ih\) in a basis of its forms. If \(n\ge r'(p-1)+1\), Olson's theorem gives a nonempty set \(J\) of holes with \(\sum_{h\in J}v_h=0\), and setting the cells \(ih\), \(h\in J\), to \(1\) gives a solution with row \(i\) nonzero.

Proof of 3. By Lemma E applied to \(\Phi|_\sigma\) there is a \(0/1\) solution \(y\) of \(\Phi|_\sigma\cup O_\sigma\) with exactly one pigeon in every free hole. Let \(d\) put at most two holes on each free pigeon; there are more than \(n/2\) free pigeons. Then pigeon \(j\)'s \(y\)-star \(A_j=\{h:y_{jh}=1\}\) has at most \(2+z_j\) holes, where \(z_j\) counts the switched cells of \(Z\) in row \(j\). The stars of distinct pigeons are disjoint, and a pigeon's star holds no other pigeon.

  • Greedy continuation. Start from \(\sigma_0=\sigma\). While \(\langle(\Phi\cup\{f\})|_{\sigma_t}\rangle\) has a dangerous subspace \(U\) modulo \(W_{\sigma_t}\), take a representative \(U'\) of dimension \(d=d_W(U)\) and a minimum cover \(K\) of its support by free rows \(K_R\) and free holes \(K_H\). Let \(J\) be \(K_R\) together with the \(y\)-pigeons of the holes of \(K_H\). Add each \(j\in J\) to the closure pigeons, with owned holes \(A_j\).
  • Well defined. The pigeon of a free hole \(h\) is free at stage \(t\): if it had joined, \(h\) would be in its star and so not free. Likewise every hole of a free pigeon's star is free.
  • The pattern agrees with \(y\). On a new closure row \(j\), \(y\) has ones exactly on \(A_j\). On a new closure column \(h\), \(y\) has exactly one one, at its owner. So the pattern of \(\sigma_t\) agrees with the full assignment, and \(y\) restricted to the free board solves \(\Phi|_{\sigma_t}\cup O_{\sigma_t}\) at every stage. No value has to be matched.
  • Size. The step zeroes the lines of \(K\), so it kills \(U'\). As in Lemma A\(_W\), the dimension of \(\langle(\Phi\cup\{f\})|_{\sigma_t}\rangle\) modulo \(W_{\sigma_t}\) drops by at least \(d\). The step adds at most \(|J|+\sum_{j\in J}|A_j|\le3|K|+\sum_{j\in J}z_j\) lines, with \(|K|<\theta d\). Each pigeon joins once, and \(\sum_jz_j\le|Z|\le l_rD\). So the potential \(|\sigma_t|+3\theta\) times the quotient dimension rises, over the whole continuation, only by the switched holes, at most \(l_rD\) in all. The quotient dimension starts at most \(D+1\), which gives the bound. The second form uses \(l_r\le\theta\).
  • Conclusion. At the end, \((\Phi\cup\{f\})|_{\sigma^*}\) is safe. For every \(\alpha\), \((\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha))|_{\sigma^*}\) has the same span, so it is safe. Let \(\alpha\) be the value of \(f\) at the pattern of \(\sigma\) together with \(y\). Then \(y\), restricted to the free board of \(\sigma^*\), solves \((\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha))|_{\sigma^*}\cup O_{\sigma^*}\). \(\square\)

The path form is easy. Along a single path the Delayer can keep one assignment. Start from the empty system with a near-matching \(y_0\): every hole holds a different pigeon, and one pigeon is empty. Answer every query by its value at \(y_0\), and extend the closure by \(y_0\)-stars as in the proof of part 3. That proof applies at every step with the same \(y_0\), whose stars have at most one hole. So each greedy step adds at most \(2|K|\) lines, and after \(T\) queries the closure has at most \(2\theta T\) lines. Neither Lemma E nor \(\theta\ge l_r\) is needed there, since \(y_0\) itself shows that no collision is implied. The content of part 3 is therefore the one-node form: a small safe star closure for every locally consistent system, including systems reached by answers that are not values at one fixed assignment. A Delayer who chooses among several good answers, as in bottleneck counting, needs that form. There, re-choosing \(y\) at a node can add up to \(l_rD\) switched holes. Along \(T\) such steps the bound can become quadratic in \(T\), unless \(Z\) can be chosen with boundedly many cells per row, a three-matroid condition not proved here.

The examples. The star closure rejects the private-hole system: each cell \(x_{ih_i}\) has cover number \(1\), so every \(h_i\) is owned, by \(i\), and then \(\psi=0\). It accepts the row-sum system, and when asked \(\mathrm{row}_{i_1}\) it answers the size of \(i_1\)'s star modulo \(p\). It rejects \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}=2\) and the calibration family, because a hole has one owner. For \(\theta\ge l_r\), every system of rank at most \(r\) it accepts has a solution with one pigeon per hole, by part 1, so it passes the rejection test automatically.

What this settles and what it does not

  • Settled for the star closure on the full board: the Delayer step in its one-node form. Hall's condition is no issue there, and the value-matching problem (MR′) is bypassed rather than solved: the pattern is read off one global solution, so nothing is left to match or place.
  • Pigeon clauses. Local consistency no longer rejects negated pigeon clauses. A path argument that accumulates the answered equations reaches a pigeon clause only at rank \(n/(p-1)\), so below that rank only hole clauses are leaves. An argument of Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's kind keeps the negated clause instead, and concludes that some line has a negation of large rank. Every refutation of unary PHP contains a pigeon clause, since hole clauses alone are satisfied by the all-zero assignment, and its negation has rank \(n\). So that conclusion is empty here.
  • Weakening. A path argument that keeps the accumulated system never weakens it, so the span-containment item is not needed there.
  • Budget. Along a path with one kept assignment the closure is linear in the number of queries. In the one-node form each step adds at most \(4\theta(D+1)\) lines, and along paths that re-choose \(y\) the total may be quadratic.
  • Open: a canonical closure for bottleneck counting, and the random walk's distribution side: the probability bound for safe systems, simulation and search hardness. The known one-defect distributions are easy (analysis), and whether the modular-collision candidate is hard is open. Row sums under a functional distribution also remain open.

Assessment

For plain unary PHP on the full board over \(\mathbb F_p\), the star closure has the per-step size bound, the hole-clause leaves and the Delayer step in its one-node form. It lacks the pigeon-clause leaf, which only a path below rank \(n/(p-1)\) avoids, and it has no canonical form. Along a single path the Delayer step is easy. So the content is that every locally consistent system has a small safe star closure, which a Delayer with several good answers needs. The key steps were to let closure pigeons own several holes and to read the pattern off one global solution. The distribution side has not moved. The known distributions are easy for linear queries, and the payoff of the sub-line is still a bounded-depth endpoint, not the goal. The sub-line stays weak, but its highest risk has moved from the closure to the distribution.

Sheaf check

Lemma E is a gluing statement. A section chooses one pigeon per hole, and the choices glue across columns whenever safety leaves enough columns on which the forms vary. Edmonds' theorem is then a Hall condition for the column cover. The star closure pins a few rows and columns to the values of one global section. So the pinned part glues to the rest by construction, which is what the earlier closures lacked. The private-hole failure was a section that was local on the closure's rows but not on their holes.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): a route review of the bounded-depth sub-line, now that the star closure has the one-step properties on the full board. The canonical closure, and whether the random walk needs the path form or the one-node form, are still open. It should state what the random walk needs from a distribution, given the star closure. That is a probability bound for safe systems, simulation of linear queries, and search hardness on a support where every hole's occupancy is \(1\) modulo \(p\) outside a known set. The review should check the modular-collision candidate against the column dichotomy and Lemma E, and weigh the bounded-depth payoff against returning to the window.

Verification gate. Re-read in full: the closure modulo the occupancy span (definitions, Lemma A\(_W\), Proposition B\(_W\), Lemma C\(_W\)), the vertex-cover closure (Proposition B, Lemma C) and the rejection argument of the forced-cell test. Before drafting, a fresh subagent checked the three statements against the record. It found none of them. The nearest records are the onto lemma with occupancy, which has a weaker conclusion under stronger hypotheses, and the rejection argument, of which the private-hole failure is an instance. Searches for matroid intersection, one pigeon per hole, private holes, row sums and pigeon-clause rank found nothing more. Edmonds' intersection theorem, the Nash-Williams union formula, Olson's theorem and Alon, Linial and Meshulam's Proposition 3.1 are imported. A fresh-context reviewer checked the draft against excerpts of these dependencies. Verdict: sound with fixes. It confirmed Lemma E, the three parts of Proposition S and both refutations. Its main finding was that along one path the Delayer can keep a single assignment, which makes the path form easy, with a linear budget. The draft's quadratic path bound was wrong as stated, and the entry now says that the content is the one-node form. Further fixes:

  • in the private-hole example: the pigeons outside \(S\) in the solution, the direct rejection argument, span weakening modulo \(W\), the rank bound and the range of \(\theta\);
  • in the row-sum example: \(n\ge p\), and the span and \(W\) steps;
  • "suggests" instead of "must" after the examples;
  • the potential form of the size bound, and safety of \(\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha\);
  • the hypotheses each part of Proposition S uses;
  • the remark that Lemma E holds on any bipartite graph;
  • (MR′) bypassed rather than solved, Hall's condition only on the full board, the remark on Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's argument now argued, and the assessment and next step narrowed.

The two added claims, the path form and the graph remark, are the reviewer's own and were checked here. The other fixes weaken or qualify claims, so no second pass was run. No computation was run.

Route review: after the star closure, the bounded-depth sub-line still meets both obstacles that Byramji and Impagliazzo name for unary PHP

22 September 2026 · Route review of the closure sub-line · Weak; the closure no longer blocks it, but sparse forms and an easy-looking distribution do; next: search hardness of the modular-collision near-bijection. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

The line's general claim. A closure theory for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\), a hard distribution and a random walk with restarts would give size lower bounds for \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutations of bounded depth. That would be the first odd-prime statement admitting arbitrarily many window lines. What the goal needs is more: the thread's goal is unrestricted refutations, and bounded depth is a restriction. Since the last review, danger is measured modulo the occupancy span, and a star closure has the Delayer step in one-node form on the full board. Route item under review: odd-prime-clause-transfer, its closure sub-line.

What the random walk needs

Section 2 of Byramji and Impagliazzo (arXiv 2511.20023v1) was re-read in the source for this review. For bit PHP with \(n+1\) pigeons they use permutation inversion: a uniform permutation of the available strings, where the goal is to find the pigeon holding a special string. The walk needs four ingredients:

  1. Simulation. Each parity query is localized to one bit that is uniform given the rest. They find the bit by pairing the pigeon with a partner whose string differs in one bit, and swapping the two. A query is simulated by revealing about two blocks in expectation.
  2. Search hardness. A tree of depth \(d\) reveals the special pigeon with probability \(O(d/n)\).
  3. A probability bound. A safe system that contains the parities fixed on permutations holds with probability \(2^{-\Omega(r)}\) in its rank \(r\) beyond those. By a closure argument, the bound is applied to the safe dimension \(|\mathrm{Cl}(\Phi)|+\mathrm{rk}(\Phi[\backslash\mathrm{Cl}(\Phi)])\).
  4. A restriction. The safe part is implied by pairs of blocks assigned pairs of strings that differ in one bit, so that fixed blocks never collide.

Their Remark A.4 gives two reasons why unary PHP resists this. Under unary distributions each cell is very likely \(0\), which defeats both simulation and the probability bound. And on near-permutations a parity tree of depth \(O(\log n)\) solves the search.

Falsification attempt: which obstacles does the star closure remove?

  • The closure and the restriction. These are what the recent entries built. The star closure gives the one-node Delayer step. Lemma E gives solutions with one pigeon per hole, which play the role of the permutation-respecting restriction. It is the plain-PHP analogue; the functional analogue is discussed below. Not an obstacle now.
  • Sparse forms and the probability bound: still an obstacle. The column-dichotomy entry recorded that the system \(\{x_{i_th_t}=0:t\le r\}\), over distinct pigeons and suitably chosen holes, holds with probability at least \(1-r/n\) under every distribution on the full board. Choosing the holes greedily also makes them distinct, at a bound of at least \(1-2r/n\) for \(r\le n/2\): the \(t\)-th pigeon has a free hole of probability at most \(1/(n-t+1)\). The cells then form a matching, so the star closure must pin at least \(r\) lines. A bound of the form \(\Pr[\Phi]\le c^{\,\text{closure size}+\text{safe rank}}\) therefore fails on the full board for every distribution. Systems of sparse forms that are each likely \(0\) behave the same way. This is Remark A.4's first reason, and the star closure does not touch it. A likely remedy is to let the witness delete cells that the system sets to \(0\), turning the board into a graph of high minimum degree, and to charge probability only for pinned lines. That is untested. On a sparse board, pigeon clauses become reachable at rank \(\deg/(p-1)\), so the star closure's empty closure pigeons would then need Hall's condition after all. With minimum degree at least \(n/2\) they do not.
  • The distribution: still an obstacle. Three candidates are on record.
    • The one-defect classes are easy (Observation).
    • So is the uniform product distribution, in which each pigeon picks a uniform hole. Its first pigeon's hole is found with \(\lceil\log_pn\rceil\) queries \(\sum_hc_hx_{1h}\), with \(c_h\) the digits of \(h\) in base \(p\). That hole holds another pigeon with probability about \(1-1/e\), and random pigeon subsets with halving, as in the proof of the column dichotomy, find it in \(O(\log n)\) further queries. This is a routine variant of the Observation.
    • The modular-collision near-bijection is untested. Fix a set \(E\) of \(p-1\) holes, and let \(\mu_E\) be uniform over maps from the \(n+1\) pigeons onto the holes outside \(E\) in which one hole \(h^*\) receives \(p+1\) pigeons and every other hole one. It is functional: every row sum is \(1\), and every column sum is \(1\) modulo \(p\) outside \(E\). These equations are consistent, since \(n+1\equiv n-(p-1)\pmod p\). Every form in the span of rows and columns is constant on its support, and so carries no information about \(h^*\). The best known tree samples pigeons, locates each hole and tests it. That needs about \(n/p\) pigeons and \((n/p)\log_pn\) queries. A tree that only reveals pigeons needs about \(n/p\) of them, the birthday bound for the \(p+1\) colliding pigeons. No lower bound for linear queries is known, and none was attempted here.
  • Functional versus plain. \(\mu_E\) is functional, so it would give a lower bound for functional PHP, which implies one for plain PHP. Under a functional distribution the row sums are fixed. The closure should then measure danger modulo rows and columns and impose the row equations. Closure pigeons then own exactly one hole, as in a matching-edge closure. The row-sum failure no longer arises, because \(\{\sum_R\mathrm{row}_i=v\}\) with \(v\not\equiv|R|\) contradicts the imposed rows. But Lemma E would then need a row constraint as well, which makes it a three-matroid problem again. The one-node Delayer step of that version is open. The path form stays easy, with a kept near-bijection, and Byramji and Impagliazzo's swapped pairs of blocks are the analogue to test.

Assessment

  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the closure sub-line: weak. The closure is no longer what blocks it, but both obstacles of Remark A.4 stand for unary PHP. Sparse forms defeat the probability bound on the full board for every distribution. And the only untested candidate distribution has a heuristic case for hardness, no proof. Both need new ingredients: a hardness proof with a simulation that handles sparse queries, and an accounting that deletes likely-zero cells. The payoff is still a bounded-depth endpoint, not the goal.
  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the window: weak, unchanged.
  • same-graph-composition: nothing open.
  • scope-and-review: complete up to external review. The write-up and the binary compiler audit await user decisions.

The highest risk is the distribution. Without a distribution that is hard for linear queries, no accounting helps, and a fast tree for \(\mu_E\) would close the sub-line.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): test the search hardness of \(\mu_E\) for linear decision trees over \(\mathbb F_p\).

  1. Look for a fast tree beyond sampling. Bilinear queries \(\sum_{i,h}a_ib_hx_{ih}\) with random \(a\), \(b\) are the first attack, then queries mixing a few pigeons' rows with column information.
  2. If none is found, attempt a lower bound of order \(n^c\) through a simulation lemma. Each query is localized either to a swap of two pigeons' holes, which changes a dense query with constant probability, or, for a query whose weight sits on few cells, to revealing the pigeon of a heavy cell. The lemma should reveal \(O(1)\) pigeons per query in expectation.

A collision is then revealed only when two of the \(p+1\) colliding pigeons are revealed, which has probability \(O((dp/n)^2)\) for \(d\) revealed pigeons. The target is thus depth \(\Omega(n/p)\) up to logarithmic factors. That is consistent with the sampling tree, the only extremal example known, and it is what a bounded-depth bound would need. The test ends with such a bound, or with a fast tree, which would close the sub-line.

Sheaf check

The walk glues along a path through a measure. The fixed forms of the distribution, here rows and columns, are global sections constant on its support, and the closure must quotient them. Sparse forms are local sections that are almost surely \(0\), so they carry no measure. The closure should delete them, not pin them. The collision is a section visible only to pairs of colliding pigeons. Whether linear readings can glue many pigeons' partial information into that pair is the open question.

Verification gate. No result is registered. Re-read in the source: Byramji and Impagliazzo's Section 2.1, on the walk with restarts, and Section 2.2, on permutation inversion, simulation, the probability bound and the restriction. Re-read in the record: the column-dichotomy entry, including its row systems and consequences; the one-defect Observation; and the star-closure entry. The product-distribution remark and the consistency check for \(\mu_E\) were verified here. Record searches for product distributions, near-bijections and switch simulations found only the Observation and the column dichotomy. No computation was run.

Search on the modular-collision near-bijection: no attack found beats sampling, two simulations for lower bounds are blocked, and a swap simulation needs a dense-graph framework

22 September 2026 · Working proofs of route obstructions and simulation lemmas; no lower bound for the \(\mu_E\) search. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The route review named the distribution as the highest risk of the bounded-depth sub-line. It asked whether linear decision trees over \(\mathbb F_p\) can find the collision of the modular-collision near-bijection \(\mu_E\) faster than sampling, and, if not, for a lower bound through a simulation lemma. The test ends with a fast tree, which would close the sub-line, or with a lower bound, or with the obstruction that stops the proof.

The problem as permutation statistics

Let \(p\ge3\), let \(E\) be a fixed set of \(p-1\) holes, and let \(H'\) be the other \(n'=n-p+1\ge2\) holes. Under \(\mu_E\), a map \(g\) from the \(n+1\) pigeons onto \(H'\) is uniform among those in which one hole \(h^*\) receives a set \(S^*\) of \(p+1\) pigeons and every other hole of \(H'\) one pigeon. The counts agree: \((p+1)+(n'-1)=n+1\). A query with coefficient matrix \(C\) has the value \(Q_C(g)=\sum_iC(i,g(i))\) modulo \(p\). The goal is two pigeons of \(S^*\).

The cells of the columns in \(E\) are \(0\) on the support. A query is constant on the support exactly when its restriction to the pigeons \(\times\,H'\) is additive: \(C(i,h)=a_i+b_h\). Such queries are constant because row sums are \(1\) and column sums are fixed modulo \(p\). Conversely, any two pigeons and any two holes of \(H'\) occur together in some support point, so invariance under swaps forces additivity. So only \(C\) restricted to the pigeons \(\times\,H'\), modulo additive matrices, carries information.

Attacks: none found beats sampling

  • Counts over all pigeons ignore \(h^*\). \(\sum_iF(g(i))=\sum_{h\in H'}F(h)\) modulo \(p\) for every hole function \(F\), because \(h^*\)'s count \(p+1\) is \(1\) modulo \(p\). So for a pigeon set \(A\), the sums over \(A\) and over its complement add up to a known constant. Sums over a subset are informative: that is how the sampling tree learns holes. Integer sums over all pigeons would locate \(h^*\), but they need carries, and carries are not linear.
  • Equality tests are cheap, but they do not help. For two pigeons \(i_1,i_2\) and random \(b\), \(\sum_hb_h(x_{i_1h}-x_{i_2h})=b_{g(i_1)}-b_{g(i_2)}\). It is \(0\) when they share a hole, and otherwise nonzero except with probability \(1/p\). Hashing holes into \(n/p\) buckets, learning bucket labels with \(\log_p(n/p)\) queries per pigeon, and testing equal labels costs about \((n/p)(\log_p(n/p)+O(1))\) queries. That is the sampling tree up to one query per pigeon. Every tree found touches about \(n/p\) pigeons individually, the birthday bound for \(S^*\).

No tree beating this was found. That is evidence, not a proof.

Two simulations that cannot give lower bounds

Observation R.

  1. Communication with players holding cells. Partition the cells among \(k\) players, each knowing its own cells. A deterministic protocol with \(O(k\log n)\) bits finds two pigeons of \(S^*\). Each player sends the integer \(\sum hx_{ih}\) over its cells. The total is \(\sum_ig(i)=\sum_{h\in H'}h+p\,h^*\), which gives \(h^*\). The players then speak in turn, each naming its pigeons in \(h^*\), and stop after two names. A depth-\(d\) linear tree gives a protocol with \(O(kd\log p)\) bits. So no communication bound obtained through this simulation can give more than \(d=O(\log n/\log p)\), for any \(k\). This covers only simulations in which the players hold actual cells. It does not cover lifted simulations, where for instance each cell is split into additive shares over \(\mathbb F_p\). There a depth-\(d\) tree still gives an \(O(d\log p)\)-bit two-party protocol, and integer sums are not available.
  2. Single-swap sensitivity. There are \(K=O(\log n)\) fixed queries that separate every support point from each of its swaps: whenever two pigeons lie in different holes, exchanging their holes changes some query. Take \(C_k(i,h)=w_k(i)\,c_k(h)\) with independent uniform \(w_k\) and \(c_k\). For pigeons \(s,u\) in holes \(h\ne h'\), the change is \((w_k(s)-w_k(u))(c_k(h)-c_k(h'))\). It is nonzero with probability \((1-1/p)^2\ge4/9\), using \(p\ge3\), independently over \(k\). The change depends only on \(s,u,h,h'\), so a union bound over at most \((n+1)^2n^2\) choices gives the claim for \(K>\ln((n+1)^2n^2)/\ln(9/5)\). So arguments that only show that a successful tree must separate the input from single swaps of its output pigeons give at most \(O(\log n)\). This does not cover arguments over longer cycles, several swaps, or adversary methods.

Both simulations lose because they ignore the modular blindness, which is what makes \(\mu_E\) plausibly hard. A proof through either kind of simulation needs arithmetic modulo \(p\) at the level of the players or the swaps.

What a swap simulation needs

Byramji and Impagliazzo localize a parity query to one bit that is uniform and independent of the rest. The unary analogue of their partner trick is to reveal an unordered pair of pigeons together with their unordered pair of holes. Given this, both orders are equally likely.

Lemma L1 (swaps detect non-additive queries). This is the easy direction of the standard four-point test for functions of the form \(a(x)+b(y)\). For \(C\in\mathbb F_p^{P\times H}\), let \(\mathrm{dist}(C)\) be the least fraction of cells where \(C\) differs from an additive matrix. For independent uniform \(i,i'\in P\) and \(h,h'\in H\), the swap difference \(\delta=C(i,h)+C(i',h')-C(i,h')-C(i',h)\) is nonzero with probability at least \(\mathrm{dist}(C)\). The same holds for a uniform bijection between \(m\) pigeons and \(m\) holes, with a uniform pair of distinct pigeons and their holes. Under \(\mu_E\), with \(H=H'\) and \(P\) all pigeons, a uniform pair of distinct pigeons gives \(\delta\ne0\) with probability at least \((1-O(p^2/m^2))\,\mathrm{dist}(C)\).

Proof. Fix \(i'\) and \(h'\). The matrix \(A(i,h)=C(i,h')+C(i',h)-C(i',h')\) is additive, and \(\delta\ne0\) exactly when \(C(i,h)\ne A(i,h)\). So \(\Pr_{i,h}[\delta\ne0]\ge\mathrm{dist}(C)\) for every \(i',h'\), and averaging gives the first claim. Under a bijection, the pigeon pair is uniform among distinct pairs, and the hole pair is independent of it and uniform among distinct pairs. That is the independent law conditioned on \(i\ne i'\) and \(h\ne h'\). Coincidences give \(\delta=0\), so conditioning on no coincidence can only raise the probability. Under \(\mu_E\) the law is invariant under permutations of \(H'\). So, given \(g(i)\ne g(i')\), which has probability \(1-O(p^2/m^2)\), the hole pair is uniform among distinct pairs, and the same argument applies. \(\square\)

Lemma L2 (localization over \(\mathbb F_p\) on many swaps). Let \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_t\) be independent uniform bits, \(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_t\in\mathbb F_p\) nonzero, and \(S=\sum_k\delta_k\beta_k\). Then \(|\Pr[S=v]-1/p|\le\frac{p-1}p\cos(\pi/p)^t\le e^{-\pi^2t/(2p^2)}\) for every \(v\). If every \(\delta_k\) is \(\pm1\), as for queries with coefficients given by a \(0/1\) rectangle, then \(\max_v|\Pr[S=v]-1/p|\ge\frac{\sqrt2}p\cos(\pi/p)^t\).

Proof. For \(\xi\ne0\), \(|\mathbb E\,\omega^{\xi\delta_k\beta_k}|=|\cos(\pi\xi\delta_k/p)|\le\cos(\pi/p)\), since \(\xi\delta_k\not\equiv0\). Fourier inversion gives \(|\Pr[S=v]-1/p|\le\frac1p\sum_{\xi\ne0}\prod_k|\mathbb E\,\omega^{\xi\delta_k\beta_k}|\), and \(\cos x\le e^{-x^2/2}\) on \([0,\pi/2]\). If every \(\delta_k=\pm1\), the transform at \(\xi=\pm1\) has modulus exactly \(\cos(\pi/p)^t\). Parseval then gives \(\sum_v(\Pr[S=v]-1/p)^2\ge\frac2p\cos(\pi/p)^{2t}\), and the maximum is at least the root mean square over the \(p\) values. \(\square\)

One swap bit gives \(S\) two values for every \(p\). Over \(\mathbb F_2\) those cover the field, so conditioning on a query leaves the rest untouched. For odd \(p\) they do not: conditioning on \(Q=v\) through one swap confines the rest of the sum to two values. By Lemma L2, about \(p^2\log(p/\eta)\) swaps with nonzero differences, among disjoint random pairs, suffice for \(\cos(\pi/p)^t\le\eta/p\). Then conditioning on the query's value changes the law of the rest by a factor \(1\pm O(\eta)\). Given the unordered data, disjoint pairs have independent orders, and their contributions add. For rectangle queries, reaching the same precision also needs about \(p^2\log(1/\eta)\) swaps. For other differences fewer can suffice: with \(\delta_k=2^{k-1}\), \(S\) is uniform on \(\{0,\ldots,2^t-1\}\) reduced modulo \(p\), and \(t\approx\log_2(p/\eta)\) is enough.

Where the simulation stops. By Lemma L1, a query with \(\mathrm{dist}(C)\ge\varepsilon\), measured on the unrevealed pigeons against the unrevealed holes of \(H'\), is localized after revealing \(O(p^2L/\varepsilon)\) pigeons, where \(L=\log(p/\eta)\). A query with \(\mathrm{dist}(C)<\varepsilon\) is an additive matrix plus a sparse part with fewer than \(\varepsilon m^2\) cells. It is decided by the pigeons that land on those cells, about \(\varepsilon m\) of them in expectation. With \(\varepsilon\approx p\sqrt{L/m}\), either way a query costs about \(p\sqrt{Lm}\) revealed pigeons. Keeping the number of revealed pigeons times \((p+1)/n\) small would give search hardness up to depth about \(c\sqrt n/(p^2\sqrt L)\). That accounting is first order only. The main gap is the sparse case. Revealing the pigeons that land on the sparse cells also conditions every other pigeon to avoid them. These conditionings accumulate, up to a constant fraction of all cells over the relevant depth, and the law of the rest drifts away from a uniform bijection. Three further steps are needed and not proved:

  1. concentration of the number of nonzero differences among disjoint pairs of one bijection. Lemma L1 gives only the expectation, and revealing pairs one by one loses about \(2r/m\) of the distance after \(r\) pigeons, which is of order \(\varepsilon\) at this balance;
  2. accumulation of the factors \(1\pm O(\eta)\) over \(d\) queries, by a hybrid argument with \(\eta\lesssim1/d^2\);
  3. conceding when a revealed pigeon lies in \(S^*\). The additive part of a sparse query is constant only while \(h^*\) is unrevealed. Pigeons or holes revealed because they lost half their cells fit the same budget.

A proof would work with uniform near-bijections inside a dense bipartite graph \(G\), revealing a pigeon or hole once it loses half its cells. The dense case changes there too. Swaps must be \(4\)-cycles of \(G\), and more queries can be nearly invariant than the additive ones: if \(G\) is close to two blocks, queries additive on each block are almost invariant. So Lemma L1 needs a version for \(G\), relative to the queries constant on the support, together with a lower bound of order \(1/m^2\) on the law of swap quadruples. The same framework, in which likely-zero cells are deleted, is what the route review proposed for the probability bound.

Assessment

The test did not end: no fast tree was found, and no lower bound was proved. It narrowed the proof. Communication simulations in which players hold cells, and single-swap sensitivity arguments, cannot give more than a logarithmic bound. Lifted simulations and adversary arguments remain open routes. Byramji and Impagliazzo's one-bit localization becomes a localization on many swaps; for rectangle queries about \(p^2\log\) of them are necessary. The main missing ingredient is a simulation for uniform near-bijections in dense bipartite graphs under cell deletions. The probability bound needs the same framework. The sub-line stays weak: its payoff is a bounded-depth endpoint, and both of its obstacles need this unproved framework.

Sheaf check

The collision is a global section that every reading modulo \(p\) of all pigeons at once misses: counts glue it away, since \(p+1\equiv1\). Integer readings would glue it back, which is why protocols whose players hold cells find it, while linear trees apparently do not. A swap is a local section of two pigeons that is invisible to additive readings. Lemma L1 measures how much of a reading lives on such local sections.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): the dense-graph simulation. Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph between the unrevealed pigeons and holes in which every vertex keeps at least a fraction \(1/2+\gamma\) of its original degree, with at most about \(c/p\) of all cells deleted. Let \(\nu_G\) be the uniform near-bijection with a \((p+1)\)-hole inside \(G\). The degree slack keeps \(\nu_G\) defined: at exactly one half, two complete blocks meet the condition, and for odd \(p\) the support can be empty.

  1. Prove the marginal bound \(\nu_G(g(i)=h)=O(1/m)\) for every edge, and that the special set stays spread.
  2. Prove the \(4\)-cycle version of Lemma L1 with a lower bound of order \(1/m^2\) on swap quadruples.
  3. Prove steps (a) to (c).

Together they would give search hardness up to depth about \(\sqrt n/p^2\), up to logarithms, far beyond the \(O(\log n)\) of the easy distributions. If the marginals fail, record the graph family that breaks them.

Verification gate. Re-read: the route review, Byramji and Impagliazzo's Section 2.2 (the partner trick and permutation inversion), and the column-dichotomy entry's sampling tree. Record searches for communication protocols, sensitivity, Fourier bounds over \(\mathbb Z_p\) and additivity tests found nothing related. A fresh-context reviewer checked the draft. Verdict: sound with fixes. It confirmed Lemmas L1 and L2 and Observations R.1 and R.2 as proved. Its fixes concern scope and completeness:

  • queries constant on the support are those additive on the pigeons \(\times\,H'\), since the columns of \(E\) are free, and distances are measured there;
  • R.1 holds for every \(k\), and for any partition of cells, but not for lifted simulations;
  • R.2 needs \(p\ge3\) and covers only single swaps;
  • Lemma L1 needs no \(2/m\) loss, and has a \(\mu_E\) version; it is the easy direction of a standard test;
  • Lemma L2 proves sufficiency; necessity holds only for \(\pm1\) differences, with a Parseval bound, and \(\delta_k=2^{k-1}\) shows that fewer swaps can suffice;
  • the simulation accounting lacked steps (a) to (c), and the dense case also changes inside \(G\);
  • the next step needs degree slack, and the assessment's claims were narrowed.

The \(\mu_E\) version of Lemma L1 and the lower bound in Lemma L2 are the reviewer's own additions, and both were checked here. The other fixes weaken or qualify claims, so no second pass was run. No computation was run.
