The modular-collision near-bijection is hard for linear trees over \(\mathbb F_p\): depth about \(n^{1/3}\), by swap localization in dense graphs

22 September 2026 · Working proof: search hardness of \(\mu_E\) for linear decision trees up to depth about \(n^{1/3}\) · odd-prime-clause-transfer. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. The last route review found the distribution to be the highest risk of the bounded-depth sub-line: no distribution was known to be hard for linear queries over \(\mathbb F_p\) on unary PHP. The search test reduced a lower bound for the modular-collision near-bijection \(\mu_E\) to a swap simulation inside dense bipartite graphs, and listed what was missing: marginals of the uniform law in such graphs, a four-cycle version of Lemma L1, and steps (a) to (c). The missing implication is: a linear tree over \(\mathbb F_p\) of small depth finds a collision under \(\mu_E\) only with small probability. The test ends with a proof of that, or with a graph family or a tree that breaks one of the steps.

Outcome. The implication holds up to depth about \(n^{1/3}\) (Theorem S). On the way, the framework proposed in the last next step turned out to be too weak: at degree fraction \(1/2+\gamma\) with \(\gamma\le1/6\), the four-cycle test can fail (Example H). Revealing a vertex once it loses a twentieth of its cells repairs this. A second issue, not listed before, is that combinations of queries must be localized jointly. It costs a factor that brings the depth from about \(\sqrt n\) down to about \(n^{1/3}\).

Setting

Let \(p\ge3\) be prime. \(E\) is a fixed set of \(p-1\) holes and \(H'\) the other \(m=n-p+1\) holes. For a bipartite graph \(G\) between a pigeon set \(A\) and a hole set \(B\) with \(|A|=|B|+p\), let \(\nu_G\) be the uniform law on maps \(g:A\to B\) with \(g(i)\in N_G(i)\) for every \(i\), in which one hole \(h^*\) receives a set \(S^*\) of \(p+1\) pigeons and every other hole exactly one. Holes other than \(h^*\) are regular. Then \(\mu_E=\nu_{G_0}\) for the complete graph \(G_0\) between the \(n+1\) pigeons and \(H'\). Write \(a=|A|\) and \(b=|B|\). We assume that every pigeon misses at most \(\mu\) holes of \(B\), and every hole misses at most \(\mu'\) pigeons of \(A\). Put \(F_1=b-\mu-\mu'-1\), \(F_2=b-\mu-\mu'-p-1\) and \(F_3=b-\mu-\mu'-3\), all assumed positive.

If \(C(i,h)=\alpha_i+\beta_h\) on the edges of \(G\), then \(\sum_iC(i,g(i))=\sum_i\alpha_i+\sum_h\beta_h+p\beta_{h^*}\) is constant modulo \(p\) on the support of \(\nu_G\). This holds for every \(G\), and it is why the modular collision is invisible to additive queries.

Marginals in dense graphs

Lemma M. Under the assumptions above, for every pigeon \(i\), every edge \((i,h)\) and every pigeon \(i'\ne i\):

  1. \(\nu_G(g(i)=h,\ h\text{ regular})\le1/F_1\);
  2. \(\nu_G(g(i)=h=h^*)\le\frac{p+1}{F_1}\nu_G(h^*=h)\), hence \(\nu_G(i\in S^*)\le(p+1)/F_1\) and \(\nu_G(g(i)=h)\le(p+2)/F_1\);
  3. \(\nu_G(i,i'\in S^*)\le p(p+1)/F_1^2\);
  4. \(\nu_G(h^*=h)\le p!\,b^p/((b-1)F_2^p)\) for every hole \(h\);
  5. \(\nu_G(g(i)=h,\ h\text{ regular})\ge\ell(G):=\frac{F_3(1-\theta)}{(b-1)(b-2)}\), where \(\theta=\frac{2p+3}{F_1}+\frac{p!\,b^p}{(b-1)F_2^p}\);
  6. for distinct holes \(h\ne h'\) with \((i,h),(i',h')\in G\), \(\nu_G(g(i)=h,\ g(i')=h',\ h,h'\text{ regular})\ge\ell(G)\,\ell(G-i-h)\).

Proof. All parts are switchings. In each, a map \(g\) together with a choice is sent to a map \(g'\) together with reverse data from which \(g\) and the choice are recovered. So the number of pairs \((g,\text{choice})\) is at most the number of pairs \((g',\text{reverse data})\).

(1), (2). Let \(g(i)=h\). Choose a pigeon \(i'\) with \(g(i')\in N(i)\setminus\{h\}\) and \(i'\in N(h)\), and exchange the holes of \(i\) and \(i'\). Hole counts and the special hole are unchanged, and both new cells are edges. Every hole has at least one pigeon, so at least \(b-\mu-1\) pigeons sit on holes of \(N(i)\setminus\{h\}\). At most \(\mu'\) of them miss \(h\), which leaves at least \(F_1\) choices. Given \(g'\), the pigeon \(i'\) is one of the pigeons of \(g'\) in \(h\): there is one if \(h\) is regular and \(p+1\) if \(h=h^*\). Hence \(F_1\,\nu(g(i)=h,\,h\text{ regular})\le\nu(g(i)\ne h,\,h\text{ regular})\le1\), and \(F_1\,\nu(g(i)=h=h^*)\le(p+1)\,\nu(g(i)\ne h=h^*)\). Summing the second bound over \(h\) gives \(\nu(i\in S^*)\le(p+1)/F_1\), and adding the two bounds gives \(\nu(g(i)=h)\le(p+2)/F_1\).

(3). Let \(g(i)=g(i')=h=h^*\). Exchange \(i'\) with a pigeon \(i''\) on a hole of \(N(i')\setminus\{h\}\) with \(i''\in N(h)\). There are at least \(F_1\) choices, and the result keeps \(g'(i)=h=h^*\) and has \(g'(i')\ne h\). The reverse data is \(i''\in g'^{-1}(h)\setminus\{i\}\), with \(p\) choices. So \(\nu(g(i)=g(i')=h=h^*)\le\frac p{F_1}\nu(g(i)=h=h^*)\). Summing over \(h\) and using (2) gives (3).

(4). Let \(h^*=h\). Choose a hole \(h''\ne h\) (\(b-1\) ways) and a pigeon \(s_0\in S^*\) (\(p+1\) ways). List \(S^*\setminus\{s_0\}\) as \(s_1,\ldots,s_p\) in a fixed order. Then choose distinct pigeons \(t_1,\ldots,t_p\) in turn, with \(t_k\in N(h'')\) and \(g(t_k)\in N(s_k)\setminus\{h,h''\}\). The holes of \(N(s_k)\setminus\{h,h''\}\) are regular and carry at least \(b-\mu-2\) pigeons. Removing those that miss \(h''\) and the earlier \(t\)'s leaves at least \(F_2\) choices for each \(k\). Set \(g'(s_k)=g(t_k)\) and \(g'(t_k)=h''\) for \(k\le p\). Then \(h\) keeps only \(s_0\), \(h''\) has \(p+1\) pigeons, and every hole \(g(t_k)\) still has one. So \(g'\) lies in the support, with special hole \(h''\). The reverse data is an ordered \(p\)-tuple \((t_k)\) from \(g'^{-1}(h'')\), at most \((p+1)!\) choices, and the holes \(g(t_k)=g'(s_k)\), at most \(b^p\) choices, since \(s_k=g'^{-1}(g(t_k))\). Hence \(\nu(h^*=h)(b-1)(p+1)F_2^p\le(p+1)!\,b^p\).

(5). Let \(\Omega_0\) be the set of maps with \(g(i)=x\ne h\) and both \(x\) and \(h\) regular. Let \(j=g^{-1}(h)\). Choose a regular hole \(y\in N(j)\setminus\{x,h\}\) whose pigeon \(k=g^{-1}(y)\) lies in \(N(x)\): there are at least \(F_3\) choices. Set \(g'(i)=h\), \(g'(j)=y\) and \(g'(k)=x\). Counts and the special hole are unchanged, and \(g'(i)=h\) with \(h\) regular. The reverse data is \((x,y)\), with at most \((b-1)(b-2)\) choices, since \(k=g'^{-1}(x)\) and \(j=g'^{-1}(y)\). So \(\nu(g(i)=h,\,h\text{ regular})\ge F_3\,\nu(\Omega_0)/((b-1)(b-2))\). By (1), (2) and (4), \(\nu(\Omega_0)\ge1-\frac{p+2}{F_1}-\frac{p+1}{F_1}-\nu(h^*=h)\ge1-\theta\).

(6). Given \(g(i)=h\) with \(h\) regular, the rest of \(g\) is distributed as \(\nu_{G-i-h}\), and \(G-i-h\) satisfies the same missing bounds. Apply (5) twice. \(\square\)

So the edge marginals are \(\Theta(1/b)\), each pigeon is special with probability \(O(p/b)\), and the special hole has marginal \(O_p(1/b)\). The constant \(p!\) in (4) is crude, but the proof below uses it only for fixed \(p\).

The four-cycle test in dense graphs

For \(C:E(G)\to\mathbb F_p\), let \(\mathrm{dist}_G(C)\) be the least fraction of edges of \(G\) on which \(C\) differs from a function \(\alpha_i+\beta_h\). Let \(\mathcal Q\) be the set of \((i,i',h,h')\) with \(i\ne i'\), \(h\ne h'\) and all four cells in \(G\). Let \(\rho_G(C)\) be the fraction of \(\mathcal Q\) on which \(\delta=C(i,h)+C(i',h')-C(i,h')-C(i',h)\ne0\).

Lemma T. Let \(G\) be any bipartite graph between \(A\) and \(B\) with the missing bounds \(\mu\) and \(\mu'\); the relation \(|A|=|B|+p\) is not used. If \(3\mu<b\), then \(\mathrm{dist}_G(C)\le K\rho_G(C)\) with

\[K=\frac{b(a-1)}{(a-\mu')(b-\mu)}\Bigl(1+\frac{3b}{b-3\mu}\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac b{b-2\mu}\Bigr)^2 .\]

Proof. For pigeons \(i\ne i'\) let \(N_{ii'}=N(i)\cap N(i')\). It has \(n_{ii'}\ge b-2\mu\) elements. Let \(D_{ii'}(h)=C(i,h)-C(i',h)\) on \(N_{ii'}\), and let \(c_{ii'}\) be a most frequent value of \(D_{ii'}\), chosen with \(c_{i'i}=-c_{ii'}\). Let \(\mathrm{err}(i,i')\) be the fraction of \(N_{ii'}\) where \(D_{ii'}\ne c_{ii'}\). If \(q_v\) are the frequencies of \(D_{ii'}\), the ordered pairs \(h\ne h'\) of \(N_{ii'}\) with \(D_{ii'}(h)\ne D_{ii'}(h')\) number \(n_{ii'}^2(1-\sum_vq_v^2)\ge n_{ii'}^2\,\mathrm{err}(i,i')\). Since \(|\mathcal Q|\le a(a-1)b^2\), the mean \(\bar e\) of \(\mathrm{err}\) over ordered pairs of distinct pigeons satisfies \(\bar e\le(b/(b-2\mu))^2\rho_G(C)\).

Fix \(i_0\) with \(\frac1{a-1}\sum_{i\ne i_0}\mathrm{err}(i,i_0)\le\bar e\). Set \(\alpha_{i_0}=0\) and \(\alpha_i=c_{i,i_0}\), and let \(\beta_h\) be a most frequent value of \(f_h(i)=C(i,h)-\alpha_i\) over \(i\in N(h)\). At a hole \(h\), the number of \(i\in N(h)\) with \(f_h(i)\ne\beta_h\) is at most \(\frac1{|N(h)|}\) times the number of ordered pairs \(i\ne\tilde\imath\) in \(N(h)\) with \(f_h(i)\ne f_h(\tilde\imath)\), by the same frequency inequality. For such a pair, \(h\in N_{i\tilde\imath}\) and \(D_{i\tilde\imath}(h)\ne\alpha_i-\alpha_{\tilde\imath}\). Call the pair coherent if \(c_{i\tilde\imath}=\alpha_i-\alpha_{\tilde\imath}\). A coherent pair contributes at most \(b\,\mathrm{err}(i,\tilde\imath)\) holes, and any pair at most \(b\). Summing over \(h\) and using \(|N(h)|\ge a-\mu'\):

\[\#\{(i,h)\in G:C(i,h)\ne\alpha_i+\beta_h\}\le\frac{b\,a(a-1)}{a-\mu'}\bigl(\bar e+P\bigr),\]

where \(P\) is the fraction of ordered pairs that are not coherent. Pairs containing \(i_0\) are coherent by construction. For \(i,\tilde\imath,i_0\) distinct, the set \(N(i)\cap N(\tilde\imath)\cap N(i_0)\) has at least \(b-3\mu>0\) elements, and on it \(D_{i\tilde\imath}=D_{ii_0}-D_{\tilde\imath i_0}\). If some hole there has all three differences equal to their chosen values, the pair is coherent. The holes where this fails number at most \(b(\mathrm{err}(i,i_0)+\mathrm{err}(\tilde\imath,i_0)+\mathrm{err}(i,\tilde\imath))\). So an incoherent pair has this sum at least \((b-3\mu)/b\). By Markov's inequality and the choice of \(i_0\), \(P\le3\bar e\,b/(b-3\mu)\). Dividing by \(|G|\ge a(b-\mu)\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

With \(\mu\le b/15\) and \(\mu'\le a/15\), \(K\le7.3\). If \(\rho_G(C)=0\), then \(C\) is additive on \(G\). So below the threshold \(\mu<b/3\), queries invariant under all swaps along four-cycles are exactly the additive ones. A finite check confirms this exact version on 72 random graphs, for \(p=3,5\) and sizes up to \(9\times9\). Its generator also caps the missing cells of holes, which the lemma does not need, and it does not test the constant \(K\).

Example H (the threshold is needed). Split \(A=A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3\) and \(B=B_1\cup B_2\cup B_3\), and let \((i,h)\) be an edge exactly when \(i\in A_k\), \(h\in B_l\) and \(k\ne l\). Every vertex is adjacent to about two thirds of the other side. Let \(C=1\) on \(A_1\times B_2\) and \(0\) elsewhere. A four-cycle uses at most two pigeon classes and two hole classes. Two distinct pigeon classes and two distinct hole classes cannot all be pairwise different in \(\{1,2,3\}\). So one of them repeats, and then \(\delta=0\). Around the six classes, \(C\) has alternating sum \(1\), so it is not additive. Its query \(\#\{i\in A_1:g(i)\in B_2\}\bmod p\) is a flow value on the six classes, with one free parameter. A computation over the full support of \(\nu_G\) finds it taking every value modulo \(3\), for \(p=3\), \(|B_l|=2,2,2\) and \(|A_k|=3,3,3\). It does the same for \(|A_k|=5,2,2\), an extra instance whose holes in \(B_1\) have degree fraction \(4/9\). A rotation along a six-cycle does change \(C\), but no simulation by four-cycle swaps can localize this query. The example sits exactly at \(3\mu=b\), degree fraction \(2/3\). So it defeats the hypothesis of the last next step, degree fraction \(1/2+\gamma\), for \(\gamma\le1/6\). The simulation below therefore reveals any vertex that misses more than \(m/20\) cells.

Lemma L1G (swaps under \(\nu_G\)). Let \(i\ne i'\) be a uniform pair of distinct pigeons and \(g\sim\nu_G\). The event Good is that \(g(i)\) and \(g(i')\) are distinct regular holes, that \((i,g(i'))\) and \((i',g(i))\) are edges, and that \(\delta\ne0\). It has probability at least \(\rho_G(C)(b-2\mu)(b-2\mu-1)\,\ell(G)\,\ell_1\), where \(\ell_1\) is the least \(\ell(G-i-h)\) over edges \((i,h)\). Proof. Sum Lemma M(6) over the elements of \(\mathcal Q\) with \(\delta\ne0\). There are \(\rho_G(C)|\mathcal Q|\) of them, and \(|\mathcal Q|\ge a(a-1)(b-2\mu)(b-2\mu-1)\). \(\square\)

Let \(\mu,\mu'\le b/15\), so also \(\mu'\le a/15\) inside Lemma T, and let \(b\) be large in terms of \(p\). Then \((b-2\mu)(b-2\mu-1)\,\ell(G)\,\ell_1\) tends to \((13/15)^4(1-\theta)^2\approx0.564(1-\theta)^2\). With \(\theta\le0.07\) and \(K\le7.3\), this gives \(\Pr[\text{Good}]\ge\mathrm{dist}_G(C)/K_0\) with \(K_0\approx12.9\le15\). On the complete board, this is Lemma L1 of the search test up to the constant. Given the unordered pair of holes \(\{g(i),g(i')\}\) and the rest of \(g\), both orientations are equally likely when the four-cycle is present, since both lie in the support. The orientation is then a uniform bit.

Systems of swap bits

Lemma F. Let \(M\in\mathbb F_p^{k\times T}\), let \(\beta\in\{0,1\}^T\) be uniform and independent of a further variable \(X\), and let \(W\le\mathbb F_p^k\) be a subspace. Suppose \(u=u(X)\in\mathbb F_p^k\), with \(\xi\cdot u(X)\) constant in \(X\) for every \(\xi\in W\). Suppose also that \(\xi^{\mathsf T}M\) has at least \(t_0\) nonzero entries for every \(\xi\notin W\). Then \(\Pr_\beta[M\beta=u(X)]=Z+\mathcal E(X)\), where \(Z\ge0\) does not depend on \(X\) and \(|\mathcal E(X)|\le\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\le e^{-\pi^2t_0/(2p^2)}\).

Proof. Fourier inversion gives \(\Pr[M\beta=u]=p^{-k}\sum_\xi\omega^{-\xi\cdot u}\prod_c\frac{1+\omega^{(\xi^{\mathsf T}M)_c}}2\). The terms with \(\xi\notin W\) have modulus at most \(p^{-k}\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\) each, as in Lemma L2. The terms with \(\xi\in W\) sum to \(Z=p^{-k}|W|\Pr_\beta[M\beta-u\in W^\perp]\ge0\), which depends on \(u\) only through the values \(\xi\cdot u\) with \(\xi\in W\). \(\square\)

Search hardness

Theorem S. For every odd prime \(p\) there are \(C_p\) and \(n_p\) such that the following holds for \(n\ge n_p\). Every linear decision tree over \(\mathbb F_p\) of depth \(d\ge1\) on the variables \(x_{ih}\) that outputs two distinct pigeons outputs two pigeons of one hole under \(\mu_E\) with probability at most \(C_p\,d\sqrt{(d+\ln n)/n}\). Its queries may be arbitrary affine forms. So success probability \(1/2\) needs depth \(\Omega_p(n^{1/3})\).

Parameters. We may assume that the bound is below \(1\). Let \(\kappa=1/n\) and \(\mu=\lfloor m/20\rfloor\). Let \(t_0=\lceil\frac{p^2}2(d\ln p+\ln(16m/\kappa))\rceil\). Since \(p^2/2\ge\max(2p^2/\pi^2,4)\), this gives \(\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\le\kappa/(16mp^d)\) and \(e^{-t_0/4}\le\kappa/(16mp^d)\). Let \(\varepsilon=\sqrt{200K_0t_0/m}\), \(q=\varepsilon/(2K_0)\) and \(T=\lceil2t_0/q\rceil\le\varepsilon m/40\).

The simulation. It runs along a path of the tree from the root, using \(g\sim\mu_E\) and its own randomness. All paths share one random tape, so the simulation along a node's path extends the simulation along each prefix. It is therefore defined along the path the tree actually takes, and failure and success below refer to that run. Along a fixed path the queries \(C_1,\ldots,C_d\) are fixed. The simulation stops with failure at the first of the events below. Its state before query \(k\) consists of:

  • the graph \(G_k\) of unrevealed pigeons \(A_k\) and holes \(B_k\), with deleted cells, in which every vertex misses at most \(\mu\) cells and \(|B_k|\ge3m/4\);
  • fully revealed pigeons with their holes, all regular;
  • a list of pairs: two pigeons \(\{i,i'\}\) and their unordered holes \(\{h,h'\}\), both regular, with the four-cycle present in the graph at the time and the orientation not revealed;
  • a subspace \(W_{k-1}\le\mathbb F_p^{k-1}\);
  • the matrix \(M\) whose entry for query \(j\) and a pair is the swap difference \(\delta_j\) of \(C_j\) on that pair.

For \(\xi\in\mathbb F_p^{k}\) write \(C_\xi=\sum_j\xi_jC_j\). The invariants are:

  1. given the revealed data \(U_{<k}\) and no failure, the unrevealed part \(X_k\) of \(g\) has law \(\nu_{G_k}\), and the orientations are independent uniform bits independent of \(X_k\);
  2. \(C_\xi\) is additive on \(G_k\) for every \(\xi\in W_{k-1}\);
  3. \(\xi^{\mathsf T}M\) has at least \(t_0\) nonzero entries for every \(\xi\in\mathbb F_p^{k-1}\setminus W_{k-1}\).

Initially \(G_1=G_0\) and \(W_0=0\). Step \(k\):

  1. Close combinations. While some \(\xi\notin W\) with \(\xi_k\ne0\) has \(\mathrm{dist}_G(C_\xi)<\varepsilon\), run a round. Take a nearest additive function and the set \(T_\xi\) of edges where \(C_\xi\) differs from it, so \(|T_\xi|<\varepsilon|G|\). First reveal, one at a time, every vertex that would miss more than \(\mu\) cells once \(T_\xi\) is deleted: a pigeon with its hole, or a hole with its pigeon. Fail if a revealed hole is \(h^*\). Then reveal every remaining pigeon \(i\) with \((i,g(i))\in T_\xi\), together with its hole, and fail if such a hole is \(h^*\). Delete \(T_\xi\) and the revealed vertices, and add \(\xi\) to \(W\). Each round raises \(\dim W\), so there are at most \(d\) rounds on the whole path. Every revelation happens in a graph that still satisfies the missing bound, because cells are deleted only after the vertices that would exceed it are gone.
  2. Pairs. Draw \(T\) times a uniform pair of distinct unrevealed pigeons, and reveal their unordered holes. Fail if the holes coincide or one is \(h^*\). If the four-cycle is absent, only one orientation is possible, and the pair is revealed in full. Otherwise it joins the list. Remove its vertices either way. Fail if some \(\xi\notin W\) with \(\xi_k\ne0\) has fewer than \(t_0\) nonzero entries in the new columns of \(\xi^{\mathsf T}M\).

Throughout, the simulation fails as soon as more than \(m/4\) pigeons have been removed from the graph, counting the pigeons of pairs. Every removal takes a pigeon and a hole, so the cap keeps \(|B_k|\ge3m/4\).

At a leaf, the tree succeeds without failure if both output pigeons lie in one hole and no failure occurred.

The invariants hold.

  • (A): every revealing step conditions on events of the unrevealed part. Given its outcome and regular revealed holes, the rest is uniform on the completions in the smaller graph. Orientations are fixed when their pair is drawn and never enter a later event.
  • (B): after a round, \(C_\xi\) equals its nearest additive function on the remaining edges. \(W\) is spanned by \(W_{k-1}\) and such \(\xi\), additivity is closed under linear combinations, and it passes to subgraphs.
  • (C): \(W_{k-1}\times\{0\}\subseteq W_k\), so a combination \((\xi',0)\notin W_k\) has \(\xi'\notin W_{k-1}\) and keeps its earlier columns. \(W_k\) may also gain vectors with \(\xi_k=0\), which is harmless. Combinations with \(\xi_k\ne0\) outside \(W_k\) are handled by the check in step 2.
  • Degrees: a deleted cell adds \(1\) to the missing count of one pigeon and one hole, and removing vertices never increases a count. So the invariant on missing cells holds.

Failure probabilities in the prior. We bound each failure given the state just before it, using Lemma M with \(\mu,\mu'\le b/15\) and \(b\ge3m/4\).

  • Phase 1 of a round, the revelations of vertices that would exceed the missing bound. Each happens in a graph that meets the bound, and fails with probability at most \(c_2(p+p!(1.2)^p)/m\) by Lemma M(2) and (4). All rounds together delete at most \(d\varepsilon ab\) cells. A vertex revealed in phase 1 would have more than \(\mu\) missing cells, and each deleted cell is missing for one pigeon and one hole. So there are at most \(2d\varepsilon ab/\mu\le45d\varepsilon m\) such revelations, each removing one pigeon.
  • Phase 2 of a round, the revelation of the pigeons on \(T_\xi\), restricted to the graph after phase 1, which meets the missing bound. It fails with probability at most \(\sum_{(i,h)\in T_\xi}\nu(g(i)=h=h^*)\le\frac{p+1}{F_1}|T_\xi|\max_h\nu(h^*=h)\le\iota:=c_1(p+1)p!\,(1.2)^p\varepsilon\). It reveals \(\sum_{(i,h)\in T_\xi}\nu(g(i)=h)\le|T_\xi|/F_1+\iota\le\varepsilon ab/F_1+\iota\le2\varepsilon a\) pigeons in expectation, by Lemma M(1) and (2).
  • A pair draw fails with probability at most \(2(p+1)/F_1\), since each of its pigeons lies in \(S^*\) with probability at most \((p+1)/F_1\).
  • The check of step 2, bounded given the state at the start of step 2. Every \(\xi\) concerned then has \(\mathrm{dist}\ge\varepsilon\). It keeps \(\mathrm{dist}\ge\varepsilon/2\) during the draws. Indeed, an additive function on a subgraph \(G'\) extends to \(G\), so \(\mathrm{dist}_{G'}\ge\mathrm{dist}_G-\Delta/|G'|\), where \(\Delta\le2T(a+b)\le4Ta\) counts the edges removed. Here \(4T\le\varepsilon m/10\) and \(|G'|\ge0.9a\cdot0.7m\), so the loss is below \(\varepsilon/6\). By Lemmas T and L1G, each draw is Good for \(\xi\) with probability at least \(q\), given the past. Draws after a failure are counted as Good. The number of Good draws then dominates a binomial \(\mathrm{Bin}(T,q)\), with \(Tq\ge2t_0\), and falls below \(t_0\) with probability at most \(e^{-t_0/4}\). A union bound over at most \(p^k\) combinations gives at most \(\kappa/(16m)\).
  • At a leaf without failure, two pigeons in one hole must both lie in \(S^*\). A revealed pigeon in \(S^*\) would have caused failure. So both are unrevealed, and by Lemma M(3) this has probability at most \(p(p+1)/F_1^2\).
  • Removed pigeons. In the prior, their expected number is at most \(2d\varepsilon a\) in phase 2, \(45d\varepsilon m\) in phase 1 and \(2dT\) in pairs, at most \(51d\varepsilon m\) in all. The cap is handled after the transfer.

From the prior to the tree. Let \(u\) be a node at depth \(k-1\) with answers \(v_u\). Along the path of \(u\), the tree reaches \(u\) exactly when \(M\beta=v_u-K(X_k)\). Here \(K\) collects the contributions of revealed pigeons, of the reference orientations of pairs, and of \(X_k\). For \(\xi\in W_{k-1}\), \(\xi\cdot K(X_k)\) is constant on the support of \(\nu_{G_k}\), by (B) and the additivity remark. By (A), \(\beta\) is independent of \(X_k\) and of the randomness of step \(k\), given \(U_{<k}\). So Lemma F applies with (C). For every event \(\mathcal D\) determined by \(U_{<k}\), \(X_k\) and the randomness of step \(k\), and contained in "no failure before step \(k\)",

\[\Pr[\text{reach }u,\ \mathcal D]=\mathbb E\bigl[1_{\mathcal D}(Z+\mathcal E(X_k))\bigr],\qquad |\mathcal E|\le\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0},\]

where \(Z\ge0\) is a function of \(U_{<k}\).

Take a sub-step \(s\), indexed globally along the run: the \(j\)-th phase-1 revelation, phase 2 of the \(j\)-th round, the \(j\)-th pair draw, the \(j\)-th check, or the leaf. At a node \(u\) at depth \(k-1\), let \(\mathcal D_u\) be "\(s\) occurs in step \(k\) without earlier failure", determined by the state at the start of \(s\), and \(\mathcal E_u\subseteq\mathcal D_u\) "\(s\) fails". For the check, the state is taken at the start of step 2. Suppose \(\Pr[\mathcal E_u\mid\text{state}]\le\beta_s\) in the prior, for a number \(\beta_s\). Since \(Z\) is known at the start of \(s\),

\[\mathbb E[1_{\mathcal E_u}Z]=\mathbb E\bigl[Z\,1_{\mathcal D_u}\Pr(\mathcal E_u\mid\text{state})\bigr]\le\beta_s\,\mathbb E[1_{\mathcal D_u}Z]\le\beta_s\bigl(\Pr[\text{reach }u,\ \mathcal D_u]+\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\bigr),\]

and so \(\Pr[\text{reach }u,\ \mathcal E_u]\le\beta_s(\Pr[\text{reach }u,\ \mathcal D_u]+\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0})+\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\). The simulations share one tape, and along the run \(s\) occurs at most once. So the events "reach \(u\) and \(\mathcal D_u\)" are disjoint over the nodes \(u\), of which there are at most \(2p^d\). Summing over \(u\), the sub-step \(s\) fails along the run with probability at most \(\beta_s+4p^d\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\le\beta_s+\kappa/(4m)\).

Since \(\varepsilon\le c_4p\sqrt{(d+\ln n)/n}\), taking \(C_p\ge204c_4p\) makes the bound trivial unless \(d\varepsilon\le1/204\), which we assume. Then there are at most \(d+45d\varepsilon m+dT+d+1\le3m\) sub-steps. The same computation with the number \(R_s\le a\) of pigeons removed at \(s\), where \(\mathbb E[R_s\mid\text{state}]\le r_s\), gives \(\mathbb E[R_s\text{ along the run}]\le r_s+(r_s+a)\,2p^d\cos(\pi/p)^{t_0}\le r_s+\kappa/2\). By Markov's inequality, the cap fails with probability at most \(\frac4m(\sum_sr_s+2)\le204d\varepsilon+8/m\). Collecting the bounds, with \(d\) rounds, at most \(45d\varepsilon m\) phase-1 revelations, \(dT\) pair draws, \(d\) checks and the leaf:

\[\Pr[\text{success}]\le d\iota+45d\varepsilon\,c_2\bigl(p+p!(1.2)^p\bigr)+dT\,\frac{2(p+1)}{F_1}+\frac{d\kappa}{16m}+\frac{p(p+1)}{F_1^2}+204d\varepsilon+\frac8m+\kappa .\]

Here \(dT\cdot2(p+1)/F_1\le0.1(p+1)d\varepsilon\), so the right side is at most \(c_3(p+1)\,p!\,(1.2)^p\,d\varepsilon+O(p^2/n^2)+O(1/n)\le C_p\,d\sqrt{(d+\ln n)/n}\), since \(\varepsilon=O(p\sqrt{(d\ln p+\ln n)/m})\). \(\square\)

What this does and does not give

  • It removes one of the two obstacles of Byramji and Impagliazzo's Remark A.4 for unary PHP, in its search form. The modular collision is a distribution on which linear trees over \(\mathbb F_p\) need polynomial depth, against \(O(\log n)\) for the one-defect classes (Observation). The sampling tree needs about \(n/p\) pigeons. So the truth lies between about \(n^{1/3}\) and \(n\).
  • It is search hardness only. The random walk also needs a probability bound for safe systems and a restriction. The proof suggests the form of the bound: the probability of a system of \(k\) answers is about \(Z\le p^{-(k-\dim W)}\), where \(W\) is the span of combinations close to additive. Their sparse parts are handled by revealing and deleting cells, not by charging probability. The system \(\{x_{i_th_t}=0\}\) that defeats a probability bound on the full board has \(W\) equal to everything, so it is charged nothing. This matches the deletion accounting proposed by the review. It is not yet a probability bound for the walk, whose systems are the lines of a refutation, not the answers of a tree.
  • Where depth is lost: the square root comes from balancing sparse revelation, \(\varepsilon m\) per round, against localization, \(t_0/\varepsilon\) pairs per step. The factor \(d\) inside \(t_0\) comes from the union bound over the \(p^k\) combinations and from the Fourier sum.

Assessment

The test ended with a proof, pending the gate below. The distribution obstacle of the sub-line is removed in search form, up to depth about \(n^{1/3}\). The sparse-forms obstacle now has a candidate accounting suggested by the same simulation: rank minus near-additive dimension. For the bounded-depth endpoint, the remaining risk is the probability bound and a restriction compatible with the star closure. The sub-line is stronger than at the review, but its payoff is unchanged, a bounded-depth endpoint, so it stays weak for the goal. The window, which the goal needs, is unchanged.

Sheaf check

The simulation glues local sections, the orientations of disjoint swaps, into a near-uniform global answer. Combinations that no swap sees are the sections that are constant up to a sparse defect, and they are glued by revelation, not by randomness. Example H is a space where the four-cycles do not generate the cycle space: a global section whose local restrictions to every swap vanish. Density above two thirds kills that first cohomology, which is Lemma T's threshold.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): the probability bound for the random walk under \(\mu_E\). For a linear system \(\Phi\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), let \(W(\Phi)\) be the span of combinations within \(\varepsilon\) of additive on the current graph. Prove that \(\Pr_{\mu_E}[\Phi]\le p^{-(\mathrm{rk}\,\Phi-\dim W(\Phi))+o(1)}\), after revealing the pigeons on the sparse parts. Then check it against the star closure: which closures the witness can afford, and whether the Delayer step survives cell deletion. Test first on the sparse systems of the review and on systems mixing one dense form with many cells. If the bound fails, record the system that breaks it.

Verification gate. Re-read in the notebook: the search-test entry's setting and its Lemmas L1 and L2, excerpted for the reviewer, and the star-closure route review. Record check: a record-check agent searched the index and the historical index. It found all four statements new and none refuted. Lemma T refines L1, and Lemma F extends L2, of the search test. The finite check (four_cycle_check.py, deterministic seed) confirmed the exact version of Lemma T on 72 random dense graphs, and Example H on three blow-ups. A fresh-context reviewer checked the draft and the code, and reproduced the output byte for byte. Verdict: sound with fixes, with no mathematical break. Its fixes:

  • the transfer needed a shared random tape across nodes, its conditions stated, the step-2 check bounded from the start of step 2, and the cap transferred explicitly on removed pigeons, pairs included;
  • base cases for invariants (B) and (C);
  • the derivations of the expected phase-2 count, the distance loss and \(K_0\);
  • the independence hypothesis of Lemma F;
  • Example H limited to four-cycle swaps and to \(\gamma\le1/6\), with the \(5,2,2\) instance marked as extra;
  • the scope of the finite check.

Unused hypotheses: Lemmas M, T, L1G and F use neither primality nor oddness, and Lemma M holds for every integer \(p\ge1\). Lemma T holds for any bipartite graph. Theorem S uses \(p\ge3\) only through \(p^2/2\ge4\) in \(t_0\), and primality only for linearity over \(\mathbb F_p\) and the span \(W\). At odd primes the walk's restriction is the binding step: restrictions keeping the modular-collision hardness imply only near-additive lines, and carrying the rest stays below the depth every refutation already has

22 September 2026 · Working proofs of a restriction lemma and a padding construction; the walk analysis is heuristic · odd-prime-clause-transfer. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. The committed next step was the probability bound of the random walk under \(\mu_E\). The route check asks first whether a probability bound would be used at all. The walk also needs, at each stage, a restriction that implies the falsifying set of the node it reaches and leaves a problem of the same kind. The missing implication tested here is: in the family where Theorem S gives hardness, a restriction of small cost implies the lines the walk reaches. The test ends with a proof or a refutation of that.

Outcome. The implication fails. In standard \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\), whose lines are disjunctions of equations, a line is falsified on a box: a conjunction of inequations \(L_j\ne a_j\). Within the dense family, a restriction implies an inequation only at a cost linear in \(n\), unless its form is close to additive (Lemma R). Every refutation can be padded, at four times the size, so that the first stage of any walk meets such an inequation (Proposition P). The alternative of carrying these inequations as conditions has, if the budget of Theorem S carries over, a reach of depth about \(n^{2/3}\). That is below the depth \(\Omega(n)\) which every refutation already needs, by a known tree-like bound. The same fact supersedes the depth bound that Theorem S gives directly.

Depth: Theorem S against a known bound

A refutation of depth \(D\) gives a linear decision tree over \(\mathbb F_p\) of depth \(D\) for the false-clause search. Start at the empty clause and keep a line falsified by the input. At a line derived from \(A\vee(L_1=a_1)\) and \(B\vee(L_2=a_2)\) by the linear-combination rule, one query of \(L_1\) finds a falsified premise. Weakening and the removal of false constant equations need no query, and Boolean axioms are never falsified. Leaves at other axioms output an arbitrary pair of pigeons. Under \(\mu_E\), only hole clauses at \(h^*\) are falsified, for the plain and the functional encoding. So Theorem S gives depth at least \(c_pn^{1/3}\), with \(c_p=(2C_p^2)^{-1/3}\).

This is superseded. Part and Tzameret (Resolution with counting, ITCS 2020, Theorem 38, read in the source) prove that every tree-like \(\mathrm{Res}_{sw}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F})\) refutation of \(\neg\mathrm{PHP}^m_n\) has size \(2^{\Omega((n-1)/2)}\), for every field. The encoding is plain, with pigeon and hole clauses, and \(\mathrm{Res}_{sw}\) simulates tree-like \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin})\). Unfolding a DAG refutation of depth \(D\) gives a tree-like one of size at most \(2^{D+1}\). So every \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutation of plain PHP already has depth \(\Omega(n)\). The novelty check of 22 September covered DAG-like size bounds only; this tree-like bound was not on record in the thread.

Restrictions in the dense family

A dense class is given by a set \(F\) of fixed pigeons, sent to distinct holes of \(H'\), and a graph \(G'\) between the remaining pigeons \(A'\) and the holes \(B'=H'\) minus those of \(F\). So \(|A'|=|B'|+p\). The graph \(G'\), and every \(G'-i-h\) for an edge \((i,h)\), satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma M with \(F_3>0\) and \(\theta<1\). Every pigeon misses fewer than \(|B'|/3\) holes. The class consists of all maps that extend \(F\) and lie in the support of \(\nu_{G'}\) on \(A'\). These are the stages on which Theorem S gives hardness. For a form \(L=\sum C(i,h)x_{ih}+c\), \(\mathrm{dist}\) is the distance of \(C\), on pigeons \(\times\,H'\), from additive matrices. Cells of the columns in \(E\) are zero on every class.

Lemma R.

  1. If \(L=a\) on the whole class, then \(C\) is additive on \(G'\).
  2. If \(L\ne a\) on the whole class, then no map in the class has \(p-1\) pairwise disjoint detecting swaps. A detecting swap is a pair of pigeons of \(A'\) in distinct regular holes whose four-cycle lies in \(G'\) and whose swap changes \(L\). Moreover \(\rho_{G'}(C)\le4(p-2)/\bigl(a'(b'-2\mu)(b'-2\mu-1)\ell(G')\ell_1\bigr)\), where \(\ell_1\) is the least \(\ell(G'-i-h)\). In the regime of Theorem S (\(\mu,\mu'\le b'/15\), \(\theta\le0.07\), \(b'\) large), this gives \(\mathrm{dist}_{G'}(C)\le4(p-2)K_0/a'\) with \(K_0\le15\).
  3. In that regime, suppose the class implies \(L=a\) or \(L\ne a\), and \(\mathrm{dist}_{G_0}(C)\ge\varepsilon\) on the complete board \(G_0\) between the \(n+1\) pigeons and \(H'\). Let \(D\) be the set of deleted cells between remaining vertices. Then \(|F|(m+n+1)+|D|\ge\varepsilon(n+1)m-4(p-2)K_0m\). In particular, \(|F|\ge\varepsilon m/4\) or \(|D|\ge\varepsilon(n+1)m/2-4(p-2)K_0m\).

Proof. On the class, \(L(g)=\mathrm{const}+\sum_{i\in A'}C(i,g(i))\).

(1). For every four-cycle \((i,i',h,h')\) of \(G'\), Lemma M(6) gives a map in the class with \(g(i)=h\), \(g(i')=h'\) and both holes regular. Exchanging the two holes gives another map in the class, and \(L\) changes by \(-\delta\). So \(\delta=0\) on every four-cycle, \(\rho_{G'}(C)=0\), and \(C\) is additive by Lemma T.

(2). Disjoint swaps commute, and each keeps the class. Take \(p-1\) disjoint detecting swaps, with changes \(-\delta_1,\ldots,-\delta_{p-1}\), all nonzero. Applying a subset \(K\) of them gives a map with value \(L(g)-\sum_{k\in K}\delta_k\). The subset sums of \(p-1\) nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_p\) cover \(\mathbb F_p\), which is the mechanism of the forced-cells lemma. Indeed, adding an element \(x\ne0\) to a set of subset sums \(\Sigma\ne\mathbb F_p\) enlarges it, since \(\Sigma+x=\Sigma\) would make \(\Sigma\) a union of cosets of \(\langle x\rangle=\mathbb F_p\). So some map in the class has \(L=a\), a contradiction.

For a map \(g\), the detecting pairs form a graph on \(A'\) with no matching of \(p-1\) edges. A maximal matching has at most \(p-2\) edges, and its at most \(2(p-2)\) vertices cover every detecting pair. So a uniform pair of distinct pigeons is detecting with probability at most \(4(p-2)/a'\), for every \(g\). The event is the event Good of Lemma L1G, whose probability under \(g\sim\nu_{G'}\) is at least \(\rho_{G'}(C)(b'-2\mu)(b'-2\mu-1)\ell(G')\ell_1\). This gives the bound on \(\rho\). In the regime, \(\Pr[\text{Good}]\ge\mathrm{dist}_{G'}(C)/K_0\) gives the bound on \(\mathrm{dist}\).

(3). An additive function on \(G'\) extends to \(G_0\), with arbitrary values on the removed vertices. So \(\mathrm{dist}_{G_0}(C)(n+1)m\le\mathrm{dist}_{G'}(C)|G'|+|G_0\setminus G'|\). The cells outside \(G'\) lie in the rows of \(F\) (at most \(|F|m\)), in the columns of the holes of \(F\) (at most \(|F|(n+1)\)), or in \(D\), and \(|G'|\le a'm\). If \(|F|<\varepsilon m/4\), then \(|F|(m+n+1)<\varepsilon(n+1)m/2\), using \(m\le n+1\). \(\square\)

What the proof uses:

  • Part (1) and the first claim of (2) use only that every four-cycle of \(G'\) occurs as a swap in the class.
  • The count in (2) is pure combinatorics.
  • The bound "fewer than \(|B'|/3\)" enters only through Lemma T.

A class implying a box must imply each of its inequations, and Lemma R bounds each one separately. The same restriction can serve several inequations, so the costs need not add.

Padding makes the first stage expensive

Proposition P. Let \(\Pi\) be a \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutation of size \(S\) and depth \(D\). Let \(L\) be a linear form and \(a\ne a'\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). There is a refutation \(\Pi'\) of size at most \(4S+2\) and depth at most \(D+3\) in which every line other than the axioms and the last two lines contains \(L=a\) or \(L=a'\) as a disjunct.

Proof. For \(c\in\{a,a'\}\), add the disjunct \(L=c\) to every line of \(\Pi\). An axiom \(A\) gives \(A\vee(L=c)\) by one weakening. The linear-combination rule, weakening and the removal of false constant equations apply unchanged with the extra disjunct carried along. So the copy derives \(L=c\). Combining \(L=a\) with \(L=a'\) by the coefficients \(1,-1\) gives \(0=a-a'\), a false constant equation, and removing it gives the empty clause. \(\square\)

Take for \(L\) the indicator of \(P_1\times H_1\), for halves \(P_1\) of the pigeons and \(H_1\) of \(H'\). On the complete board with \(a\) pigeons and \(b\) holes, a cell lies in a fraction \(4/(ab)\) of the four-cycles. Every four-cycle with \(\delta\ne0\) contains a cell where \(C\) differs from a given additive matrix. Hence \(\mathrm{dist}\ge\rho/4\). A uniform four-cycle splits both halves with probability about \(1/4\) and then has \(\delta=\pm1\), so \(\mathrm{dist}_{G_0}(C)\ge1/16-o(1)\). A walk on \(\Pi'\) descends at least three levels in its first stage. Unless the search is solved, it reaches a line containing \(L=a\) or \(L=a'\). So the first stage's class implies \(L\ne c\) for some \(c\), and by Lemma R(3) it fixes at least about \(m/64\) pigeons or deletes about \(nm/32\) cells. Nesting \(k\) paddings, with forms supported on disjoint blocks of pigeons, multiplies the size by \(4^k\) and should make \(k\) stages expensive; that is not proved here.

What the walk needs at odd primes (heuristic)

  • The restriction, not the probability bound, is binding. Within the dense family, the walk can neither imply far inequations cheaply (Lemma R) nor avoid them (Proposition P). With stages of depth about \(n^{1/3}\), reaching depth beyond \(n\) takes more than \(n^{2/3}\) stages, and each stage then has a budget below about \(n^{1/3}\) pigeons.
  • Carrying inequations. The alternative is to condition on the far inequations of each node instead of implying them. Sparse literals would still be handled by restrictions, which Lemma R does not exclude; a single literal \(x_{ih}=1\) is implied by fixing pigeon \(i\) to \(h\). Conditioning on far forms leaves the swap simulation untilted only under four conditions:
    1. the main term must be exactly \(p^{-k}\), the \(\xi=0\) term of Lemma F, since \(M\) depends on the unrevealed part;
    2. the bound \(t_0\) must hold outside a set of much smaller probability than the conditioning event;
    3. the claim concerns the pair structure, not the orientation bits, which the answers constrain;
    4. \(t_0\gg p^2J\ln p\) for \(J\) carried inequations.
    None of these is proved.
  • Its reach. Suppose Theorem S's budget carries over, so that carried far rank plus depth stays below about \(n^{1/3}\), up to constants depending on \(p\). This extrapolates the \((J+d)^{3/2}/\sqrt n\) form of Theorem S and is not justified. Then about \(n^{1/3}/(p\ln S)\) stages of depth \(n^{1/3}\) give \(D\ln S\gtrsim n^{2/3}/p\). That is vacuous, because every refutation already has depth \(\Omega(n)\). A useful carrying walk would need carried rank of order \(n^{2/3+\Omega(1)}\) at depth \(n^{1/3}\), far outside what the swap simulation handles.

Assessment

The test ended with a refutation of the implication as posed. Proposition P makes it rigorous for the first stage. The probability bound was the wrong next obligation.

  • Within the family where hardness is proved, restrictions cannot imply the far inequations that a padded refutation puts in the walk's way.
  • Carrying the inequations instead reaches, heuristically, only depths that every refutation exceeds.
  • The direct depth bound of Theorem S is superseded by a known tree-like bound.

For the closure sub-line, the random walk at odd \(p\) now needs a restriction family outside the dense classes, one that keeps a far inequation implied at bounded cost. Classes with affine links between cells would be an example. No candidate is known. Theorem S keeps its value as the first hard distribution for linear search at odd \(p\), but its route to a proof-system bound is blocked at the restriction. The sub-line is weak, and a route review is due before further work on it.

Sheaf check

A restriction is a local section that must glue to the whole falsifying set of a line. On the dense family, the four-cycles transport values across the class. So a far inequation cannot be glued from sections of the family: every section implying it is near-additive, or removes a linear part of the board. The box is not a flat, so no product of cell sections covers its complement. Carrying inequations replaces gluing by conditioning. Conditioning is consistent only while swaps keep the carried values independent of the rest, and its budget is where that fails.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): a route review of the closure sub-line and of the thread. It should weigh three new facts: Theorem S, Lemma R with Proposition P, and the known \(\Omega(n)\) depth bound. It should ask two questions:

  • whether any restriction family beyond dense classes can imply far inequations at odd \(p\) at bounded cost, for instance affine links between cells or bit-like gadgets inside unary rows;
  • whether the sub-line has any payoff beyond depth \(n\).

It should also say where the window line stands after the pause-review override.

A fresh-context reviewer checked the first draft. Verdict: sound with fixes, with the depth corollary and Lemma R standing. Its fixes:

  • Lemma R's hypotheses: Lemma M for every \(G'-i-h\), the regime for (2) and (3), \(K_0\le15\), and the holes of \(F\) in \(H'\);

Route review: restrictions cannot imply far inequations cheaply, and walks that carry them are capped a logarithmic factor above the depth floor; back to the window's decisive calibration

22 September 2026 · Route review of odd-prime-clause-transfer · Closure sub-line: restriction blocked heuristically, carrying capped near the depth floor; window: weak, unchanged; next: the decisive calibration by swap-averaged designs. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

The lines' general claims. The closure sub-line claims that a random walk in the style of Byramji and Impagliazzo gives size lower bounds for \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutations of unary PHP of bounded depth. It would combine a hard distribution, a closure and restrictions. The window line claims that dense-support blocks of intermediate projected rank can be excluded by a gluing of weighted pieces at additive degree cost. What the goal needs is superpolynomial size for unrestricted DAG-like refutations. The statement set leaves open refutations with more than \(Cn\) window lines of nonlocal dimension above \(n^{1/(p-1)-\varepsilon}\). A bounded-depth result helps the goal only as a partial endpoint, and it is meaningful only beyond depth \(\Omega(n)\): Part and Tzameret's tree-like bound, unfolded, gives every refutation that depth. Route item under review: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The user's override of the pause review stands: window work continues.

Evidence since the last review

  • Theorem S: under the modular collision \(\mu_E\), linear trees over \(\mathbb F_p\) need depth about \(n^{1/3}\) to find a collision. This is the first hard distribution for linear search on unary PHP at odd \(p\), with dense-graph marginals (Lemma M) and a four-cycle test with a sharp two-thirds threshold (Lemma T).
  • Lemma R and Proposition P: restrictions that keep this hardness imply a far inequation only at linear cost. Padding puts such an inequation into the first stage of every walk, at four times the size.
  • The known tree-like bound gives every refutation depth \(\Omega(n)\). It supersedes Theorem S's direct depth bound.

Falsification attempt 1: restrictions beyond the dense classes

The previous entry asked whether restrictions outside the dense classes can imply far inequations at bounded cost. Four kinds were examined.

  • Graph classes of any density. Such a class fixes some pigeons and confines each other pigeon to a set of holes, given by a graph \(G'\); it consists of all admissible maps on \(G'\) extending the fixed part. Bit-like gadgets inside rows are of this kind: fixing each pigeon's side of a cut is a confinement. The first claim of Lemma R(2) uses three facts only. The class is closed under swaps along four-cycles of \(G'\) between regular holes. A regular hole holds one pigeon, so swaps on disjoint pairs use disjoint holes, commute, and keep each other's holes regular. And \(L(g)=\mathrm{const}+\sum_iC(i,g(i))\) for every map. So that claim holds for every graph class: a class implying \(L\ne a\) has no map with \(p-1\) disjoint detecting swaps. The distance bounds of Lemma R(2) and (3) need Lemma M's hypotheses and the regime of Theorem S, and do not carry over. That is why the next step is heuristic. Take the cut form \(L=\mathbf 1[P_1\times H_1]\) of Proposition P. Among swaps along four-cycles of \(G'\) between regular holes, a swap detects exactly when it exchanges a pigeon of \(P_1\) and a pigeon outside \(P_1\) whose holes lie on opposite sides of the cut. So, heuristically, once at most \(2(p-2)\) pigeons per map are set aside, \(G'\) has no crossing four-cycle: none with one pigeon in each half and one hole on each side. One way is to confine every pigeon of \(P_1\) to its side, which fixes \(L\). Another is to send \(P_1\) and its complement to disjoint hole sets \(X\) and \(Y\). Every hole is occupied, with occupancy \(\equiv1\pmod p\), so then \(L\equiv|X\cap H_1|\).
  • Nesting. The previous entry noted that nested paddings, with forms on disjoint blocks of pigeons, should make \(k\) stages expensive. That design cannot accumulate confinement, since each pigeon meets one cut. Use instead \(k\) independent random cuts on all pigeons, and pad directly. Weaken every axiom by all \(k\) disjuncts \(L_j=c_j\), and run one copy of \(\Pi\) for each of the \(2^k\) choices \(c_j\in\{a_j,a_j'\}\). At the bottom, eliminate the cut forms one at a time: combining two lines that differ only in \(c_1\) gives a false constant equation, and removing it drops \(L_1\). The size is about \(2^kS\) and the depth \(D+2k\). Every line other than an axiom and the bottom \(2k\) levels contains all \(k\) disjuncts. So a walk that passes depth \(2k\) needs classes implying a box of \(k\) cut inequations. By the previous bullet, heuristically, each block of pigeons and holes within which the class allows swaps is, for each cut, one-sided in the pigeon cut or in the hole cut. A block of \(s\) pigeons and \(s\) holes then has \(s\lesssim\sqrt{nm}\,2^{-k/2}\), where \(m\) is the number of holes, and disjoint hole sets as above attain this. With \(k=C\log_2n\) the size grows by the factor \(n^C\), and for \(C>2\) a typical pigeon keeps \(O(1)\) holes.
  • Affine restrictions, such as affine links between cells. An affine function that is not constant on a flat takes every value there. So a flat that implies \(L\ne a\) by linear algebra alone, that is on the whole flat over \(\mathbb F_p\), fixes \(L\), and this is carrying \(L\) as an equation. The class is only the maps inside the flat, and implications that use Booleanity or the hole axioms are not covered. They include every graph class, since fixing or deleting a cell is an affine restriction.
  • Nonlinear gadgets. The walk recurses on a \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutation of a smaller unary PHP, and a nonlinear gadget turns linear lines into polynomial lines of higher degree. An affine gadget cannot help: realizing the unit vectors of a row with \(a\) allowed holes needs at least \(a-1\) free variables, so shrinking a row means deleting holes, which is confinement.

So, heuristically and within these scopes, no kind implies far inequations at bounded cost. Graph classes pay by confinement, which random nested cuts make total. Affine classes whose implication is linear-algebraic reduce to carrying. Nonlinear gadgets are excluded by the recursion, not refuted.

Falsification attempt 2: can a walk that carries inequations pass the floor?

The walk must then carry far inequations as conditions. Stage \(i\) works under \(\mu_E\) conditioned on a box of \(J\) carried far inequations, and runs the refutation for \(d\) levels. Depth \(D\) takes \(D/d\) stages. A line reached with probability at least \(1/(4S)\) has at most about \(p\ln(4S)\) near-independent far inequations, and a refutation can make each stage add that many. So the analysis must tolerate \(J\approx(D/d)\,p\ln S\).

Stage failures add. A stage fails when its \(d\) levels reach a falsified axiom. Under \(\mu_E\) that means they find a collision. A refutation of depth \(D\) sends the walk to an axiom within \(D\) levels. So if each stage fails with probability at most \(\delta\), a walk says something about depth \(D\) only when \((D/d)\,\delta<1\). Theorem S gives \(\delta\approx C_pd\sqrt{(d+\ln n)/n}\). Then \(D\lesssim\sqrt{n/(d+\ln n)}/C_p\), at most about \(\sqrt n\), and the walk covers no refutation at all, since every refutation has depth \(\Omega(n)\).

No stage lemma about arbitrary trees does much better. Under \(\mu_E\) each pigeon lies in \(h^*\) with probability \((p+1)/(n+1)\).

  • A tree finds a pigeon's hole by binary search with the \(0/1\)-valued queries \(\sum_{h\in A}x_{ih}\), in about \(\log_2n\) queries.
  • It then looks for a second pigeon in that hole by column counts over subsets of the other pigeons. If the hole is \(h^*\), a random subset holds a number of the other \(p\) pigeons that is nonzero modulo \(p\) with probability \(1-2^{1-p}\). Once a count lies strictly between \(0\) and \(p\), halving is exact.
  • So \(O(\log n)\) queries find a collision with probability about \((p+1)/n\). A tree of depth \(d\) makes about \(d/\log n\) such attempts on distinct pigeons, and succeeds with probability about \(dp/(n\log n)\).

Hence \(\delta\gtrsim dp/(n\log n)\) for every lemma about arbitrary linear trees, and \(D\lesssim n\log n/p\). That is at most a logarithmic factor above the floor. Passing it would need a stage bound that uses the refutation's size, and no recorded analysis does.

The carried box within that window. A first count charged every close combination of an adaptive query with carried forms the whole \(\ell_1\) weight \(2^J\) of the box. In the Fourier expansion of the box's normalized indicator \(f\) over the carried forms \(L\), the coefficients have absolute value \((p-1)^{-|\mathrm{supp}\,\xi|}\). The fresh-context reviewer argued that this over-charges, since the tilt from \(sQ+\xi\cdot L\) is \(|\hat f(\xi)|\le1\) times its bias. Its finer heuristic count has three regimes:

  • combinations below Theorem S's threshold are revealed;
  • a band up to the far scale \(\tau\) of the carried span holds at most one \(\xi\) for each \(s\);
  • one batch of swaps covers everything above \(\tau/2\), and \(J\) enters only there, fitting when \(J\lesssim\tau m/(K_0p^2)\).

Clusters \(L_0+\sigma_j\) of mutually close forms seem to cost about \(p^2J\) up to logarithms as well. With disjoint rows, detections add over \(\mathrm{supp}\,\xi\). With shared rows, one reveal serves the whole cluster. So the box is probably affordable. With a stage lemma of the optimal order \(\delta\approx dp/(n\log n)\), at \(d\) up to about \(n^{1/3}\), the count \(\ln S\gtrsim md/(p^3D)\) would give superpolynomial size throughout the window. That lemma is far stronger than Theorem S.

So this attempt caps the carrying walk rather than refuting it. At best it gives size bounds for depths between the floor \(\Omega(n)\) and about \(n\log n/p\), and only through a sharp stage lemma that is not in hand.

Assessment

  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, closure sub-line: weak, and capped near the floor. Theorem S stands as an independent result: the first hard distribution for linear search on unary PHP at odd \(p\). The restriction route is blocked on the dense classes by Lemma R, and heuristically on every graph class by random nested cuts. The carrying route is capped at depth about \(n\log n/p\) by the generic collision search. Even its best case, a sharp stage lemma, gives bounded-depth bounds only in a logarithmic window above the floor. The named obligation is kept on record: a stage bound of order \(dp/(n\log n)\) under a carried box.
  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, window: weak, unchanged since the pause review. No restart condition of that review has been met; the user's override keeps the line open. Its decisive calibration asks whether the weighted replay can absorb one dense block of rank \(\Theta(N)\) at degree \(o(N)\). One analogy from the walk suggests a design-side mechanism. There, a carried box appears to be absorbed by one batch of swaps at a cost linear in its rank, even when its forms cluster. Reweighting by its selector instead costs degree multiplicatively, like the product split (SPLIT).
  • same-graph-composition: nothing open.
  • scope-and-review: a novelty gap was found. The novelty check of 22 September covered DAG-like size bounds only, and missed tree-like results. Part and Tzameret's bound supersedes Theorem S's depth corollary. It does not touch the DAG-like endpoints of the statement set. Any write-up must cite the tree-like literature (Itsykson and Sokolov over \(\mathbb F_2\), Part and Tzameret over every field). The write-up and the binary compiler audit still await user decisions.

Correction to the closure-walk route review: its window calibration was already met; the next step moves to the dense side at \(p\ge5\)

22 September 2026 · Correction of a route review, odd-prime-clause-transfer · Withdraws its window assessment and next step; next: a dense-rank criterion for \(p\ge5\). Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

What is corrected. The closure-walk route review stated two things about the window. It said that no restart condition of the pause review had been met. And it set as next step that review's "decisive calibration": exclude one random dense block of rank \(\Theta(N)\), jointly with the recorded weight, at degree \(o(N)\). Both are wrong. The block-count review had already settled the calibration. The recorded old-consequence transfer with target \(1\) removes one fresh block of any rank and accuracy from any base, at \((p-1)\delta=4\) degrees. So a single dense block is excluded jointly with any exclusion that holds four degrees higher, and that review concluded: "The real calibration is the number of window blocks." The statement set then replaced the restart conditions with three. None of them is met, as the thread review after the audits checked:

  • a batched mechanism for non-nested dense blocks that uses PHP structure;
  • a proof of the level-one conjecture with a depth-independent use;
  • outside work on DAG-like proofs with dense linear lines.

The review's window assessment and its next step, swap-averaged certification of one block, are withdrawn. Its analyses of restrictions and of carrying walks do not depend on this and stand as recorded, heuristic where marked. The error came from restating the calibration from the pause review without searching for later entries that met it.

The distributional analogy against the real calibration

The review's analogy was that a walk absorbs a carried box cheaply. Against the number of window blocks it offers nothing. A walk never handles a refutation's lines jointly. It meets them one path at a time. At the end of a stage it conditions on one line's box, whose far rank is at most about \(p\ln(4S)\) for a line reached with probability at least \(1/(4S)\). It pays for the polynomially many lines through a union bound over lines. The block-count review recorded the same shape for the compile-and-exclude framework. Its size-sensitive exclusions work through one matching restriction and a union bound, dense window blocks survive such restrictions, and no recorded mechanism replaces the union bound for them. So the analogy transfers the obstruction, not a mechanism.

The walk cap and Byramji and Impagliazzo's Remark A.4

The review capped every walk with restarted stages at depth about \(n\log n/p\). The reason is that a linear tree finds a collision with probability about \(dp/(n\log n)\) under any collision distribution on the plain unary encoding. This is the randomized odd-prime counterpart of Remark A.4 of Byramji and Impagliazzo (arXiv 2511.20023, read in the source). There, for near-permutations over \(\mathbb F_2\), a deterministic parity tree finds the doubled hole by binary search over holes and then its two pigeons, in \(O(\log n)\) queries. Over \(\mathbb F_p\) the modular collision \(\mu_E\) defeats the binary search over holes, because every column sum outside \(E\) is \(1\) modulo \(p\). That is why Theorem S holds at all. The randomized search locates one pigeon's hole and then tests for a partner, and it still succeeds with probability about \(p/n\) per \(O(\log n)\) queries. The known bounds beyond depth \(n\), theirs and those of Bhattacharya, Chattopadhyay and Byramji, are for bit PHP and for a block-lifted unary functional PHP. That is consistent with the cap, since in those encodings linear queries find a collision much more slowly. Those proofs were not checked here.

Assessment and next step

Both lines of odd-prime-clause-transfer are weak. The window has no candidate for any restart condition, and the user's override keeps it open for one. The closure sub-line on the plain encoding is capped near the floor. One open piece of this route item can be attacked with recorded tools: the dense side at \(p\ge5\). For \(p=3\), dense projected rank is excluded on separated graphs by the clique-head criterion, above a threshold \(\Theta(N\log N)\). For \(p\ge5\) the low side holds, through Corollary NDp and the all-prime quotient-rank exclusion, but no dense-rank criterion is recorded. So at \(p\ge5\) the open case is everything above nonlocal dimension \(n^{1/(p-1)-\varepsilon}\).

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): a dense-rank criterion for \(p\ge5\).

  • State the \(p\ge5\) analogue with its threshold, and prove it or name the prime-specific obstruction.

Evaluate the threshold first on the two extremal inputs of the ternary proof, a random dense block and a clique-head block, and compare it with \(n^{1/(p-1)}\). Success narrows the open case at \(p\ge5\) to an intermediate window, as at \(p=3\). It does not reach the goal.

A head count for heads of any degree: at \(p\ge5\) the dense threshold of the kernel method is about \(N^{p-3/2}\)

22 September 2026 · Working proof and finite check · Lemma HDH bounds independent sets for heads of degree up to \(p-1\); the \(p\ge5\) dense side reduces to transcribing the ternary criterion. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. At \(p\ge5\) the low side of the window holds through Corollary NDp, but no dense side is recorded. So the open case there is everything above nonlocal dimension \(n^{1/(p-1)-\varepsilon}\). The ternary dense side is the low-or-dense graph criterion. It finds one weight \(f\) in a separated matching space \(W_k\) that lies in the kernel of every block's reduction map. Its dense step counts the distinct leading monomials (heads) of a block's input span, which are pairs at \(p=3\). At \(p\ge5\) the inputs \(1-L^{p-1}\) have degree \(\delta=p-1\), so their heads are sets of up to \(\delta\) coordinates. The missing implication tested here is the count: do many heads of degree up to \(\delta\) force a small reduction image, as many pairs do? A counting lemma with a nonvacuous threshold answers yes for the count. A family of large rank whose heads defeat every count would answer no.

The counting step of the ternary criterion

If polynomials have distinct squarefree leading monomials, monomial-by-monomial reduction by them and Booleanity, in a fixed degree-compatible order, has an image of degree-\(\le k\) monomials divisible by no head. Its dimension is at most \(J_{\le k}\), the number of sets of at most \(k\) coordinates containing no head. The ternary criterion bounds \(J_{\le k}\) for pairs by (DH-count), \(J_{\le k}\le4\binom sk\exp(k^2/s-qk/s^2)\) for \(q\) distinct pairs. It needs the image of each dense block to be at most \(4\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N-\Lambda}\), where \(\Lambda=\log(64(M+1))\) for \(M\) blocks, \(s=15(N+1)\) and \(k=\lceil\sqrt{N\Lambda}\rceil\). Then the images of all blocks together stay below \(\dim W_k\ge\frac12e^{-5k^2/N}\binom sk\).

Lemma HDH (distinct heads of bounded degree)

Let \(\delta\ge2\) and \(k\le s/4\). Let \(\mathcal H\) be a family of \(q\) distinct subsets of \([s]\), each of size between \(1\) and \(\delta\). Let \(\mathcal E\) be the family of \(\delta\)-subsets of \([s]\) that contain a member of \(\mathcal H\), and put \(\theta=|\mathcal E|/\binom s\delta\). Then \(\theta\ge q/(2^\delta\binom s\delta)\), with \(\theta=q/\binom s\delta\) when every member has size \(\delta\). The number \(J_{\le k}\) of subsets of \([s]\) of size at most \(k\) that contain no member of \(\mathcal H\) satisfies

\[ J_{\le k}\ \le\ \sum_{j<\delta}\binom sj\;+\;2.3\binom sk\exp\Bigl(\frac{k(\delta-1)}{s}-\frac{k\theta}{\delta}\Bigr).\tag{HDH} \]

When \(k<\delta\) the first term alone bounds \(J_{\le k}\). The application uses heads of size at least \(2\).

Proof. A \(\delta\)-set contains at most \(2^\delta\) members of \(\mathcal H\), and each member lies in some \(\delta\)-set, so \(q\le2^\delta|\mathcal E|\). For \(|K|\ge\delta\), the set \(K\) contains a member of \(\mathcal H\) exactly when it contains a member of \(\mathcal E\): a member inside \(K\) extends inside \(K\) to a \(\delta\)-set. So for \(j\ge\delta\), \(J_j\) counts the \(j\)-sets all of whose \(\delta\)-subsets lie in \(\mathcal F\), the complement of \(\mathcal E\) among the \(\delta\)-sets.

If \(\mathcal F\) is empty, \(J_j=0\) for \(j\ge\delta\). Otherwise write \(|\mathcal F|=\binom x\delta\) with real \(\delta\le x\le s\). Apply Lovász's form of the Kruskal–Katona theorem (Lovász, Combinatorial Problems and Exercises, 13.31, imported) to the family of those \(j\)-sets, whose \(\delta\)-shadow lies in \(\mathcal F\). If \(J_j\ge1\), write \(J_j=\binom yj\) with real \(y\ge j\). Then \(\binom y\delta\le|\mathcal F|=\binom x\delta\), so \(y\le x\) and \(J_j\le\binom xj\). In particular \(J_j=0\) when \(x<j\). The factors \((x-i)/(s-i)\) decrease in \(i\), so \(1-\theta=\prod_{i<\delta}\frac{x-i}{s-i}\ge\bigl(\frac{x-\delta+1}{s-\delta+1}\bigr)^\delta\). Hence \(x\le\delta-1+s(1-\theta)^{1/\delta}\), and

\[ \frac xs\le\frac{\delta-1}s+1-\frac\theta\delta\le\exp\Bigl(\frac{\delta-1}s-\frac\theta\delta\Bigr). \]

For \(x\ge j\) every factor of \(\binom xj/\binom sj=\prod_{i<j}\frac{x-i}{s-i}\) lies in \([0,x/s]\), so \(\binom xj\le\binom sj(x/s)^j\). This gives \(J_j\le T_j:=\binom sj\exp\bigl(j(\delta-1)/s-j\theta/\delta\bigr)\). For \(\delta\le j<k\), \(T_j/T_{j+1}=\frac{j+1}{s-j}\,e^{\theta/\delta-(\delta-1)/s}\le\frac13e^{1/2}<0.55\), because \(k\le s/4\) and \(\theta/\delta\le1/2\). So \(\sum_{\delta\le j\le k}T_j\le T_k/0.45\le2.3\,T_k\), and the sets of size below \(\delta\) contribute at most \(\sum_{j<\delta}\binom sj\). \(\square\)

For \(\delta=2\), every head is a pair, and the exponent is \(k/s-kq/(s(s-1))\). That is slightly sharper than (DH-count), whose first term is \(k^2/s\).

The dense threshold at \(p\ge5\)

Keep \(s,\Lambda,k\) as in the ternary criterion, and put \(\delta=p-1\) and

\[ Q^{(p)}_*=\Bigl\lceil2^\delta\,\delta\binom s\delta\Bigl(\frac{\delta-1}s+\frac{5k}N+\frac{\Lambda+1}k\Bigr)\Bigr\rceil . \]

Suppose a block supplies at least \(Q^{(p)}_*\) combinations with distinct squarefree heads of degrees \(2\) to \(\delta\). Then \(k\theta/\delta\ge k(\delta-1)/s+5k^2/N+\Lambda+1\), so the second term of (HDH) is at most \(2.3e^{-1}\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N-\Lambda}\). For a polynomial inventory \(M\), the first term is at most \(\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N-\Lambda}\) for large \(N\), since \(e^{5k^2/N+\Lambda}\) is then polynomial in \(N\). So \(J_{\le k}\) is below the ternary requirement \(4\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N-\Lambda}\). The reduction meaning carries over: reducing by polynomials with distinct squarefree heads of degree up to \(\delta\), with multipliers of degree at most \(k\) minus the head's degree, keeps the degree ceiling and has image at most \(J_{\le k}\). Which old relations the heads are taken modulo at degree \(\delta\), and the lower bound on \(\dim W_k\) at \(p\ge5\), belong to the transcription and are not checked here. For a polynomial inventory, \(Q^{(p)}_*=O_p(N^{\delta-1/2}\sqrt{\log N})\). A block's span can have up to \(\sum_{2\le j\le\delta}\binom sj=\Theta_p(N^\delta)\) heads, so the threshold is not vacuous. When every head has degree \(\delta\), the factor \(2^\delta\) can be dropped. At \(p=3\) this is the ternary \(Q_*=\Theta(N^{3/2}\sqrt\Lambda)\) up to constants. If the heads are taken in the quotient where Corollary NDp bounds the rank, \(q\le r_a\le\binom{v+\delta}{\delta}\), and a block reaching \(Q^{(p)}_*\) has nonlocal dimension \(v\) of at least about \(N^{1-1/(2\delta)}\).

This settles only the counting step. The rest of the ternary criterion has not been checked at \(p\ge5\), and the next step lists what must be.

Observation SH: a sunflower family (control)

A rank of order \(s^2\), which counts as dense at \(p=3\), gives no useful count at \(p\ge5\). Take distinct Boolean coordinates \(y_1,\dots,y_a\), \(y'_1,\dots,y'_b\) and a set \(Z\) of at least \(p-3\) further ones, and an affine form \(z\) with support exactly \(Z\). Consider the block with inputs \(q_{ij}=1-(y_i+y'_j+z)^\delta\). Put \(B=(2+z)^\delta-2(1+z)^\delta+z^\delta\) and \(A=(1+z)^\delta-z^\delta\). Booleanity gives

\[ q_{ij}=1-z^\delta-(y_i+y'_j)A-y_iy'_jB,\qquad q_{ij}-q_{i1}-q_{1j}+q_{11}=-(y_i-y_1)(y'_j-y'_1)B . \]

Here \(B\) has degree exactly \(p-3\) in \(z\), with leading coefficient \((p-1)(p-2)\ne0\). After multilinear reduction, every \((p-3)\)-subset of \(Z\) appears in its top part with a nonzero coefficient. The same holds for the top parts of \(A\), of degree \(p-2\), and of \(z^\delta\), of degree \(p-1\), whenever \(Z\) is that large. For \(z=\sum_tc_tz_t+c_0\), each such coefficient is \((p-1)!\prod c_t=-\prod c_t\).

Fix a degree-compatible monomial order, and label the coordinates so that \(y_1\) and \(y'_1\) are the smallest in their groups. Under any monomial order the largest \(j\)-subset of \(Z\) is the set of its \(j\) largest coordinates, so these sets are nested. Let \(m^*\) be the \(p-3\) largest coordinates of \(Z\), which is the head of \(B\). The \(ab\) elements

  • \((y_i-y_1)(y'_j-y'_1)B\) for \(i,j\ge2\), with heads \(y_iy'_jm^*\);
  • \((y_i-y_1)(A+y'_1B)\) for \(i\ge2\), and \((y'_j-y'_1)(A+y_1B)\) for \(j\ge2\), whose heads are \(y_i\) or \(y'_j\) times a set containing \(m^*\);
  • and \(q_{11}\), whose head is \(u\) times the top \((p-1-|u|)\) coordinates of \(Z\) for some \(u\subseteq\{y_1,y'_1\}\);

have pairwise distinct heads. So they form an echelon basis of the span, which therefore has dimension \(ab\), and every head of the span contains \(m^*\). Heads of products of polynomials in disjoint variables multiply. A \(k\)-set contains \(m^*\) with probability at most \((k/s)^{p-3}\), so the head count gives no useful bound for this block, although its span has dimension \(ab\), up to about \(s^2/4\), with no affine element. This does not contradict Lemma HDH: \(ab\) stays far below \(Q^{(p)}_*\).

At \(p=3\), \(B\) is the constant \(2\) and the heads \(y_iy'_j\) are spread pairs. The family is consistent with the threshold above, since \(ab\le s^2\) lies far below \(N^{p-3/2}\). It is the \(p\ge5\) selector instance of the recorded common-factor controls (the clique-head entry's structured controls, and the shared-factor cubic barrier). It is also a one-probe case: fixing \(z=c\) leaves inputs of degree at most two. The dimension is that of the span in the Boolean ring. Its certified rank modulo the old relations and the affine image is not computed.

Checks

  • hypergraph_head_count.py enumerates all sets exactly on 90 families: uniform, mixed-size, split (all \(\delta\)-sets meeting a set \(T\)), clique-type and sunflower. The parameters are \(s\) from 12 to 16 and \(\delta\) from 2 to 4, with deterministic seed 20260922. The summed bound is tested wherever \(\delta\le k\le s/4\), in 89 cases, 13 of them at \(\delta=4\) on 16 coordinates. It checks the Kruskal–Katona step, the per-size bound, the summed bound (HDH) and \(q\le2^\delta|\mathcal E|\). All hold. The Kruskal–Katona step is attained (ratio 1.0) in the clique and split cases. The largest ratio \(J_k/T_k\) is 0.85.
  • sunflower_heads.py computes the span exactly over \(\mathbb F_5\) and \(\mathbb F_7\), with \(\mathbb F_3\) as control, for up to 20 inputs. It uses eight monomial orders per instance: \(Z\) first, \(Z\) last, and six random rankings. It confirms the identity, the degree of \(B\), dimension \(ab\), all heads of degree \(\delta\), and every head containing \(m^*\), the \(p-3\) largest coordinates of \(Z\). At \(p=3\) all heads are spread pairs.

Assessment

The count transfers. Lemma HDH replaces (DH-count) for heads of any bounded degree, and at \(p\ge5\) it gives a dense threshold of order \(N^{p-3/2}\sqrt{\log N}\) inside the possible range \(N^{p-1}\). The sunflower family shows the count is needed in this form. At \(p\ge5\), blocks of span dimension up to about \(N^2\) can have all heads through a fixed set, so no rank threshold below that can come from counting heads. Such blocks are one-probe cases. The dense side at \(p\ge5\) is not proved: the ternary criterion has other steps whose degrees and certificates depend on \(p\). Even when proved, it leaves a window from \(N^\sigma\) to \(N^{p-3/2}\) in quotient rank, far wider than at \(p=3\), and it does not touch the goal.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): transcribe the ternary low-or-dense graph criterion to every odd prime, with Lemma HDH in its dense step. Check each \(p\)-dependent step against its source:

  • the field scope of the separated space \(W_k\);
  • the reduction of degree-\(2\) to \(\delta\) coefficient columns modulo the old \(I_\delta\), with certified representatives;
  • the product map with images \(\beta_i=f^{p-2}c_i\), giving the product \(1-f^{p-1}+f^{p-2}E\) and weighted companions \(g_i(f-f^p)+f^{p-1}g_iE\), with certificate and field degrees;
  • the low side's exact prefix \(\prod_j(1-G_j^{p-1})\) and Fermat zero indicators for small affine cores;
  • the affine-core restriction bound;
  • the final budget \(TD+k\le N/10^6\) at the compiler degree \(4p-1\).

The step ends with an all-prime criterion with explicit thresholds, or with the step that fails.

Sheaf check

The kernel method glues one section, the weight, across all blocks by dimension counting: each block removes at most its image from \(W_k\). Lemma HDH bounds that removal for sections of any degree. The sunflower family is a block whose removal is nearly total, because its sections share a common factor. It is glued instead by a probe that fixes the factor.
