Logarithmic partial prefixes reduce ordinary unary PHP at odd primes to an odd-prime wide-clause statement; the degree-three first moment needs a thinness theorem

22 September 2026 · Conditional reduction theorem and an entropy lemma · The ordinary-PHP lower bound follows from an odd-prime analogue of the recorded wide-clause statement. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The route review sent this cycle to the recorded degree-three obstruction of the main record's wide-clause line. It proposed a partition-rank first moment. Reading the record first showed that the degree-three program went further on 20 September than the parking decision suggested:

  • an exact dimension of the degree-three conflict space, cubic dimension (lem:cubic-conflict-space-dimension);
  • nontrivial relative cubic kernels forced below \(d\approx\sqrt6N^{3/2}\);
  • kernels of factor rank up to about \(N^{1/4}\) excluded (thm:bounded-factor-rank-relative-cubic-kernels), with a ceiling of that order for the method;
  • an exact identity reducing the relative kernel to the rank of \(E\otimes K\to\Lambda^3E\) under quadratic faithfulness (lem:faithful-quadratics-syzygy-injection);
  • a fixed six-hole example whose affine system has a degree-three PC refutation although the Nullstellensatz level sees no contradiction.

The last point made the affine, no-fall model too strong, and the cubic endpoint review parked it in favour of the actual wide-companion obligation. This cycle asks two things. What does a first moment at degree three need? And can the odd-prime problem use that obligation directly?

1. The logarithmic partial prefix

The substitution-capacity entry defined the partial prefix of size \(k\) on sets \(S_b\): each block's product becomes \(Q_b=\prod_{j\in S_b}L_{b,j}^{p-1}\). By the constant-row clamp's argument there, a degree-\(D\) refutation of the source gives a refutation of the base plus the images \(g_{b,i}Q_b\), \(i\notin S_b\), of degree at most \(B_k=\max(D\max(1,(p-1)(k-1)),(p-1)(k+1))\). That entry took \(k\) constant, for random inventories. Here \(k\) grows logarithmically, and the inventory is arbitrary.

The odd-prime wide-clause statement. For an odd prime \(p\) and constants \(K,c\), consider the following system. It consists of the ordinary weak unary base \(\Gamma_{\rm w}\) for \(\mathrm{PHP}^{n+1}_n\) (Booleanity, column collisions and the linear row equations modulo \(p\), with no same-row exclusions and no onto axioms, as in the weak-base compiler) together with the axioms \(g_{b,i}\prod_{j\in S_b}L_{b,j}^{p-1}\), for \(M\le n^K\) families of affine forms \(L_{b,1},\dots,L_{b,h_b}\), subsets \(S_b\) with \(|S_b|=\min(k,h_b)\), \(i\notin S_b\), and \(g=1-L^{p-1}\). The parameters satisfy \[ M\Big(1-\frac1p\Big)^{k}<1,\qquad k\le c\log n . \] The statement is that for every such family of forms there is a choice of the sets \(S_b\) for which this system has no PC refutation of degree \((4p-1)(p-1)k\).

Each block's product \(Q_b\) is the indicator that the forms \(L_{b,j}\), \(j\in S_b\), are all nonzero, that is, that the inputs \(g_{b,j}\) all vanish. The axioms say that on that set every other input \(g_{b,i}\) of the block vanishes too. For independent forms with uniform values the set has density \((1-1/p)^k\), and the condition \(M(1-1/p)^k<1\) is then the analogue of the recorded \(M2^{-h}<1\). The proof below uses it only as a parameter condition. The statement does not require independence, and on Boolean points the actual density can be larger: \(X-1\) is nonzero exactly when \(X=0\).

It is an analogue of the recorded wide-clause statement, not a special case of it. The two differ in four ways. The recorded statement uses the functional base where this one uses the weak base; the weak base is smaller, so this statement is not implied by it. It lets the chooser take any flat cut out by forms in the block's span, where this one allows only subsets of the given inputs; the chooser here has less freedom. It asks for polylogarithmic degree, where this one fixes degree \((4p-1)(p-1)k\), which is weaker. And it requires \(h\ge c'\log_2N\). Over odd \(p\) the sets are not flats.

Theorem (logarithmic-prefix reduction). Fix an odd prime \(p\) and \(K\). Suppose the odd-prime wide-clause statement holds with \(M=n^K\) and \(k=\lceil(K+1)\log n/\log\frac p{p-1}\rceil\). Then for all large \(n\), no \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutation of ordinary unary \(\mathrm{PHP}^{n+1}_n\) has at most \(n^K\) lines. So if the odd-prime wide-clause statement holds for every \(K\), unary PHP needs superpolynomially many lines.

Proof. A refutation with \(S\le n^K\) lines compiles, by the weak-base compiler, into a source of at most \(S\) complete accuracy-one blocks, each with old affine inputs, that has a PC refutation of degree \(D=4p-1\). Apply the partial prefix of size \(k\) on the sets \(S_b\) that the odd-prime wide-clause statement supplies. Blocks with \(h_b\le k\) receive the full prefix, and their companions map into the Boolean ideal. Each block has its own fresh coefficients, so the substitution is well defined. The compiler adds no other axioms: initial-value lines are derived inside the refutation, and the optional rank-one bridge is not used. The substitution maps every fresh coefficient to \(0\) or to a product of at most \(k-1\) selector complements of degree \(p-1\) each. These are idempotent modulo Booleanity: \(L^p-L\) follows from Booleanity at degree \(p\). So each field image \(\beta^p-\beta\), of degree \(p(p-1)(k-1)\le D(p-1)(k-1)\), is derivable within the bound. Every line of degree at most \(D\) in the old variables and the coefficients maps to one of degree at most \(D\max(1,(p-1)(k-1))\). The companions \(g_{b,i}P_b\) map to \(g_{b,i}Q_b\), of degree \((p-1)(k+1)\), which is zero modulo Fermat for \(i\in S_b\) and an axiom of the odd-prime wide-clause statement for \(i\notin S_b\). The old axioms are unchanged. The image is a PC refutation of the the odd-prime wide-clause statement system of degree at most \((4p-1)(p-1)k\), with \(M\le n^K\) and \(M(1-1/p)^k\le n^K\cdot n^{-(K+1)}<1\), contradicting the odd-prime wide-clause statement. The degree is \(O(\log n)\), far below PHP's own barrier of about \(n/2\). \(\square\)

The reduction makes no assumption on the inventory: no window, no randomness, no rank condition. It covers ordinary unary PHP; the functional variant would need the functional compiler and the statement over the functional base. It moves the entire difficulty into the odd-prime wide-clause statement, a statement of the same type as the main record's central wide-companion obligation. The binary side of that obligation is open. So this is a conditional theorem, and it tells which statement to prove. The recorded all-prime affine source exclusion does not already give it. That theorem covers blocks whose inputs are old affine forms, while compiled blocks have selector inputs \(1-L^{p-1}\) of degree \(p-1\), which are affine only for row- or column-local \(L\).

The sets \(S_b\) must be chosen suitably. The recorded row-clause failure does not carry over to the weak base, which has no same-row exclusions. Here is one that does. For each hole \(t\), take a block with forms \(X_{jt}-1\) over all pigeons \(j\), and use the same set \(S\) of \(k\) pigeons in every block. Then \(g_{j}=X_{jt}\) and \(L^{p-1}=1-X\) on Boolean points, and modulo collisions each image \(X_{it}\prod_{j\in S}(1-X_{jt})\) is \(X_{it}\). So every cell of a pigeon outside \(S\) is zero, and that pigeon's row equation gives \(1=0\), at degree about \((p-1)(k+1)+1\). A random choice of \(S_b\) per hole leaves an expander-like graph PHP instead, so the statement is not trivially false on this family. The density condition uses the size, as a sufficient condition must. It fails for exponentially many blocks, consistent with the exponential refutations that completeness gives.

2. What a degree-three first moment needs

Work in the recorded setting over \(\mathbb F_2\): \(n=N^2-1\), \(\bar K\subseteq\Lambda^2V\) the conflict two-forms, \(\bar K_3=V\wedge\bar K\), and \(U\) a uniform \(d\)-subspace of \(V^*\) with \(\bar W=U^\perp\). A nontrivial relative cubic kernel is an element of \(\bar K_3\) that vanishes on \(U\) and lies outside \(\bar W\wedge\bar K\).

The entropy lemma. Let \(S\subseteq\bar K_3\) be the elements whose event "vanishes on \(U\) and is not in \(\bar W\wedge\bar K\)" is nonempty. Then the per-element first moment \(\sum_{\xi}\Pr[\ldots]\) is at least \(|S|/(3.5\cdot2^{d(n-d)})\), and \(d(n-d)\le n^2/4<N^4/4\).

Proof. A nonempty event over uniform \(d\)-subspaces has probability at least one over their number, which is at most \(3.5\cdot2^{d(n-d)}\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). \(\square\)

By the recorded dimension formula, \(\dim\bar K_3=\binom{(N+1)(N-1)}3-\binom{N+1}3(N^3-6N^2+8N-1)=\Theta(N^5)\). For example, the same-row pairs of basis cells times a basis cell of another row already give \(\tfrac12N^5(1-o(1))\) independent elements. So a union bound over single elements below one needs \(|S|<3.47\cdot2^{d(n-d)}\le3.47\cdot2^{N^4/4}\): the elements that can vanish nontrivially on some \(d\)-subspace must be an exponentially thin part of \(\bar K_3\). At degree two the entropy count does not obstruct: there \(\dim\bar K=\Theta(N^3)\) is below \(d(n-d)\), about \(\sqrt2N^{7/2}\) at the degree-two forced dimension \(d\approx\sqrt2N^{3/2}\). The obstruction applies only to union bounds over single elements. Unions over coarser witnesses are not covered, such as classes modulo \(\bar W\wedge\bar K\), kernel subspaces, or the restrictions \(\xi|_U\). The recorded exclusion of factor rank up to \(N^{1/4}\) proves a piece of the needed thinness. Its method's ceiling at that rank means the remainder needs a different argument. With the exact formula, the ratio \(\dim\bar K_3/(n^2/4)\) is \(55.6,247,1015,4087\) at \(N=16,64,256,1024\), and \(\dim\bar K_3/N^5\) is \(0.86,0.97,0.99,1.00\).

The imported regularity results. Janzer's bound (imp:Janzer-finite-field-partition-rank) concerns one tensor's bias, not the joint vanishing of many values. Kazhdan–Ziegler effective universality (imp:KZ-effective-affine-universality) has a rank threshold polynomial in the target dimension, the family size and the uniformity exponent. Here the joint event has \(\binom d3\) values at \(d\) of order \(N^{3/2}\), and a three-form on \(V\) has partition rank at most \(n<N^2\). Whether the imported exponents admit that rank was not checked in this cycle, so it is open whether these tools supply the high-rank side. Either way, a thinness theorem for the low-rank side needs structure specific to \(\bar K\).

Assessment and next step

Part 1 is the main result. The lower bound for ordinary unary PHP, not only the window or the random calibration, follows from the odd-prime wide-clause statement, the odd-prime analogue of the main record's central open obligation. The two threads therefore need the same kind of statement: hardness of PHP under polynomially many wide clauses of logarithmic codimension and total density below one. Part 2 explains, with exact counts, why the recorded random-case approach stalls at degree three. The recorded affine and no-fall models are stronger than the odd-prime wide-clause statement needs.

The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is a choice rule for the sets \(S_b\), stated and proved against structured families: the hole family above, collision-derived lines and occupancy lines. The proof should show that a random or balanced choice turns each such family into a graph PHP whose recorded degree bounds apply. Exact closures cannot test this. At \(p=3\) the density condition allows only one block at \(k=1\). Two blocks need \(k=2\), with images of degree 6 and PHP hard at degree 7, so \(n\ge13\), far beyond exact elimination. The step is therefore a proof, with the hole family as its first case.

Process. Reading the recorded degree-three program before drafting replaced a planned partition-rank attempt, which cannot close, by an exact statement of what is missing. Asking what the odd-prime problem could use directly then produced the reduction, which the capacity entry had one parameter away.

Verification gate. Re-read from the main notebook: the wide-clause statement with its falsification attempts, the cubic dimension formula and relative-kernel bound, the bounded-factor-rank theorem's statement, the syzygy-injection lemma, the cubic endpoint review, and the imported Janzer and Kazhdan–Ziegler statements. From this notebook: the weak-base compiler's degree and block form, and the partial-prefix substitution. Claim searches covered sequential exposure, restriction rank, matrix spaces, Cartan's lemma, entropy first moments, and the odd-prime wide-companion and density vocabulary. They found the recorded cubic program, now cited, and no odd-prime wide-clause statement. One exact computation compared the size of \(\bar K_3\) with the entropy ceiling at four board sizes. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer checked the reduction's proof in full: the degree bound, the telescoping of the product, the Fermat vanishing for inputs in \(S_b\), and the final degree for all \(k\ge1\). It found the reduction correct and not trivially true or false on the families it tested. It required the following, all adopted:

  • correct the comparison with the binary statement, which differs in base, chooser freedom, degree and width;
  • describe the density as a parameter condition, with the correct indicator;
  • name the weak base and restrict the scope to ordinary PHP;
  • state the proof's omitted checks;
  • replace the binary row-clause failure mode by the hole family, which works over the weak base;
  • redo the next step's nonvacuity count;
  • recompute the Part 2 ratios from the exact formula, and narrow the entropy lemma to single-element unions;
  • weaken the Kazhdan–Ziegler remark to an unchecked exponent question;
  • distinguish the all-prime affine source exclusion;
  • replace a letter-suffix name.

The corrections weaken or restate, apart from the hole-family example, which is a direct degree computation, so no second pass was run.

Choosing the prefix sets: random sets make the hole family a sparse graph PHP, but padding refutes the uniform rule

23 September 2026 · Conditional proposition and a refutation · The uniform random rule fails under padding; the choice rule must see which inputs can vanish. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The logarithmic-prefix reduction makes the odd-prime wide-clause statement sufficient for the ordinary-PHP goal, provided the prefix sets \(S_b\) are chosen suitably. The reviewer's hole family shows that one shared set refutes at low degree. The general implication at stake: a uniformly random choice of \(S_b\) keeps every polynomial family hard. The recorded random-conditioning and wide-clause evidence covers the generic extreme, uniformly random forms. This cycle studies the opposite extreme, literal-like forms, for the mechanism rather than as one more case, and tests the uniform rule. It ends with a conditional result for the hole family and a refutation of the uniform rule.

The hole family under a random choice

For each hole \(t\le n\) take the block \(b_t\) with the \(n+1\) inputs \(L_{t,j}=X_{jt}-1\), and choose \(S_t\), a \(k\)-subset of the pigeons, uniformly and independently. On Boolean points \(L^{p-1}=1-X\) and \(g=1-L^{p-1}=X\), with certificates of degree \(p-1\). So the image for \(i\notin S_t\) is \[ X_{it}\prod_{j\in S_t}(1-X_{jt})\;\equiv\;X_{it}\pmod{\text{collisions}}, \] because every other term of the product's expansion contains a collision \(X_{it}X_{jt}\). This holds at degree \(k+1\le(p-1)(k+1)\). Conversely each image is a multiple of \(X_{it}\). So at any degree at least \((p-1)(k+1)\), the base plus the images has the same PC closure as the base plus \(\{X_{it}=0:(i,t)\notin G_S\}\), where \(G_S=\{(i,t):i\in S_t\}\). That is the weak graph PHP on the random bipartite graph \(G_S\). Every hole has degree exactly \(k\), and each pigeon has binomial degree with mean \(kn/(n+1)\).

Proposition (hole family). Let \(k=\lceil(K+1)\ln n/\ln\frac p{p-1}\rceil\) be the reduction's value. Since \(1/\ln\frac p{p-1}>1\), this exceeds \((1+\varepsilon)\ln n\), so isolated pigeons, of probability about \(e^{-k}\) each, are absent with high probability. For smaller \(k\), below \((1-\varepsilon)\ln n\), they exist and the family is refuted at degree \(O(k)\). Suppose \(G_S\) is, with high probability, an \((s,\delta)\)-boundary expander on the pigeon side with maximum pigeon degree \(d=O(\log n)\) and \(\delta s/(2d)\) above \((4p-1)(p-1)k+d\). Then with high probability the hole family's image system has no PC refutation of degree \((4p-1)(p-1)k\).

Proof. By the equivalence above, a refutation of the image system at that degree is one of the weak graph PHP on \(G_S\): set the deleted variables to 0, which does not raise degree and leaves each row equation over the pigeon's neighbours. The functional graph PHP's axioms derive the weak base's: \(1-\sum_{t\in N(i)}X_{it}\) follows from the pigeon clause and the row exclusions at degree \(d_i\). So such a refutation gives a functional one of degree at most \((4p-1)(p-1)k+d\). The imported Miksa–Nordström bound (ctx:php-linear-constraints-literature) excludes it. \(\square\)

The expansion hypothesis is heuristic here. For random bipartite graphs of logarithmic degree one expects unique-neighbour expansion with \(\delta\approx k\) for pigeon sets up to \(s\approx n/k\), and \(d\approx k\). That gives \(\delta s/(2d)\) of order \(n/k\), far above the needed degree, but it is not proved here. The imported Miksa–Nordström statement was not rechecked for the exact hypotheses: the side of the expansion, whether \(d\) is the maximum left degree, whether their functional graph PHP includes row exclusions, and whether it holds over \(\mathbb F_p\). So the proposition is conditional on both, and covers this one family.

The mechanism in this family

In the hole family, \(Q_{b_t}=\prod_{j\in S_t}(1-X_{jt})\) is the indicator that no pigeon of \(S_t\) sits in hole \(t\), which holds on almost all PHP-like points, far from the parameter density \((1-1/p)^k\). The images do not act as generic clauses there. Modulo the base they collapse to cell deletions, and a random choice leaves an expanding graph. Together with the shared-set example of the reduction entry, this shows that the density condition is not sufficient by itself. For this family the working measure is the expansion of the surviving graph.

Padding refutes the uniform rule

The fresh-context reviewer found a counterexample to the uniform random rule, which the draft had conjectured for all families. Take \(M=n\) blocks. For each hole \(t\), block \(b_t\) has one real input \(B_t=X_{1t}-1\) and \(N\approx n^2\) filler inputs that never vanish on Boolean points, for instance the distinct forms \(2-X_v\) over the other cells, with values 2 and 1. A uniform \(k\)-subset contains \(B_t\) with probability \(k/(N+1)\approx k/n^2\). So with probability at least \(1-k/n\), every \(S_{b_t}\) consists of fillers only. Then \(Q_{b_t}\equiv1\) at degree \((p-1)k\), since each filler's \(L^{p-1}\) is 1 on Boolean points. The fillers' own images vanish, because their \(g\) is 0. The real input's image is \(g_{B_t}\equiv X_{1t}\). All of pigeon 1's cells are deleted, and its row equation gives \(1=0\) at degree about \((p-1)(k+1)\), far below \((4p-1)(p-1)k\).

So a uniform choice can be turned back into the adversary's fixed choice by padding with forms that never, or almost never, vanish. The existential wide-clause statement survives this example: put \(B_t\) in \(S_{b_t}\). Any choice rule must see which inputs can vanish. Every candidate rule should be tested against padding by forms that are never zero, and by forms that are zero only on a vanishing fraction of points.

Assessment and next step

This cycle gives a conditional result for one family and refutes the natural uniform rule. The existential wide-clause statement, which the logarithmic-prefix reduction needs, stands. It needs a choice rule that looks at the inputs. The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is to define a rule that weights inputs by how often they vanish, and test it against the padding counterexample and the hole family. One candidate draws inputs with probability proportional to their vanishing mass under a fixed PHP design, one of degree above the image degree, so that the design sees each \(g_i\). The step also has to decide whether such a weighted rule reduces the literal-like part to cell deletions and the generic part to clauses. If no input-weighted rule survives padding by forms that vanish only on a polynomially small fraction, the existential statement needs a choice that depends on the whole family, and that is the next object.

Process. Stating the uniform rule as a general conjecture let the reviewer refute it in one step. That was worth more than extending the hole family. A padding test belongs in every future choice-rule statement.

Verification gate. Re-read: the logarithmic-prefix reduction and its hole-family remark, the imported Miksa–Nordström statement as recorded, and the recorded separated-space lemma, which is for a constructed sixteen-neighbour graph and so is not used. The collision reduction \(X_{it}\prod(1-X_{jt})\equiv X_{it}\) and the equivalence of closures were checked directly. Claim searches for random graph PHP, boundary expansion and choice rules found the imported literature context and the separated-space lemma, and no prior choice-rule statement. A fresh-context reviewer confirmed the hole-family algebra, the closure equivalence and the conditional proof. It refuted the uniform-rule conjecture by padding, and required the reduction's exact \(k\), the isolated-pigeon threshold, the imported hypotheses to be named, and the overclaims removed. All were adopted, and the entry is reframed around the refutation.

Measure-based choice rules fail: collision padding refutes the density rule, and a choice rule must be invariant modulo the base

23 September 2026 · Two working lemmas and a refutation · Any rule measuring vanishing under a fixed measure can be padded against. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The choice-rule entry refuted the uniform choice of prefix sets by padding with never-zero forms. The logarithmic-prefix reduction needs some suitable choice. The general implication at stake: a choice rule that sees which inputs can vanish makes the images of every block family either generic clauses of small total density, or structured constraints that a recorded mechanism handles. This cycle defines such a rule and tests it against padding. It ends with the rule refuted and with the property any rule must have.

The rule

Let \(\mu\) be the product measure on cell assignments in which each pigeon independently picks a uniform hole. The row equations hold; collisions may fail. Under \(\mu\) an affine form is \(L=c+\sum_if_i(U_i)\), with \(U_i\) the hole of pigeon \(i\) and \(f_i(t)\) the coefficient of \(X_{it}\). For a set \(S\) of a block's inputs let \(q(S)=\mu(\text{every }L_j,\ j\in S,\text{ is nonzero})\), the reference density of \(Q_S=\prod_{j\in S}L_j^{p-1}\). The density rule chooses \(S_b\), of size \(\min(k,h_b)\), minimizing \(q\), with ties broken uniformly at random.

Lemma (padding immunity). Let \(R\) be a set of a block's inputs, and suppose every other input has vanishing mass \(\mu(L=0)\le m_0\). Then, with \(k\) replaced by \(\min(k,h_b)\), the rule's density satisfies \(\min_{|S|=k}q(S)\ge\min_{T\subseteq R,\,|T|\le k}q(T)-k\,m_0\). In particular, inputs of \(\mu\)-mass 0 cannot lower the density below what \(R\) achieves; in that case \(q(S)=q(S\cap R)\). The immunity covers only \(\mu\)-null padding, not padding that is null modulo the base, as the next section shows.

Proof. \(q\) is non-increasing under enlarging \(S\). By the union bound, \(q(S)\ge q(S\cap R)-\sum_{j\in S\setminus R}\mu(L_j=0)\ge q(S\cap R)-k\,m_0\), and \(|S\cap R|\le k\). \(\square\)

In the padding counterexample, the real input's own density is about \(1-1/n\) and every filler has mass 0. A set containing the real input has density \(1-1/n\), strictly below the fillers' density of 1, so the rule does choose it. With the real input chosen, the filler images vanish modulo the Boolean axioms at degree \((p-1)(k+1)\), the real input has no image, and the padding refutation disappears. In the hole family every \(k\)-subset has the same density, \((1-1/n)^k\) under \(\mu\), so ties make the rule a uniform random choice, and the conditional hole-family proposition applies. The lemma removes padding as a way of hiding inputs; it does not by itself make every family good.

When the density is small

Lemma (anti-concentration under \(\mu\)). Call a row function \(f\) \(\eta\)-robust if every value class has at most \((1-\eta)n\) labels. Let \(L_1,\dots,L_k\) be forms such that every nonzero \(\mathbb F_p\)-combination has at least \(t\) \(\eta\)-robust rows. Then for every \(v\in\mathbb F_p^k\), \[ \big|\mu(L=v)-p^{-k}\big|\le(1-c_p\eta/2)^t,\qquad c_p=1-\cos(2\pi/p), \] and hence \(q(\{L_1,\dots,L_k\})\le(1-1/p)^k+p^k(1-c_p\eta/2)^t\).

Proof. For one row with value frequencies \(q_v\) and \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/p}\), \[ \Big|\sum_vq_v\omega^v\Big|^2=1-\sum_{u<v}2q_uq_v\big(1-\cos\tfrac{2\pi(u-v)}p\big)\le1-c_p\Big(1-\sum_vq_v^2\Big)\le1-c_p\eta, \] since \(\sum q_v^2\le\max q_v\le1-\eta\). So \(|E\omega^{f(U)}|\le1-c_p\eta/2\). For \(a\ne0\), the combination \(a\cdot L\) has at least \(t\) robust rows, the rows are independent under \(\mu\), and so \(|E\omega^{a\cdot L}|\le(1-c_p\eta/2)^t\). Fourier inversion over \(\mathbb F_p^k\) gives the first bound, and summing over the \((p-1)^k\) nonzero vectors \(v\) gives the second. \(\square\)

So for \(k\) inputs whose span is robustly wide, with \(t\gg k\log p/(c_p\eta)\), which is of order \(kp^2\log p/\eta\), that set has density at most \((1-1/p)^k+p^k(1-c_p\eta/2)^t\). The rule takes a minimum, which other inputs may push lower, as the next section shows.

Collision padding refutes the density rule

The fresh-context reviewer found padding that the rule prefers. For hole \(t\), keep the real input \(B_t=X_{1t}-1\), of \(\mu\)-mass \(1/n\). For every other hole \(s\), add the filler \(F_s=C_s-2\), with \(C_s=\sum_iX_{is}\) the column sum. Modulo collisions and Booleanity \(C_s\) is idempotent, so \(F_s\in\{-2,-1\}\) and \(F_s^{p-1}\equiv1\) at degree about \(p-1\): modulo the base, the fillers never vanish. Under \(\mu\), however, \(C_s\) is about Poisson(1), so \(\mu(F_s=0)\) is about \(e^{-1}/2\approx0.18\). Any \(k\) fillers have density about \(0.82^k\). Every set containing \(B_t\) has density about \((1-1/n)\,0.82^{k-1}\), which is larger, so the rule picks fillers only. Then \(Q\equiv1\) modulo the base, the fillers' images vanish, \(g_{B_t}Q\equiv X_{1t}\), pigeon 1 loses every cell, and the system is refuted at degree about \((p-1)(k+1)\). This is the draft-7 failure again. The cause is that \(\mu\) satisfies the rows but not the collisions, so \(\mu\)-mass is not invariant modulo the base.

The same objection applies to every fixed measure, because none is supported on solutions of the base: there are none. For instance, under "a random injection with pigeon \(n+1\) unplaced", the forms \(R_{n+1}+(R_i-1)\) vanish with mass 1 and are \(\equiv1\) modulo the base. So a choice rule must measure vanishing modulo the base, up to the substituted degree \(B=(4p-1)(p-1)k\). An input that the base proves nonzero within degree \(B\) must never be counted as helping. A fixed measure cannot do that. A degree-\(B\) object of the base, such as a design, might, but the anti-concentration lemma would have to be re-proved for it, since rows are no longer independent.

What the classification survives as

The draft classified blocks as generic (\(k\) robustly wide inputs), narrow (low nonlocal dimension, covered by the recorded endpoints), and a rare-local remainder described as Res(\(t\)) lines. The last description is wrong. The lemma with \(k=1\) gives only that an input of mass below \(1/(2p)\) has fewer than about \(2\ln(2p)/(c_p\eta)\) robust rows, and few robust rows does not mean few pigeons. The column form \(C_s-3\) at \(p=5\) has mass about \(0.06\), no robust row, and depends on every pigeon. The remainder also contains correlated inputs of mass about \(1/p\) each, such as one wide form plus local perturbations. What survives is the generic class, with the anti-concentration bound, and the narrow class, with the recorded endpoints. The rest is unclassified.

Assessment and next step

Two measure-based rules have now been refuted by padding: the uniform rule by never-zero forms, and the density rule by forms that vanish only on collisions. Each failure has the same cause, a measure that disagrees with the base. The general requirement is a base-invariant choice: the rule's notion of "this input can vanish" must be unchanged by adding base consequences of degree at most \(B\). The reduction needs only the existence of a good choice, not a computable rule. So the next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is to formulate the existential choice directly in base-invariant terms. Exclude every input the base proves nonzero within degree \(B\), and characterize the good sets by a condition on the degree-\(B\) closure. Then test the formulation against both padding types and the hole family. If the characterization turns out to be the wide-clause statement restated, that shows the choice problem cannot be separated from the hardness problem, and the next object is the hardness problem itself.

Process. A second padding refutation, of the same kind as the first, shows that the next rule must be tested against base-null padding before it is written down, not after.

Verification gate. Re-read: the choice-rule entry's padding counterexample and hole-family proposition, the logarithmic-prefix reduction, and the nonlocal-dimension endpoint statements with their exceptional-line tolerance. The anti-concentration bound was derived directly, with explicit constants. Claim searches for Res(\(k\)) and \(k\)-DNF PHP bounds and for rare local events found no imported Res(\(k\)) result. A fresh-context reviewer confirmed both lemmas' proofs, including every step of the character bound. It refuted the density rule with collision padding, showed the rare-local description wrong with the column form, and required the threshold to include \(c_p\) and the density claim to become an upper bound. All were adopted, and the entry is reframed around the refutation.

Route review: every open line of the thread now meets at one statement, polynomial calculus under many wide constraints

23 September 2026 · Route review · Choosing the prefix sets cannot be separated from hardness; the next step is the three-predicate case of the core statement. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

The line's general claim. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The logarithmic-prefix reduction proves that the superpolynomial lower bound for ordinary unary PHP in \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) follows from the odd-prime wide-clause statement. For every polynomial family of blocks there is a choice of prefix sets \(S_b\) of logarithmic size such that the weak base plus the images \(g_{b,i}\prod_{j\in S_b}L_{b,j}^{p-1}\) has no PC refutation of degree \((4p-1)(p-1)k\). What the goal needs is exactly that statement.

Choice and hardness cannot be separated

The last two cycles tried to split the statement into a choice rule plus a hardness theorem for the chosen system.

  • The uniform rule was refuted by never-zero padding.
  • The density rule was refuted by collision padding. No fixed measure agrees with the base, because the base has no solutions.
  • A fixed design is the base-invariant substitute for a measure. It helps only where the images are structured. For the hole family it works if chosen correctly: take a design \(\Lambda_0\) of graph PHP on a fixed random graph \(G\) of hole degree \(k\), and choose each \(S_t\) as hole \(t\)'s neighbourhood in \(G\). The images then delete exactly the cells outside \(G\), which \(\Lambda_0\) annihilates. For generic blocks it fails. An image \(g_iQ_S\) of a collectively wide set is annihilated, with all its multipliers, by a fixed functional only by accident. Each such constraint cuts the space of designs, which is the capacity count of the substitution entry. So polynomially many generic constraints need a design built for them, not chosen in advance.

So for generic blocks, a certificate that a choice is good is a design of the chosen system itself. There the choice problem is the hardness problem, and the wide-clause statement cannot be reduced to a choice rule plus a hardness theorem with a fixed witness. Structured blocks, literal and occupancy types, can be handled by fixed designs of restricted boards.

The core statement

Collecting the thread's lines shows they meet at one statement. Call it the core statement. PHP stays hard at polylogarithmic degree under polynomially many constraints, each asserting that a collectively wide family of forms avoids a small set of values, with total density below one. It appears in each line below.

  • The \(p\)-complex. The one-predicate and two-form lifts prove it for one or two constraints. The three-selector control refutes assembling it from pairs when the forms are dependent. Family compatibility is exactly its many-constraint case.
  • Random conditioning. The random-conditioning law and the recorded \(\mathbb F_2\) uniform degree-two theorem prove or support it for random affine constraints at degrees two and three. The entropy lemma explains why their counting method stops at degree three.
  • The logarithmic-prefix reduction. Its images are constraints of this kind.
  • The main record. Its central open obligation, the binary wide-clause statement, has this form.

The recorded endpoints handle narrow and occupancy-type constraints. The hole family shows that literal-type constraints reduce to graph PHP. What is left is the collectively wide case. The core statement is shared with the main goal, so progress on it serves both threads.

Falsification attempt

Could the core statement be false for polynomially many wide constraints of small total density? The recorded attacks all fail in ways that avoid it:

  • the structured row-clause example needs badly chosen flats;
  • the paddings defeat choice rules, not the existential statement;
  • the six-hole affine example has density above one;
  • the forced falls of the counting line occur beyond the density threshold.

No recorded construction refutes it inside its hypotheses. It is consistent with completeness, since it quantifies over polynomially many constraints. It also uses the size, as a sufficient condition must.

Assessment of this line

This line is weak in what it can deliver now, but clear in what it needs. The thread's goal rests on one statement, open in both characteristics. It is supported by consistent evidence at small degree and small size, and by proofs for one or two constraints. No known PC lower-bound technique handles dense constraints in quantity: expansion arguments need sparse constraints, and the counting method stops at degree three. The main record put its own version at about 3 percent. The odd-prime thread adds no counterevidence, and its reduction makes the statement sufficient for its whole goal.

Next step: the three-constraint case, aiming at the induction

The smallest open case of the core statement is three constraints whose forms are collectively wide and linearly independent. The recorded three-selector control only covers dependent forms. The two-form lift handles pairs through the \(p\)-complex's exactness for two commuting operators. For three it needs exactness of the Koszul-type complex of three operators, where the recorded projective proof does not port, since \(H^2(\mathbf P^2,\mathcal O(-3))\ne0\) in characteristic three.

The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is to prove joint extension for three independent, collectively wide ternary predicates. The point of the case is not the number three but the inductive step from \(r\) to \(r+1\) constraints: a proof that adds one wide constraint to a system already known to extend, at a degree cost that does not grow with \(r\). A proof at \(r=3\) that uses only the \(r=2\) statement and the new constraint's width would be that induction. A proof that needs all three at once shows where the cost enters. The coded-row induction of the amplitude theorem, which adds one active row at a time with forced rows, is the model to adapt. Its analogue would add one constraint at a time with the earlier constraints forced.

One requirement follows from the size rule. An induction whose hypothesis is the joint width of all forms added so far reaches at most about \(n^2\) constraints, because beyond the dimension ceiling the forms span everything and joint width fails. The core statement needs polynomially many constraints. So the inductive step must rely on each new constraint's own width together with a density or genericity condition relative to the earlier ones, not on the joint width of all of them. The three-constraint case should be proved in that form, or the proof should show why it cannot be.

Process. Choice rules were refuted three times: by two paddings, and by a fixed design for generic blocks. The review makes the point general: the choice cannot be split off, and the thread's lines have one common core.

Verification gate. Re-read: the logarithmic-prefix reduction, both padding refutations, the hole-family proposition, the \(p\)-complex family review, the three-selector control, the random-conditioning entry and the entropy lemma. A first draft claimed that no fixed design handles the hole family. That is wrong: a design of graph PHP on a fixed random graph, with each \(S_t\) adapted to it, handles it. The section now restricts the inseparability to generic blocks. A claim search for simultaneous extension of many wide predicates found the recorded one- and two-predicate results and no three-predicate statement.

Closed tuples need not lift for three or more forms at odd primes; symmetric targets lift on free modules, and the lift obstruction is an Ext group

23 September 2026 · Refutation and a working lemma · The many-operator lift holds for symmetric targets on free modules only. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The core-statement review asked for an inductive step of joint extension from \(r\) to \(r+1\) wide constraints. The \(p\)-complex's tool for joint extension is the polarized common lift of the two-parameter lemma. The review noted that its projective proof does not port to three operators, since its third twist is \(-p\), which equals \(-3\) at \(p=3\), and \(H^2(\mathbf P^2,\mathcal O(-3))\ne0\). The implication at stake: exactness of every pencil direction, which width supplies through the amplitude theorem, gives an \(r\)-operator common lift. This cycle tests that on the free module, where every pencil is exact at every degree. It ends with the implication refuted, its correct form proved on free modules, and the remaining obstruction identified.

Width does not replace density

The cycle first checked whether width in every row, without density, controls the threshold. Take random occupancy forms \(L=\sum_sc_sC_s\), where \(C_s\) is the column sum and \(c\) is uniform in \(\mathbb F_3^n\). Add the predicates \(1-L^2\) (that is, \(L\ne0\)) to the weak base over \(\mathbb F_3\). Every nonzero combination is again an occupancy form, active on every row and robust unless its coefficients are nearly constant; the forms span at most \(n-1\) dimensions modulo rows and constants. The fast closure driver found the least refuted count at degree two: \(8\) and \(13\) at \(n=6\), and \(21\) and \(21\) at \(n=8\) (two seeds each). The general-form law is \(16\) and \(36\). These forms are refuted earlier than general ones, although they are as wide as possible. Each predicate forbids the set \(L=0\), of density \(1/3\); the core statement's density hypothesis bounds the total density of the forbidden sets below one, so these systems are far outside it. The check shows only that width does not substitute for density. Files: research/results/odd_prime_twise_width_20260923/occupancy_predicates.py and occupancy_n6.json, occupancy_n8.json.

Setting

Let \(k\) have prime characteristic \(p\) (odd, except in the remarks on \(p=2\)), and put \(\delta=p-1\) and \(R=k[D_1,\dots,D_r]/(D_1^p,\dots,D_r^p)\). This is the group algebra of \((\mathbb Z/p)^r\), with \(D_i=g_i-1\). Let \(C=\bigoplus_sC_s\) be a finite-dimensional graded \(R\)-module with each \(D_i\) of degree \(-1\). The \(p\)-complex with \(r\) forms is such a module. The weighted marginal \(\delta_i^f\) is linear in the row function \(f\); marginals on different rows commute, and on the same row both orders vanish, since \(\delta_i\) kills summands without row \(i\). So the forms' operators \(D_j=\sum_i\delta_i^{f^{(j)}_i}\) commute, and each \(\Theta_u\) is a sum of commuting square-zero maps, so \(\Theta_u^p=0\). Let \(A=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^r:|\alpha|=\delta\}\) and \(m(\alpha)=\delta!/\alpha!\), a unit mod \(p\). Put \(\Theta_u=\sum_iu_iD_i\). The polarized lift of \(w\in C_{d+\delta}\) is the tuple \(\Lambda w=(m(\alpha)D^\alpha w)_{\alpha\in A}\) in \(C_d\), the coefficients of \(\Theta_u^\delta w\). A tuple \(z=(z_\alpha)\) in \(C_d\) is

  • closed if \(\Theta_u\sum_\alpha u^\alpha z_\alpha=0\) identically in \(u\), i.e. \(\sum_{i:\,b_i\ge1}D_iz_{b-e_i}=0\) for every \(|b|=p\). This is the two-parameter lemma's condition (TP-closed) for \(r=2\).
  • symmetric if \(D_iz_\alpha/m(\alpha)=D_jz_\beta/m(\beta)\) whenever \(\alpha+e_i=\beta+e_j\), and \(D_iz_{\delta e_i}=0\) for each \(i\).

Every lift is symmetric: \(D_iD^\alpha w=D^{\alpha+e_i}w\) depends only on \(\alpha+e_i\), and \(D_i^p=0\). Every symmetric tuple is closed. If \(\mu_b\) is the common value of \(D_iz_{b-e_i}/m(b-e_i)\), the closedness sum for \(b\) is \(\mu_b\sum_im(b-e_i)=\mu_b\,p!/b!\), since \(\sum_i\delta!\,b_i/b!=\delta!\,p/b!\). This is \(0\) mod \(p\) unless \(b=pe_i\), where the second symmetry condition applies. For \(r=2\) the two notions coincide, and so they do for \(p=2\) and every \(r\), where closedness reads \(D_iz_j+D_jz_i=0\) and \(D_iz_i=0\): this is the self/cross closedness of the recorded characteristic-two projective family lemma. For \(r=2\), the two preimages of \(b=(b_1,b_2)\) have \(m(b-e_1)/m(b-e_2)=b_1/b_2=-1\) mod \(p\), so the one symmetry equation is the closedness equation. For \(r\ge3\), a \(b\) with three nonzero coordinates has three preimages, and closedness gives one equation where symmetry gives two.

The closed-tuple lift fails for three or more operators

Proposition (closed-tuple failure). Let \(N_j=\binom{j+r-1}{r-1}\) count monomials of degree \(j\) in \(r\) variables. Suppose \(d\ge1\) and the map \(\pi:C_d\to C_{d-1}^r\), \(v\mapsto(D_iv)_i\), is surjective. Then the closed tuples in \(C_d\) exceed the lifts \(\Lambda C_{d+\delta}\) in dimension by at least \[ \dim C_{d-1}\cdot\Delta(p,r),\qquad \Delta(p,r)=rN_{p-1}-2N_p+r=N_{p-1}\,\frac{(r-2)(p-2)-2}{p}+r . \] \(\Delta(p,r)>0\) for every odd \(p\) and \(r\ge3\), and \(\Delta=0\) when \(r=2\) or \(p=2\).

Proof. Apply \(\pi\) to every entry. A tuple \(z\) maps to \(x_{\alpha,i}=D_iz_\alpha\in C_{d-1}\), and closedness depends only on \(x\): \(\sum_{(\alpha,i):\alpha+e_i=b}x_{\alpha,i}=0\) for each \(|b|=p\). These \(N_p\) equations involve disjoint sets of unknowns, each nonempty, and \(\pi\) is surjective, so the closed tuples map onto a space of dimension \(\dim C_{d-1}(rN_{p-1}-N_p)\). A lift maps to \(x_{\alpha,i}=m(\alpha)D^{\alpha+e_i}w\), which is determined by the moments \(D^bw\) with \(|b|=p\) and \(b\ne pe_i\), since \(D_i^p=0\). So the lifts map into a space of dimension at most \(\dim C_{d-1}(N_p-r)\). Lifts are closed, so the codimension is at least the difference. For the sign, \(N_p=N_{p-1}(p+r-1)/p\) gives the second form of \(\Delta\). If \(r\ge4\) or \(p\ge5\) (with \(r\ge3\)), then \((r-2)(p-2)\ge2\) and \(\Delta\ge r\). At \(p=r=3\), \(\Delta=-6/3+3=1\). For \(r=2\), \(N_{p-1}=p\) gives \(\Delta=-2+2=0\). For \(p=2\), \(\Delta=r^2-r(r+1)+r=0\). \(\square\)

In the matching complex. Take the top moment-correction spaces \(K\) of the amplitude theorem with \(r\) forms whose row functions are linearly independent modulo rows and constants. Then \(K_0=k\), and \(\pi:K_1\to k^r\) is given by \(r\) independent functionals, so it is surjective. Hence, at \(d=1\), there is a closed tuple indexed by \(A\) with no polarized lift, for every \(r\ge3\) and every odd \(p\), however wide the forms are. No width or robustness hypothesis can give the closed-tuple form of the \(r\)-operator lemma. For the free module \(R\) itself the pencil hypothesis holds at every degree: over \(\bar k\), a linear change of the \(D_i\) makes \(\Theta_u\) a coordinate, since \((\sum a_{ij}D_j)^p=\sum a_{ij}^pD_j^p=0\). The finite check agrees with \(\Delta\) exactly. It uses \(R\) with the monomials of degree \(e\) placed in degree \(r(p-1)-e\), so that the \(D_i\) lower degree. The table is lemma degree \(d=1\), where \(\dim C_0=1\):

\(p,r\)closedlifts\(\Delta\)

5, 324186

Failures also occur at higher lemma degrees (for \(p=7,r=3\), at \(d=1,\dots,5\)); the binary cases and \(r=2\) fail nowhere. Files: free_module_lift.py, free_module_lift_graded.py and their JSON outputs in the same directory.

Symmetric targets lift on free modules

Lemma (symmetric lifting). Let \(F\) be a finitely generated graded free \(R\)-module. Every symmetric tuple \(z\) in \(F_d\) is \(\Lambda w\) for some \(w\in F_{d+\delta}\).

Proof. Put \(\zeta_\alpha=z_\alpha/m(\alpha)\). Let \(J\subset R\) be the ideal generated by the monomials \(D^\alpha\), \(\alpha\in A\). It has the \(k\)-basis of nonzero monomials \(D^\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|\ge\delta\) and all \(\gamma_i\le p-1\). Define \(\varphi(D^\gamma)=D^{\gamma-\alpha}\zeta_\alpha\) for any \(\alpha\in A\) with \(\alpha\le\gamma\).

  • Well defined. Two choices \(\alpha,\alpha'\le\gamma\) in \(A\) are joined by moves \(\alpha\to\alpha-e_j+e_i\) that stay below \(\gamma\): move one unit at a time from a coordinate where the current index exceeds \(\alpha'\) to one where it falls short. For one move, write \(\alpha=\beta+e_j\) and \(\alpha'=\beta+e_i\). Then \(\gamma-\beta\ge e_i+e_j\), and both values equal \(D^{\gamma-\beta-e_i-e_j}\) applied to \(D_i\zeta_{\beta+e_j}=D_j\zeta_{\beta+e_i}\), which is the symmetry condition.
  • \(R\)-linear. If \(\gamma_k<p-1\), then \(\varphi(D_kD^\gamma)=D_k\varphi(D^\gamma)\) with the same \(\alpha\). If \(\gamma_k=p-1\), then \(D_kD^\gamma=0\), and choosing \(\alpha=\delta e_k\le\gamma\) gives \(D_k\varphi(D^\gamma)=D^{\gamma-\delta e_k}D_k\zeta_{\delta e_k}=0\) by the second symmetry condition.

So \(\varphi:J\to F\) is an \(R\)-module map. The group algebra \(R\) is a Frobenius algebra, hence self-injective, so the free module \(F\) is injective and \(\varphi\) extends to \(R\to F\). Put \(w=\tilde\varphi(1)\). Then \(D^\alpha w=\varphi(D^\alpha)=\zeta_\alpha\), that is, \(z=\Lambda w\). The equations are homogeneous, so the degree-\((d+\delta)\) component of \(w\) is also a solution. \(\square\)

The finite check found symmetric tuples equal to lifts at every degree of \(R\) for \((p,r)=(3,3),(3,4),(5,3),(7,3),(5,4)\) (symmetric_lift.py, symmetric_lift.json).

The obstruction for a general module. The proof identifies symmetric tuples in \(C\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(J,C)\) in the matching degree, and lifts with the image of \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(R,C)=C\). From \(0\to J\to R\to R/J\to0\), the symmetric tuples modulo lifts form \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/J,C)\) in that degree, with \(J=\mathfrak m^{p-1}\). By Dade's lemma (E. C. Dade, Ann. of Math. 108, 1978), a finite-dimensional \(R\)-module is free exactly when its restriction to every cyclic shifted subgroup \(k[\Theta_u]/(\Theta_u^p)\), \(u\in\bar k^r\setminus0\), is free. That is pencil exactness at every degree. So pencil exactness at every degree implies symmetric lifting at every degree, for every \(r\): freeness holds after extension to \(\bar k\), and solvability of the lifting equations descends to \(k\) because the ranks of a finite linear system and its augmented matrix do not change under field extension, as in the two-parameter lemma. Dade's lemma is imported and is not used in the lemma's proof.

What this does to the inductive step

The \(r\)-operator lift must be stated for symmetric targets. The closed form is false for every \(r\ge3\), so the missing step was never a proof technique for a true statement. For \(r=2\), and for \(p=2\), the two forms coincide, which is why the recorded lemmas needed only closedness.

Two gaps remain before this gives joint extension for many forms.

  • A degree window. The amplitude theorem gives pencil exactness only at degrees \(d\) with \(t\ge2d+p-a\) robust rows, not at every degree. So Dade's lemma does not apply as stated, and the matching complex need not be free. What is needed is a window version: vanishing of \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(R/\mathfrak m^{p-1},C)_d\) from pencil exactness in a bounded range of degrees around \(d\). The two-parameter lemma is such a statement for \(r=2\), using degrees \(d\), \(d+\delta\) and \(d+p\). At \(p=2\) the recorded projective family lemma uses exactness through degrees \(d,\dots,d+r-1\), a range that grows with \(r\). Whether it must grow at odd \(p\) is open. That is the point where the inductive step's cost may depend on \(r\).
  • The quadratic ceiling. Pencil exactness is needed for every direction in the span of all \(r\) forms. The span of more than about \(N^2\) forms contains narrow forms (the dimension bound \(d_t<N^2\)). So even with a window lemma, and even if symmetric lifting yields joint extension, which is not shown, this module route reaches the wide-conditioning conjecture's quadratic range, not polynomially many constraints. The core statement needs a mechanism that uses each constraint's own width with density, which the module lift does not supply.

Assessment and next step

This cycle settles the three-operator question in the \(p\)-complex line: the closed-tuple lift is false, the symmetric lift is the right statement, it holds on free modules, and its obstruction is an Ext group. A window lemma would be the local ingredient of joint extension for up to quadratically many wide forms; turning symmetric lifts into joint extension is a further unproved step, and the reach would still be short of the goal. Any mechanism for the core statement that works on at most \(t=\operatorname{polylog}\) constraints at a time needs this ingredient at a degree cost independent of \(t\). The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is to decide the window question at the smallest nonvacuous size, then bound it.

Start at \(r=3\), \(p=3\) and \(d=1\), where the proposition lives. There \(K_0=k\), and a symmetric 6-tuple splits into its moment part, the values \(D^bw\) for the \(N_3-3=7\) mixed \(b\), and a part in \(\bigcap_j\ker D^{(j)}\subset K_1\). Decide by hand whether both parts lift from \(K_3\) under the two-parameter lemma's hypotheses. A computation is costly here: the robustness condition needs \(N>\tfrac32(3d+3p-1)=16.5\) labels, so labels \(\mathbb F_3^3\), and with eight rows \(\dim K_3\le\binom83\cdot27\cdot26\cdot25\approx9.8\times10^5\). A smaller board is useful only if pencil exactness is checked on it directly. If symmetric lifting fails at \(d=1\), pencil exactness at the two-parameter lemma's degrees is not enough for three operators, and the window must widen. If it holds, try the window lemma by induction on \(r\), with the two-parameter lemma as the base and the free-module proof as a guide. The cycle ends with the window's size as a function of \(r\), or with a counterexample.

Verification gate. Re-read: the two-parameter lemma and its proof, the amplitude theorem's statement, the family-transversal entry's dimension bound, and the ternary pair theorem's claim record. Claim searches (many-operator lifting, Dade and rank varieties, constant Jordan type, polarized three-operator lift) found the characteristic-two projective family lemma, the two-parameter lemma, the ternary pair theorem and the wide-conditioning conjecture, and no three-operator result at odd \(p\). The proposition's count was checked against the free-module computation at four \((p,r)\), with exact agreement. The lemma was checked at five \((p,r)\), at every degree. A fresh-context reviewer confirmed the projection count, the formula and sign of \(\Delta\), the table, the symmetric-lift construction including the boundary case, the Ext identification and the statement of Dade's lemma. It required: commutation of different forms' operators to be proved, the characteristic-two family lemma and its growing window to be cited, descent to \(k\), the freeness assertion weakened, the claim about joint extension marked unproved, the ternary pair comparison dropped, and the tuple sizes and the density convention stated. All were adopted.

Symmetric lifting follows from adding one form at a time with the earlier forms forced; in the matching complex no growth of the needed width is seen up to five forms

23 September 2026 · Working reduction lemma and a finite check · The forced-forms exactness it needs is unproved. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The symmetric-lift entry showed that the \(p\)-complex's many-operator lift holds for symmetric targets on free modules, and asked whether it holds in the matching complex \(K\) from pencil exactness in a degree window whose size does not grow with the number \(r\) of forms. Any mechanism for the core statement that treats polylogarithmically many constraints at a time needs that. At \(p=2\) the recorded projective family lemma and the collective parity-trade theorem (thm:collective-parity-trade-lift) need width \(d+s-1\) for \(s\) forms, which grows with \(s\). This cycle measures the width the matching complex actually needs, and looks for a proof whose window is independent of \(r\). It ends with a reduction whose number of levels is independent of \(r\), and with the measurement.

Finite check: the width threshold does not grow with \(r\)

Work at \(p=3\) and lemma degree \(d=1\), in the matching complex with the definitions of the amplitude theorem: \(K_s\) is the direct sum over \(s\)-row sets of arrays on injections into the labels with zero ordinary marginal in every row, and \(\delta_i\) is the \(f_i\)-weighted marginal. The script computes the symmetric tuples in \(K_1\) exactly, and the rank of the polarized lift map \(K_3\to K_1^{A}\), block by block over 3-row sets. First, dense random row functions on \(R\) rows and \(N\) labels:

  • At \(R=N=6\) the symmetric tuples have dimension 169 and all lift; the closed tuples have dimension 170, the one-dimensional deficit of the closed-tuple failure. At \(R=N=9\): 421 symmetric, all lift, 422 closed.
  • Narrow controls fail: \(R=N=3\) lifts none of 25; \(R=6,N=4\) lifts 20 of 97.

Then \(r\) forms with disjoint supports of \(t\) rows each, random row functions, \(N=7\) labels. The table gives symmetric dimension and lift rank; \(t=3\) fails and \(t=4\) lifts for every \(r\) tested (\(t\le2\) was run only for \(r\le3\)).

For \(r=2\) symmetric equals closed, so the first row is the recorded two-parameter regime. The threshold is one board and one seed per cell, at one degree, so it is evidence, not a theorem. No growth is seen for \(r\le5\) at \(d=1\) with \(N=7\). A linear law such as \(d+r-1\) would be separated only at \(r=5\), and logarithmic growth, or growth at higher \(d\), is not excluded. Larger runs of the same test would sharpen constants off the critical path, so the series stops here. Reduction: symmetric lifting from first-order cocycles

Use the setting of the symmetric-lift entry: \(R=k[D_1,\dots,D_r]/(D_i^p)\), a graded \(R\)-module \(C\) with each \(D_i\) of degree \(-1\), \(\delta=p-1\), \(A=\{|\alpha|=\delta\}\), and symmetric tuples. Call \((c_1,\dots,c_r)\in C_{s-1}^r\) a cocycle if \(D_jc_i=D_ic_j\) for all \(i,j\) and \(D_i^{p-1}c_i=0\) for all \(i\). Say \(C\) has cocycle lifting at level \(s\) if every cocycle in \(C_{s-1}^r\) equals \((D_ic)_i\) for some \(c\in C_s\). For \(p=2\) cocycles are the self/cross-closed tuples of the recorded characteristic-two lemmas, and there \(\delta=1\) makes the first lemma below trivial: cocycle lifting at \(p=2\) is the recorded collective parity-trade theorem's conclusion.

Lemma (cocycle reduction). If \(C\) has cocycle lifting at levels \(d+1,\dots,d+\delta\), then every symmetric tuple in \(C_d\) is a polarized lift \(\Lambda w\), \(w\in C_{d+\delta}\).

Proof. Let \(\zeta_\alpha=z_\alpha/m(\alpha)\). The symmetric-lift entry's construction gives a well-defined \(R\)-linear map \(\varphi\) from \(J=\mathfrak m^{\delta}\) to \(C\) with \(\varphi(D^\alpha)=\zeta_\alpha\). Its proof uses only the symmetry conditions, not freeness. We build, for \(q=0,\dots,\delta\), elements \(u^{(q)}_\gamma\in C_{d+q}\) for \(|\gamma|=\delta-q\), with \(u^{(0)}_\alpha=\zeta_\alpha\) and \[ D_iu^{(q)}_\gamma=u^{(q-1)}_{\gamma+e_i}\qquad(1\le q\le\delta,\ |\gamma|=\delta-q,\ 1\le i\le r). \] By induction this gives \(D^\beta u^{(q)}_\gamma=\zeta_{\gamma+\beta}\) for \(|\beta|=q\). Here \(\gamma+\beta\in A\), because \(\gamma_i+\beta_i\le\delta\). Suppose \(u^{(q-1)}\) is built, and fix \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|=\delta-q\). Put \(c_i=u^{(q-1)}_{\gamma+e_i}\in C_{d+q-1}\).

  • Cross condition: for \(q=1\), \(D_jc_i=D_j\zeta_{\gamma+e_i}\) and \(D_ic_j=D_i\zeta_{\gamma+e_j}\) agree by symmetry. For \(q\ge2\), both equal \(u^{(q-2)}_{\gamma+e_i+e_j}\).
  • Self condition: \(D_i^{p-1}c_i=D_i^{p-q}\,D_i^{q-1}u^{(q-1)}_{\gamma+e_i}=D_i^{p-q}\zeta_{\gamma+qe_i}=\varphi(D_i^{p-q}D^{\gamma+qe_i})\). The last monomial has \(i\)-exponent \(\gamma_i+p\ge p\), so it is \(0\) in \(R\).

So \((c_i)\) is a cocycle, and cocycle lifting at level \(d+q\) gives \(u^{(q)}_\gamma\in C_{d+q}\) with \(D_iu^{(q)}_\gamma=c_i\). At \(q=\delta\), \(w=u^{(\delta)}_0\in C_{d+\delta}\) satisfies \(D^\alpha w=\zeta_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in A\), which is \(z=\Lambda w\). \(\square\)

Lemma (forced-forms cocycle lifting). Put \(M_j=\bigcap_{l>j}\ker D_l\), with \(M_r=C\). Suppose that for each \(j\), every \(x\in M_j\cap C_{s-1}\) with \(D_j^{p-1}x=0\) equals \(D_jy\) for some \(y\in M_j\cap C_s\). Then \(C\) has cocycle lifting at level \(s\).

Proof. Let \((c_i)\) be a cocycle. Since \(c_r\in M_r\) and \(D_r^{p-1}c_r=0\), write \(c_r=D_ry_r\) and replace \(c_i\) by \(c_i-D_iy_r\) for every \(i\). This is again a cocycle, now with \(c_r=0\). Then \(D_rc_i=D_ic_r=0\), so every \(c_i\in M_{r-1}\). Next \(c_{r-1}\in M_{r-1}\) and \(D_{r-1}^{p-1}c_{r-1}=0\), so \(c_{r-1}=D_{r-1}y_{r-1}\) with \(y_{r-1}\in M_{r-1}\). Subtracting \((D_iy_{r-1})_i\) keeps \(c_r=0\), because \(D_ry_{r-1}=0\), and makes \(c_{r-1}=0\). By the cross condition the remaining \(c_i\) then lie in \(M_{r-2}\). Continue down to \(j=1\). The subtracted gradients sum to \((D_ic)_i\) with \(c=\sum_jy_j\). \(\square\)

The elimination is the standard argument for first cohomology of commuting operators. Its hypothesis, lifting inside the joint kernel of other forms, is the odd-prime counterpart of the recorded binary relative coded parity lift: global targets in the common top kernel of local codes lift within that kernel, at width \(d+s-1\). That proof goes through the projective lemma, not through elimination. So the lemma is recorded as a refinement of the odd-prime route with a binary analogue, not as a new mechanism.

Together: symmetric lifting at degree \(d\) follows from the hypothesis of the second lemma at the \(p-1\) levels \(d+1,\dots,d+\delta\). The number of levels does not depend on \(r\). The dependence on \(r\) now sits in the forced-forms hypothesis, where \(M_j\) carries \(r-j\) forced forms; in the binary analogue the width needed grows with exactly that number, so the width this hypothesis needs may still grow with \(r\). The hypothesis is one statement about one form at a time: the form \(D_j\) is exact, in the position \(\ker D^{p-1}=\operatorname{im}D\), on the joint kernel of the forms added before it. This is the shape the core-statement review asked for: an inductive step from \(r\) to \(r+1\) with the earlier constraints forced. On a free module the hypothesis holds: for \(F=R\), \(M_j=R_j\prod_{l>j}D_l^{p-1}\) with \(R_j=k[D_1,\dots,D_j]/(D_i^p)\), which is free over \(R_j\), hence over \(k[D_j]/(D_j^p)\), so \(\ker D_j^{p-1}=\operatorname{im}D_j\) inside \(M_j\), degree by degree. In the matching complex it is unproved. The amplitude theorem's forced-row version forces the weighted marginals of individual rows, not the vanishing of a whole form's operator, so it does not apply directly.

What this changes

Symmetric lifting, the local ingredient of joint extension, now has a sufficient condition: forced-forms exactness at \(p-1\) levels. It is only sufficient; it may fail where cocycle or symmetric lifting holds. The measured threshold shows no growth with \(r\) up to five forms at \(d=1\). The two gaps of the symmetric-lift entry change as follows.

  • The window gap becomes forced-forms exactness in the matching complex, whose width may still depend on the number of forced forms.
  • The quadratic ceiling is unchanged. The joint kernels shrink as forms are added, and once the forms span everything no wide form is left. The joint extension step from symmetric lifts to designs is also still unproved.

Assessment and next step

The local ingredient now has a one-form-at-a-time sufficient condition, and the data at \(d=1\) show no growth in \(r\) up to five forms. The route to the core statement still lacks a mechanism for density. The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is forced-forms exactness. First test it directly in the matching complex at \(p=3\), \(r=3\), disjoint supports of \(t=4\) rows and \(N=7\) labels, at the levels \(s=2,3\) the reduction uses, together with cocycle lifting itself at those levels, so that a failure of the stronger condition is not mistaken for a failure of the reduction's hypothesis. \(K_2\) has \(66\cdot29=1914\) dimensions and \(K_3\) has \(220\cdot104=22{,}880\), so level 3 needs the compiled GF(3) elimination, not the Python one. If it holds, adapt the amplitude theorem's forced-row induction so that the forced object is a whole form's operator. The test ends the question for this size; the proof attempt ends with forced-forms exactness at a width independent of \(r\), or with the point where the forced form's width enters.

Verification gate. Re-read: the amplitude theorem's statement and the definitions of \(K\) and \(\delta_i\) (moment-correction spaces as top chessboard cycles), the symmetric-lift entry's lemma and construction of \(\varphi\), and the recorded binary claims found by the search (projective family lemma, collective parity-trade theorem, relative coded parity lift). Claim searches for cocycle and gradient lifting, self/cross-closed tuples and forced-row exactness on joint kernels found those binary results and no odd-prime reduction. The lift ranks are exact computations over \(\mathbb F_3\), with closed-tuple dimensions as a control. A fresh-context reviewer confirmed both inductions, the free-module claim and the scripts. It required: the binary analogues to be cited in the body and the lemma labelled as their odd-prime counterpart, the statement that the forced-forms width may still grow with \(r\), "sufficient" instead of an equivalence, no binary contrast, the finite-check conclusion limited to \(r\le5\) at \(d=1\), the untested small \(t\) stated, the control file regenerated with its closed-tuple count, and cocycle lifting added to the next test. All were adopted.

Forced-forms exactness in the matching complex: in these checks additional forced forms do not raise the width, which coincides with the amplitude theorem's one-form row count

23 September 2026 · Finite check · Three forms on seven labels, levels two and three. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The cocycle reduction derives the symmetric many-operator lift at degree \(d\) from forced-forms exactness at the levels \(s=d+1,\dots,d+\delta\): every \(x\in M_j\cap K_{s-1}\) with \(D_j^{p-1}x=0\) is \(D_jy\) with \(y\in M_j\cap K_s\), where \(M_j=\bigcap_{l>j}\ker D_l\). It left open whether this holds in the matching complex, and whether the width it needs grows with the number \(r-j\) of forced forms, as the width of the binary analogues does. This cycle computes both sides exactly at the smallest nonvacuous size, \(p=3\), \(d=1\) (levels 2 and 3), together with cocycle lifting itself, the reduction's actual hypothesis. It ends with the width at which each holds, with and without forced forms.

The computation

The matching complex is as in the amplitude theorem. \(K_s\) is spanned by arrays on injections of \(s\)-row sets into \(N=7\) labels with zero ordinary marginal in every row, and \(D_l\) is the sum of the \(f^{(l)}_i\)-weighted marginals. The script builds \(D_l:K_s\to U_{s-1}\) block by block in per-set bases of \(K_s\). Here \(U_{s-1}\) is the full array space; it contains \(K_{s-1}\). All ranks are exact over \(\mathbb F_3\) with the recorded bit-sliced elimination. For each level and each \(j=r,\dots,1\) it compares

  • \(\dim(\ker D_j^{2}\cap M_j\cap K_{s-1})\) with \(\dim D_j(M_j\cap K_s)\): forced-forms exactness holds when they are equal;
  • the cocycles in \(K_{s-1}^r\) with the gradients of \(K_s\): cocycle lifting.

At level 2, \(D_j^2\) maps \(K_1\) to zero, so the kernel side is all of \(M_j\cap K_1\). Forms have disjoint supports of \(t\) rows each, or are dense (every form on all \(rt\) rows), with random row functions. The largest case has \(\dim K_3=47{,}320\). Each case ran in under 90 seconds on 12 threads.

Results

Level 3 entries are kernel / image for \(j=r,\dots,1\), then cocycles / gradients. Level 2 was exact in every case with \(N=7\), including \(t=3\) (\(54/54,53/53,52/52\) and \(159/159\)), matching its row condition \(|I|\ge3\). Seeds are recorded in the JSON outputs (0, 24, 25, 33, 34, 35, 104, 105).

A tiny control (\(r=2\), \(t=2\), \(N=5\)) fails at both levels.

What the numbers say

  • The threshold coincides here with the one-form row count. At level 3 the case \(j=r\) has no forced form. It is plain exactness of one form in the position \(\ker D^2=\operatorname{im}D\) on \(K_2\). The amplitude theorem's row condition for that position is \(|I|\ge2\cdot2+1=5\). With disjoint supports it first holds at \(t=5\), and there every forced case holds too, for one and for two forced forms. Its robustness condition, \(Q=8\) deletions, cannot hold with seven labels, and fails at level 2 too. So exactness holds although the robustness hypothesis fails: that hypothesis is not necessary at this size. With one label count and one seed per case, the data cannot separate the row count from label effects.
  • Below the threshold, forced positions can fail by more. At \(r=3\), \(t=4\) the deficits for \(j=3,2,1\) are \(1,1,4\). At \(r=2\), \(t=4\) they are \(1,4\), so a single forced form already reaches four. The deficit is not a function of the number of forced forms. At \(r=3\), \(t=3\) every position fails by 16. No forced position failed at a width where the unforced position holds.
  • The reduction costs one level of width, not more. Symmetric lifting at \(d=1\) held already at \(t=4\) (previous entry). The reduction's hypothesis needs \(t=5\) with disjoint supports, because it uses exactness on \(K_{d+\delta-1}\) in the position \(\ker D^{p-1}=\operatorname{im}D\). That costs \(2(d+\delta-1)+1\) rows by the amplitude theorem. The recorded two-parameter lemma uses the \(K_{d+\delta}\) position, which costs \(2(d+\delta)+1\), more than the reduction. Dense forms at 12 rows satisfy everything.

So, at this size, the dependence on \(r\) that the cocycle reduction moved into the forced-forms hypothesis does not appear: the width needed coincides with the amplitude theorem's row count for one form. The evidence is one seed per case, one label count, \(d=1\) and at most two forced forms. The case \(r=4\) would need about 8 GB for the stacked operators and would only extend a prediction that already failed at two forced forms, so the series stops here.

Assessment and next step

The local ingredient of the core statement now has a concrete target. Prove forced-forms exactness in the matching complex at the one-form width of the amplitude theorem, uniformly in the number of forced forms. The data at the smallest size support that target. A proof would give the symmetric many-operator lift for any number of wide forms at a degree cost independent of that number, within the quadratic ceiling. The step from symmetric lifts to joint extension and the density mechanism would remain open.

The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is that proof for disjoint supports. Decompose \(K\) by the set \(A\subseteq I_l\) of rows of a forced form's support that an array uses. The other forms' operators preserve this grading, and \(D_l\) is the differential of a cube over subsets of \(I_l\), built from commuting square-zero maps \(\delta_i\). The plan has three parts:

  • show that each graded piece is exact for \(D_j\) at the amplitude theorem's width, as a forced-row statement with ordinary rather than weighted marginals on \(A\);
  • show that the kernel of the cube differential inherits exactness;
  • induct on the number of forced forms.

The cycle ends with the proof, or with the step where the forced forms' number enters.

Verification gate. Re-read: the cocycle-reduction entry's two lemmas and next step, the amplitude theorem's statement with its row and robustness conditions, and the definition of \(K\). The script reuses the matching-complex conventions of the previous entry's check. The tiny and \(t=3\) cases fail at level 3 as controls, and in every output the image is at most the kernel and the gradients at most the cocycles. No mathematical claim is made beyond the finite check. A fresh-context reviewer confirmed that the script computes the stated quantities, including the level-2 handling of \(D_j^2\) and kernels taken in the full array space, and that the table and row counts are right. It required the level-2 threshold corrected to \(t\ge3\), the deficit pattern stated for both \(r\), "coincides" instead of "is" for the threshold, the robustness remark clarified, "additional" instead of "earlier" forced forms, and the seeds recorded. All were adopted.

Route review: the local-lift line has a sharp target but does not reach density; the next step moves to how density enters

23 September 2026 · Route review · The forced-forms proof met two obstacles; linear window growth in the number of forced forms is enough for a local mechanism. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, high effort).

The line's general claim. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The last three cycles built a local ingredient for the core statement. They found:

  • the \(p\)-complex's many-operator lift holds for symmetric targets;
  • it follows from forced-forms exactness, where each form is exact on the joint kernel of the forms already added;
  • that hypothesis holds in the matching complex at \(p=3\), \(d=1\), from the amplitude theorem's one-form row count, with up to two forced forms.

The line's claim is that joint extension for many wide constraints can be built from this ingredient. What the goal needs is the core statement: polynomially many collectively wide constraints of total density below one, at polylogarithmic degree.

The proof attempt, and a correction of the requirement

This cycle opened on a proof of forced-forms exactness for forms with disjoint supports. The smallest case is one forced form: \(\Theta\) exact, in the position \(\ker\Theta^{p-1}=\operatorname{im}\Theta\), on \(\ker D\). Two routes stopped.

  • The projective route gives nothing at odd \(p\). A solution is a constant section \(y\) of \(M_s\otimes\mathcal O\) with \((u\Theta+vD)y=u\,x\) for all \((u:v)\). With exact pencils, the obstruction to lifting \(u\,x\) lies in \(H^1\) of the kernel bundle of \(u\Theta+vD\) on \(M_s\). That bundle is resolved by \(M_{s+\delta}\otimes\mathcal O(-\delta)\), and \(H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(-\delta))\) has dimension \(\delta-1\), nonzero for \(p\ge3\). At \(p=2\) it vanishes, which is why the binary lemmas go through. So the vanishing argument of the two-parameter lemma gives no proof in this position at odd \(p\). This is a limit of the method, not a counterexample: the computed cases hold.
  • Row insertion does not preserve a forced form. The amplitude theorem's induction inserts an active row \(i\) by tensoring with a vector \(c\) on row \(i\), chosen outside the labels of each small tensor of a coded-trade expansion. A weighted marginal on a forced row \(k\) then acquires the correction \(c(\omega)f_k(\omega)\) at the collision label. So insertion commutes with \(D_l\) only when one \(c\) avoids the labels of every tensor, which is impossible for targets of large support. The forced-row version of the theorem avoids this by forcing individual weighted marginals, which \(\bigcap_{i\in I_l}\ker\delta_i\subsetneq\ker D_l\) does not capture.

The requirement was also overstated. The earlier entries asked for a degree cost independent of the number of forced forms. A local mechanism handles at most \(t=\operatorname{polylog}n\) constraints at a time. So a window that grows by \(O(p)\) per forced form costs \(O(pt)\) extra degree and \(O(pt)\) extra rows of width. Both are polylogarithmic, within the core statement's degree and far below the forms' width. Linear growth is enough; that is what an induction over forced forms using the two-parameter lemma at each step would give, if the one-forced-form position could be handled.

Falsification attempt: does anything in the record refute the line's use of density?

The core statement's density condition is the one hypothesis the local line never uses. The record's refutations and falls all sit at total density at least one:

  • the random affine thresholds, whose equations each forbid density \(1-1/p\);
  • the occupancy predicates of the symmetric-lift entry, refuted from 8 predicates of density \(1/3\) each;
  • the three-selector control, whose selectors \(a\ne0\), \(b\ne0\), \(a+b\ne0\) forbid density \(1/3\) each, total exactly one. The degree fall there derives the consequence \(a=b\), not a refutation, and the satisfying set \(a=b\ne0\) keeps density \(2/9\).

So no recorded example refutes the core statement, and the three-selector control sits exactly at the density boundary. But none of the line's results uses density either. A principle deriving joint extension from local lifts alone would hold at every density. It would then contradict the occupancy and affine refutations, provided their small subfamilies have local designs; the next step checks that. So the local line cannot be the whole mechanism. Density has to enter in the gluing.

Assessment of this line

The local-lift line has made steady progress on its own question:

  • a refutation of the closed-tuple lift;
  • the symmetric lift on free modules;
  • a reduction to forced-forms exactness;
  • finite evidence that the hypothesis holds at the one-form width.

Its remaining proof is harder than expected at odd \(p\). More importantly, it is not the highest-risk part. Even complete, it supplies local lifts for polylogarithmically many constraints, or at most about \(N^2\) wide forms. It is silent on density, which the occupancy and affine examples show is indispensable. Continuing to refine it would be refining a sufficient sub-step while the necessary one stays untouched. The line is set aside with a restart condition: a density mechanism that consumes local lifts of \(O(\operatorname{polylog})\) forms.

Next step: how density enters the gluing

The next step on odd-prime-clause-transfer is to state a density-weighted local-to-global principle precisely, and test it against the record before any proof. Its shape: if every subfamily of at most \(t\) constraints has a degree-\(D+O(pt)\) design, and the constraints' total density is below one, then the whole family has a degree-\(D\) design. Density must enter through counting over \(\mathbb F_p\): through the number of value patterns of the forms that avoid all forbidden sets, not through probabilities, which a finite-field design cannot use.

  • First, check the principle against the occupancy predicates, the random affine thresholds and the three-selector control. For each, compute the total density and the size of the subfamilies a refutation uses. The principle must exclude each refuted case through the density hypothesis alone.
  • Then find its simplest nontrivial case. The candidate is constraints on disjoint row blocks, where local lifts are available. There, compare total density just below one with just above one at the same local data.

The cycle ends with a principle consistent with the record and a named first case, or with a recorded example that no density-weighted principle can accommodate.

Process. Three cycles refined one sub-step before this review asked whether it is the critical one. The route check in CLAUDE.md already requires that question when a line produces special cases without moving the general implication; it applied a cycle earlier than it was asked.

Verification gate. Re-read: the core-statement review, the last three entries, the two-parameter lemma's proof, the amplitude theorem's forced-row induction, and the three-selector control. The \(H^1\) computation uses \(h^1(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(m))=-m-1\) for \(m\le-2\). The density values are those of the cited entries. This review proves nothing new and registers no claim.
